cases.audioScript: On December seventh, 2003, thirteen-year-old Daniel Morcombe was waiting for a bus under the Kiel Mountain Road overpass at Woombye, on Queensland's Sunshine Coast. He never came home. For nearly eight years, his family had no answers, and a coroner's inquest was held in Maroochydore and Brisbane. Then, on August thirteenth, 2011, police arrested a forty-one-year-old man named Brett Peter Cowan. In the weeks that followed, police and State Emergency Service volunteers crawled shoulder to shoulder through bushland off Kings Road in the Glass House Mountains. They found a pair of shoes and human bones. DNA confirmed they were Daniel's. In March 2014 a Supreme Court jury in Brisbane found Cowan guilty of murder, indecent treatment of a child and interfering with a corpse. Justice Roslyn Atkinson sentenced him to life in prison with a minimum of twenty years before parole, and said she did not believe he should ever be released.
cases.summary: Daniel Morcombe, 13, vanished Dec. 7, 2003 while waiting for a bus under the Kiel Mountain Road overpass at Woombye on the Sunshine Coast. Brett Peter Cowan was arrested Aug. 13, 2011; searches off Kings Road in the Glass House Mountains found shoes and bones that DNA confirmed were Daniel's. A Supreme Court jury found Cowan guilty on March 13, 2014 of murder, indecent treatment of a child and interfering with a corpse; he was sentenced to life with a 20-year non-parole period. He confessed to undercover police officers; the Queensland Court of Appeal dismissed his appeal in May 2015, and the High Court refused special leave on March 11, 2016.
cases.solvedHow: Solved with Cowan's August 2011 arrest, followed by recovery of Daniel's remains in the Glass House Mountains, DNA confirmation and a 2014 jury trial. (Investigative method leading to the arrest is not detailed in fetched sources.)

cases.audioScript: On Australia Day, January twenty-sixth, 1966, three children from Adelaide set off for Glenelg beach, a short bus ride from home. Jane Beaumont was nine. Her sister Arnna was seven, and their brother Grant was four. They never came home. Police found witnesses who had seen the children near the beach with a tall, thin-faced, sun-tanned man in his mid-thirties. They were confirmed at Colley Reserve and at a cake shop in Glenelg. After that, they vanished. Police believe the children were abducted and murdered. Their remains have never been found. Over the decades, detectives have followed thousands of leads. In 2013 and again in 2018, police dug at a factory site in North Plympton after new tips. Nothing of interest was found. A privately organized dig in 2025 also found no remains. The South Australian government offers a one-million-dollar reward for information leading to a conviction, or to finding the children. Nearly sixty years later, the Beaumont children remain one of Australia's most enduring mysteries.
cases.summary: On Australia Day, Jan. 26, 1966, Jane (9), Arnna (7) and Grant (4) Beaumont took a short bus trip from their home in Somerton Park to Glenelg beach in Adelaide and failed to return (National Missing Persons Coordination Centre). Witnesses saw the children near the beach with a tall, thin-faced, sun-tanned man in his mid-30s; confirmed sightings were at Colley Reserve and a cake shop in Moseley Street, Glenelg. Police suspect the children were abducted and murdered (NMPCC). In 2014 the South Australian government raised the reward to A$1 million, payable for information leading to a conviction or the recovery of remains (Sydney Morning Herald; Guardian/AAP). SA Police excavated part of the New Castalloy factory site in North Plympton in 2013 and again in February 2018 after Channel Seven supplied geophysical results; the 2018 dig found only animal bones and was called off (Guardian/AAP; ABC). A seven-day dig at the site organized by independent MP Frank Pangallo ended on March 1, 2025, without finding remains; SA Police said the theory behind it was not supported by evidence (ABC). Tips: Crime Stoppers 1800 333 000 (AFP National Missing Persons Coordination Centre listing; reward A$1,000,000 listed).
cases.solvedHow: Unsolved. Remains never found.

cases.audioScript: On July twenty-ninth, 2023, Erin Patterson hosted a lunch at her home in Leongatha, a small town in South Gippsland, Victoria. Her guests were her former parents-in-law, Don and Gail Patterson, both seventy, Gail's sister Heather Wilkinson, sixty-six, and Heather's husband, Ian, a church pastor. She served beef Wellington. Within days, Don, Gail and Heather were dead. Ian spent nearly two months in hospital with critical organ damage before he recovered. The dish contained death cap mushrooms. In July 2025, after a trial in the Supreme Court of Victoria, a jury found Erin Patterson guilty of three counts of murder and one count of attempted murder. In September 2025, Justice Christopher Beale sentenced her to life in prison with a non-parole period of thirty-three years. She appealed. On October thirtieth, 2026, Victoria's Court of Appeal dismissed her appeal and went further, resentencing her to life without parole. Her only remaining avenue is an application to the High Court of Australia. Today the case is remembered for Don, Gail and Heather, three people who were loved in their community.
cases.summary: On July 29, 2023, Erin Patterson served a beef Wellington lunch at her Leongatha home to her former parents-in-law Don and Gail Patterson, both 70, Gail's sister Heather Wilkinson, 66, and Heather's husband Ian Wilkinson. The meal contained death cap mushrooms. Don, Gail and Heather died; Ian spent nearly two months in hospital and recovered (SBS). Patterson was tried in the Supreme Court of Victoria and on July 7, 2025 a jury found her guilty of three counts of murder and one count of attempted murder. On Sept. 8, 2025 Justice Christopher Beale sentenced her to life imprisonment with a 33-year non-parole period (ABC; AustLII sentence R v Patterson [2025] VSC 557). On Oct. 30, 2026 the Victorian Court of Appeal dismissed her appeal against conviction and upheld a prosecution appeal, setting aside the non-parole period and resentencing her to life without parole (SBS, ABC). ABC reported her remaining avenue is a High Court of Australia special-leave application. Separate attempted-murder charges concerning her estranged husband were dropped before trial and are not part of the convictions.
cases.solvedHow: Solved by police investigation and jury trial; convictions upheld on appeal (2026).

cases.audioScript: In May 2005, eighteen-year-old Natalee Holloway of Mountain Brook, Alabama, was in Aruba with classmates, celebrating their high school graduation. She was set to attend the University of Alabama on a scholarship. At about one thirty in the morning on May thirtieth, she was last seen leaving a nightclub in Oranjestad with three young men, the FBI has said. She was never found. A judge declared her dead in 2012. Years later, one of those men, Joran van der Sloot, demanded money from her mother in exchange for information, and he was indicted in the United States for extortion and wire fraud. In October 2023, as part of his guilty plea in Birmingham, he admitted killing Natalee on a beach in Aruba and pushing her body into the sea. He was sentenced to twenty years for extortion and wire fraud. Because of Aruba's statute of limitations, he cannot be prosecuted there for her death. Her mother said: Her case is solved.
cases.summary: Natalee Holloway, 18, of Mountain Brook, Ala., was last seen about 1:30 a.m. May 30, 2005, leaving Carlos 'N Charlie's nightclub in Oranjestad, Aruba, during a graduation trip. Her body has never been found; she was declared dead in 2012. On Oct. 18, 2023, Joran van der Sloot pleaded guilty in federal court in Birmingham to extortion and wire fraud tied to her case and, in his plea agreement, admitted killing her on a beach; he was sentenced to 20 years. He has never been charged with her death: Aruba's limitation period has expired. In 2026, Aruban prosecutors offered their case file to Amsterdam prosecutors evaluating a complaint filed by her mother.

cases.audioScript: On the afternoon of Saturday, February second, 2008, twenty-four-year-old real estate agent Lindsay Buziak went to show a home in Saanich, British Columbia. The house sat on a quiet cul-de-sac in the Gordon Head neighbourhood. She arrived for a five-thirty showing with a couple who said they were buyers. Police say Lindsay was stabbed to death in an upstairs bedroom. Investigators later said the couple had arranged the meeting with a cellphone registered under a fake name in Metro Vancouver. They have never been identified, and no one has ever been arrested. In 2021, Saanich police formed a new task force. Working with the FBI and the RCMP, they began retesting evidence with DNA technology that did not exist in 2008. In late 2025, Lindsay's mother said she had heard the investigation was ending. Police answered that the case remains active and ongoing. Every February second, her father leads a Walk for Justice from Saanich Municipal Hall to the B.C. Legislature. He is still asking for someone to come forward.
cases.summary: Lindsay Buziak, a 24-year-old real estate agent, was stabbed to death on Feb. 2, 2008, while showing an empty home on a cul-de-sac (De Sousa Place) in Saanich's Gordon Head neighbourhood (CBC; Saanich News). Her father leads an annual Walk for Justice each Feb. 2 (Saanich News). Tips: Saanich Police, 250-475-4321 (Saanich News, Nov. 2025; CHEK News).

cases.audioScript: Through the late 1990s and into 2001, women kept disappearing from Vancouver's Downtown Eastside. Many were poor, many struggled with addiction, and many were Indigenous. For years, their families said no one was listening. In February 2002, police searched a pig farm in nearby Port Coquitlam owned by Robert William Pickton. What they found turned it into the largest crime scene in Canadian history. Pickton was charged with murdering twenty-six women. In December 2007, a jury in New Westminster found him guilty of second-degree murder in the deaths of six: Sereena Abotsway, Mona Wilson, Andrea Joesbury, Brenda Wolfe, Georgina Papin and Marnie Frey. He was sentenced to life in prison, with no chance of parole for twenty-five years. In 2010, the Supreme Court of Canada upheld the convictions, and prosecutors decided not to try him on the other twenty charges. A provincial inquiry later found blatant failures by police. In May 2024, Pickton was attacked in a Quebec prison and died. Many families of the missing women are still waiting for answers.
cases.summary: Robert William Pickton, a pig farmer from Port Coquitlam, B.C., was arrested in 2002 after the Project Evenhanded task force (Vancouver Police and RCMP) searched his farm beginning Feb. 5, 2002 (Canadian Encyclopedia; CBC). He was eventually charged with 26 counts of murder of women from Vancouver's Downtown Eastside (Canadian Encyclopedia; CBC). On Dec. 9, 2007, a B.C. Supreme Court jury in New Westminster found him not guilty of first-degree murder but guilty of second-degree murder in the deaths of Sereena Abotsway, Mona Wilson, Andrea Joesbury, Brenda Wolfe, Georgina Papin and Marnie Frey (CBC; Globe and Mail; Guardian). On Dec. 11, 2007, he was sentenced to life with no parole eligibility for 25 years, the maximum (CBC). The Supreme Court of Canada dismissed his appeal and affirmed the convictions on July 30, 2010 (SCC docket 33288; CBC). Prosecutors announced on Aug. 4, 2010 that they would not proceed on the 20 remaining charges (Canadian Encyclopedia). The Missing Women Commission of Inquiry's 2012 report found "blatant failures" by police (Canadian Encyclopedia; CBC). Pickton was assaulted at Port-Cartier Institution in Quebec on May 19, 2024, and died May 31, 2024 (CBC).
cases.solvedHow: A tip about illegal firearms gave police grounds for a search warrant at the farm; evidence found there led to murder charges. Convicted at trial in 2007.

cases.audioScript: On the evening of May twenty-fifth, 1989, forty-four-year-old nurse Cindy James deposited her paycheque at a bank machine at the Blundell Shopping Centre in Richmond, British Columbia. Then she vanished. Her car turned up in a mall parking lot with drops of blood on the door, her groceries and a wrapped gift still inside. On June eighth, a city worker found her body beside an abandoned house. Her hands and feet were tied behind her back, and a black nylon stocking was around her neck. An autopsy found a lethal overdose of morphine and other drugs. For seven years before her death she had reported nearly one hundred incidents of harassment, including threatening calls, notes and five violent attacks. Over time, police came to doubt her accounts, and the RCMP concluded she had taken her own life. Her parents never accepted that. In 1990, after a forty-day inquest, a coroner's jury could not decide, and ruled that she died of an unknown event. No one has ever been charged.
cases.summary: Richmond, B.C. nurse Cindy James, 44, vanished May 25, 1989 after visiting the Blundell Shopping Centre; her body was found June 8, bound, with a stocking around her neck and a lethal drug overdose. She had reported nearly 100 incidents of harassment over seven years; the RCMP concluded suicide. A 1990 coroner's inquest ruled her death an "unknown event"; no one has been charged.
cases.solvedHow: Not solved. The RCMP investigated years of reported harassment and her death, concluded suicide and closed the file in July 1989; a 1990 coroner's inquest could not determine the manner of death (unknown event). No forensic link to any person was found (per Neal Hall).

cases.audioScript: On June twelfth, 1999, fifteen-year-old Sharmini Anandavel left her family's Toronto apartment. She told her parents she was going out to see about a new job. She never came home. Days later, police found a phony employment application in her room, and came to believe that whoever killed her had used the promise of a job to lure her away. Four months later, in October 1999, her skeletal remains were found in a shallow grave in a wooded ravine beside the Don River, in a park in northeast Toronto. Toronto police have said they had a suspect in mind and questioned that person several times, but did not have enough evidence to lay a charge. Her parents, who had come to Canada in 1993, stood beside detectives and begged for anyone with information to come forward. More than twenty-five years later, no one has been charged in Sharmini's murder. If you know anything about what happened to Sharmini Anandavel in the summer of 1999, contact the Toronto Police Service Homicide Squad, or Crime Stoppers at one eight hundred, two two two, tips.

Her skeletal remains were found in October 1999 (Oct. 9 per the Toronto Police homicide page; the Globe and Mail reported Oct. 12) in a shallow grave in a wooded ravine next to the Don River in a northeast Toronto park. Toronto police said they had a suspect but that the evidentiary standard to proceed had not been met; in 2024 Det. Stella Karras told CityNews that officers had questioned an individual multiple times but did not have enough evidence to lay a charge. Police offered a $50,000 reward (Globe and Mail). No one has been charged. Tips: Toronto Police Homicide, 416-808-7400 or homicide@torontopolice.on.ca (Toronto Police Service, Homicide #36/1999).

cases.audioScript: In August 2007, twenty-year-old Christina Calayca of Toronto was on a camping trip with friends at Rainbow Falls Provincial Park, along Highway Seventeen near Schreiber, Ontario, on the north shore of Lake Superior. At about six thirty on the morning of August sixth, she told a companion she was going for a jog. She was last seen on a roadway in the park's campground. She never came back. The Ontario Provincial Police launched a huge search, on the ground, from the air, on the water, and with specialist teams trained in high-angle rope rescue on the steep, rugged terrain west of the park. They found no trace of her. Police say it is not known whether her disappearance involved foul play, but it cannot be ruled out. In 2023, the OPP renewed its appeal, asking anyone in the area to report bones or clothing matching what she wore: a blue hoodie, a maroon and purple striped shirt, black pants and white running shoes. If you have any information about Christina Calayca, contact the Ontario Provincial Police, or Crime Stoppers.

The OPP conducted extensive ground, air, marine and specialist searches; a planned continuation by the Provincial Emergency Response Team, with high-angle rope searches west of the park, was cancelled for weather in November 2007. In 2023 the OPP renewed its appeal, saying foul play could not be ruled out and asking people to report any remains or clothing matching what she wore. She has never been found. Tips: OPP, 1-888-310-1122, or Crime Stoppers, 1-800-222-TIPS (8477) (Toronto Sun, 2023). Canada's Missing lists the Nipigon OPP file as TP07020640.

cases.audioScript: On the evening of May sixth, 2013, Tim Bosma, a thirty-two-year-old husband and father from Ancaster, Ontario, took two men on a test drive of the pickup truck he was selling online. He never came home. His burned remains were found days later. The two men were Dellen Millard and his friend Mark Smich. In 2016, a jury in Hamilton found them both guilty of first-degree murder. Prosecutors said the pair planned to steal the truck and kill its owner, and that Bosma's body was burned in an animal incinerator Millard had bought. Investigators then looked back. Laura Babcock, a twenty-three-year-old Toronto woman who had been involved with Millard, had vanished in July 2012. In 2017, Millard and Smich were convicted of her murder too. Her remains have never been found. And in November 2012, Millard's father, Wayne, had been found shot in his Toronto home. Police first deemed it a suicide. In 2018, a judge found Dellen Millard guilty of murdering him. Three victims, three trials, three first-degree murder convictions. Ontario's top court later upheld the conviction for his father's murder.
cases.summary: Laura Babcock, 23, vanished from Toronto in July 2012. On Nov. 29, 2012, Wayne Millard, 71, a wealthy aviation executive, was shot in the eye while he slept in his Etobicoke home; police first deemed his death a suicide (CBC; Globe and Mail). On May 6, 2013, Tim Bosma, 32, of Ancaster, disappeared after taking Dellen Millard and Mark Smich on a test drive of a pickup truck he had listed for sale online; his burned remains were found days later (CityNews; Globe and Mail). The Crown said the pair planned to steal the truck and kill its owner, and that Bosma's body was burned in an animal incinerator Millard had bought (CityNews; CBC). On June 17, 2016, an Ontario Superior Court jury in Hamilton found Millard and Smich guilty of first-degree murder in Bosma's death; both received life sentences (CBC; National Post). In 2017 a Toronto jury convicted both of first-degree murder of Babcock, whose body was burned in an animal incinerator and never found; the judge ordered their life sentences served consecutively to the Bosma sentences (CBC). In September 2018, Justice Maureen Forestell found Dellen Millard guilty of first-degree murder of his father, finding he bought the gun used and set up a false alibi (Globe and Mail; CBC). The Ontario Court of Appeal dismissed his appeal of that conviction, calling the evidence "overwhelming" (CBC, April 2023).
cases.solvedHow: The Bosma test-drive disappearance led to Millard and Smich; later investigations connected Millard to the earlier disappearance of Laura Babcock and the death of his father, initially ruled a suicide.

cases.audioScript: On December fifteenth, 2017, billionaire philanthropists Barry and Honey Sherman were found dead in the basement pool area of their home in Toronto's North York neighbourhood. Barry, seventy-five, founded the generic drug giant Apotex. Honey was seventy. They were found side by side, with belts looped around their necks and tied to a pool railing. Autopsies found they died of ligature neck compression, and police said there were no signs of forced entry. Police believe they were killed on the evening of December thirteenth. In December 2021, detectives released a short video of a person walking near the home that night. Of everyone caught on nearby cameras, it was the only person police could not identify and rule out. The person is between five foot six and five foot nine, and kicks up the right foot with each step. Police could not determine their sex or race. Detectives asked anyone who recognizes the walk to come forward. Eight years later, the case remains unsolved.
cases.summary: Barry Sherman, 75, founder of Apotex, and his wife Honey, 70, were found dead Dec. 15, 2017 in the basement pool area of their North York home; both died of ligature neck compression. In Dec. 2021, Toronto police released video of an unidentified suspect with a distinctive gait seen near the home on the night of Dec. 13, 2017. No arrests have been made.

cases.audioScript: In March 1998, twenty-three-year-old Amy Lynn Bradley of Virginia was on a Caribbean cruise with her family aboard Royal Caribbean's Rhapsody of the Seas. On March twenty-third, the ship left Aruba, headed for Curaçao. In the early morning hours of Tuesday, March twenty-fourth, as the ship sailed toward port, Amy went missing. According to the Charley Project, she and her brother had sat on their cabin balcony until about five-thirty that morning, and two passengers later reported seeing her on an elevator to the top deck. She has never been found. The FBI still lists Amy among its missing persons and is offering a reward of up to one hundred thousand dollars for information leading to her recovery, or to the identification, arrest and conviction of anyone responsible. Amy was born in Petersburg, Virginia. She played basketball in college and loved her family. Over the years there have been reported sightings, but none has led to her. If you were on that cruise, or you have seen anyone you believe could be Amy, the FBI asks you to submit a tip at tips dot F B I dot gov.
cases.summary: Amy Lynn Bradley, 23, of Chesterfield County, Virginia, was traveling with her family on Royal Caribbean's Rhapsody of the Seas in March 1998. The FBI says the ship departed Aruba on Monday, March 23, 1998, bound for Curaçao, and that Bradley went missing in the early morning hours of Tuesday, March 24. The ship then called at Curaçao, St. Maarten and St. Thomas before returning to San Juan on March 28. The Charley Project, citing case records, says she and her brother sat on their suite's balcony until about 5:30 a.m. and that two passengers saw her riding an elevator toward the top deck around 6 a.m.; those sequence details come from a database summary and are stamped accordingly. The FBI lists the case under Kidnappings and Missing Persons and offers a reward of up to $100,000. Reported sightings over the years have not been confirmed. Netflix's three-part docuseries Amy Bradley Is Missing premiered July 16, 2025. No one has been charged. The case is filed under Curaçao because the disappearance occurred on the approach to Willemstad; her Virginia home county is a secondary location. Tips: the Bradley family takes tips at 804-789-4269 or amybradleyismissing@gmail.com (WTVR CBS 6); this is a family line, not a police line.

cases.audioScript: In early April 2014, two young Dutch women, twenty-one-year-old Kris Kremers and twenty-two-year-old Lisanne Froon, disappeared from the town of Boquete, Panama. They had gone hiking in the forest surrounding the town and never came back. Residents of Boquete held vigils as the search went on. More than two months later, a backpack containing two mobile phones thought to belong to the women was found, and soon police found bones and a pair of boots in Bocas del Toro province. Forensic tests confirmed the remains were Kris and Lisanne. It was still not clear how they died. A team of Dutch forensic specialists traveled to Panama at the families' request. In March 2015, the families said the team had concluded the women most likely died in an accident, possibly a fall, and considered a crime very unlikely. No definitive cause of death was ever established, and the case remains widely debated.
cases.summary: Kris Kremers, 21, and Lisanne Froon, 22, Dutch women traveling in Panama, disappeared from Boquete in early April 2014 while hiking in the forest around the town. In June 2014 a backpack with two phones and then bones and boots were found in Bocas del Toro province; forensic tests identified both women. A Dutch forensic team working for the families concluded in March 2015 that an accident, possibly a fall, was most likely and that a crime was very unlikely. The cause of death was never definitively determined.
cases.solvedHow: Not solved as a crime. Remains identified by forensic/DNA testing (June 2014). A Dutch forensic team working for the families concluded a fatal accident, possibly a fall, was most likely and a crime very unlikely (March 2015).

cases.audioScript: Just after midnight on June twenty-sixth, 2014, Anchorage police got a 911 call from a home on the city's Hillside. The caller said twenty-year-old Breanna Moore, known as Bree, had just been shot. Officers found Bree dead of a single gunshot wound to the head. Her boyfriend, twenty-two-year-old Joshua Almeda, was taken in for questioning. Police arrested him that same day and charged him with second-degree murder. Almeda told police he had found the gun with her body. But in 2015, he pleaded guilty to second-degree murder. In April 2016, an Anchorage judge sentenced him to seventy-five years in prison, saying the killing was closer to a deliberate shooting than a reckless one. Bree's family turned their grief into action. Her parents pushed for a state law on teen dating violence. In 2018, Alaska's governor signed a bill renaming the state's school program the Bree Moore Teen Dating Violence Awareness and Prevention Program. Bree was a curly-haired young woman with her whole life ahead of her. Today her name is used to teach Alaska's teenagers the warning signs.
cases.summary: At about 12:30 a.m. on June 26, 2014, Anchorage police received a 911 call from a home in the 10600 block of Treeline Court reporting that Breanna Richelle Moore, 20, had been shot. Officers found her dead of a single gunshot wound to the head (APD). Her boyfriend, Joshua Almeda, 22, was questioned and that day arrested and charged with second-degree murder and weapons offenses. The Anchorage Daily News reported he told police he had found the gun with her body. Almeda pleaded guilty to second-degree murder in 2015. On April 19, 2016, Anchorage Superior Court Judge Philip Volland sentenced him to 75 years, within a 10-to-99-year range, saying the killing was closer to a deliberate shooting than a reckless one and citing his criminal history (ADN). Her parents campaigned for dating-violence education; in July 2018 Gov. Bill Walker signed HB 214, renaming the school program the Bree Moore Teen Dating Violence Awareness and Prevention Program and funding training (KTUU).

cases.audioScript: On February first, 2012, eighteen-year-old Samantha Koenig was working at the Common Grounds coffee stand on Tudor Road in Anchorage, Alaska. That night a man abducted her and took her to a white pickup truck parked across the street. Federal prosecutors say he killed her early the next morning. He then used her stolen debit card, sent texts from her phone to hide what had happened, and later demanded ransom. The man was Israel Keyes, a thirty-four-year-old contractor, and he was arrested in March 2012. In April, FBI divers searched Matanuska Lake for Samantha's body. Keyes confessed, and told FBI agents he had also killed a Vermont couple, Bill and Lorraine Currier, and others across the country. But on December second, 2012, before he could stand trial, Keyes killed himself in his Anchorage jail cell. The FBI has released his travel history and is still asking anyone with information about him to call 1-800-CALL-FBI.
cases.summary: Samantha Koenig, 18, was abducted Feb. 1, 2012 from the Common Grounds coffee stand on Tudor Road in Anchorage and killed early the next morning, according to the federal indictment. Israel Keyes, 34, used her debit card, texted from her phone and sent a ransom demand; he was arrested in March 2012 and indicted April 18, 2012. He confessed and told FBI agents he had killed Bill and Lorraine Currier in Vermont in 2011 and others. Keyes died by suicide in the Anchorage Correctional Complex on Dec. 2, 2012; the FBI continues to seek information about other victims.
cases.solvedHow: Investigators tracked Keyes through use of Koenig's stolen debit card after a ransom demand; he was arrested in March 2012 and confessed.

cases.audioScript: On November thirteenth, 1996, thirty-five-year-old Carrie Loraine Bowles was shot and killed at her home in Cottondale, in Tuscaloosa County, Alabama. A family member found her dead inside the residence. Investigators have said it is unknown whether she knew her attacker. Nearly thirty years later, no one has been arrested, and the Tuscaloosa County Sheriff's Office still lists the case among its unsolved homicides. The county district attorney's office worked with investigators and the governor's office to bring the reward back. In August 2026, Governor Kay Ivey signed a proclamation offering a ten-thousand-dollar reward for information leading to an arrest and conviction. A five-thousand-dollar governor's reward first issued in 1998 had expired. The new proclamation states that the case remains unsolved and that there are no suspects. The reward is limited to private citizens who are not law-enforcement employees or their relatives. If you know anything about what happened to Carrie Bowles, call the Tuscaloosa County Metro Homicide Unit at 205-464-8690, or leave a confidential tip with Crime Stoppers at 205-752-7867.

cases.audioScript: In the early morning of August 23, 1987, the crew of a Union Pacific train spotted the bodies of two teenagers on the tracks near the Crooked Creek trestle in Alexander, Arkansas. The train could not stop in time. The boys were seventeen-year-old Kevin Ives and sixteen-year-old Don Henry, best friends who had been out hunting late the night before. They were identified through dental records. The state medical examiner first treated the deaths as accidental, saying the teens had been so affected by marijuana that they fell asleep on the tracks. Their parents rejected that ruling, and other medical experts said it was highly unlikely. After a second autopsy and a grand jury, the deaths were ruled a probable homicide. Theories about drug trafficking have circulated for decades, including a later witness claim that remains unproven. No one has been charged. Linda Ives, Kevin's mother, spent decades seeking records and answers. She died in 2021, with the case still unsolved.
cases.summary: On Sunday, August 23, 1987, at about 4:00 a.m., the crew of a Union Pacific locomotive spotted the bodies of two teenagers near the Crooked Creek trestle in Alexander, a community in Pulaski and Saline counties, Arkansas. The Encyclopedia of Arkansas, citing the historical record of the case, states that the bodies were lying between the tracks, that the crew reported they were wrapped in a pale green tarp with a gun nearby, and that the train was unable to avoid running over them. The crew reported the incident to railroad officials and to local law enforcement at Benton, where the train came to a full stop; by 4:40 a.m., local and state police were at the scene. The victims were 17-year-old Kevin Ives and 16-year-old Don Henry, best friends who had been out hunting late on Saturday night, August 22. When they could not be found the next morning, their parents began searching. They were identified conclusively through dental records on Monday. The encyclopedia reports that police took in a shattered .22-caliber rifle as evidence and that, according to some accounts, no tarp was found by police at the scene. Arkansas state medical examiner Dr. Fahmy Malak ruled the deaths an apparent suicide and then 'two accidental deaths due to THC intoxication,' a theory that the boys had been so affected by marijuana that they fell asleep on the tracks. All four parents disputed the ruling. KATV reported that other medical experts from around the country objected and concluded the boys were likely murdered. The encyclopedia describes second opinions in 1988 that rejected the idea that THC exposure would have had the effects Malak described, and a second autopsy by Georgia medical examiner Dr. Joseph Burton. After a hearing at the Saline County Courthouse in Benton, the official cause was changed from accidental to undetermined on February 26, 1988. A grand jury later that year ruled the deaths a probable homicide. The encyclopedia records that the deaths were again described as homicides after further investigation in March 1990, and that, as reported then by the Arkansas Gazette, there were no reported arrests. Linda Ives, Kevin's mother, became the public face of the effort to reopen and document the case. In 2016 she filed a federal Freedom of Information Act lawsuit; a 2017 order required some formerly redacted documents from certain federal defendants to be turned over for private review, other agencies were dismissed, and the suit itself was dismissed in 2019. KATV reported that she and her attorney did not find anything related to the boys' deaths in the material they obtained, and that she had believed the deaths could have been related to a drug-trafficking ring; that belief is not treated here as a proven fact. In 2017, former professional wrestler Billy Jack Haynes recorded an account in which he claimed to have witnessed the murders during a drug drop and to have helped place the bodies on the tracks. KATV reported in 2021 that his account, like other drug-trafficking theories, remains unproven and that no charges have been filed. Linda Kay Ives died on June 3, 2021, at age 71, in Benton, without a charging decision in the case. The Encyclopedia of Arkansas, last updated September 17, 2026, states that the case remains unsolved.
cases.solvedHow: Unsolved. No one has been charged. The official cause of death was changed from a medical-examiner accidental ruling to undetermined and then to a grand-jury finding of probable homicide after a second autopsy. Later FOIA litigation and unofficial witness claims have not produced charges. The case remains open in the public record as unsolved.

cases.audioScript: On the morning of April tenth, 2001, a ranch house in Scottsdale, Arizona, exploded and caught fire. When firefighters dug through the debris, they found Mary Fisher and her two children, twelve-year-old Brittney and ten-year-old Bobby. Police say all three had been killed before the fire, and that a gas line to the house had been severed and rigged to explode. The husband and father, Robert Fisher, was gone, and so was the family dog, Blue. The evening before, surveillance video showed him withdrawing two hundred eighty dollars from an ATM, the last confirmed sighting. Ten days later, on April twentieth, investigators found the family's Toyota 4Runner in the woods near Payson, in the Tonto National Forest. Blue was waiting under the vehicle. Robert Fisher was not. He is charged with three counts of first-degree murder and arson, and the FBI still lists him as wanted. He has never been found, and he has never been tried. Scottsdale detectives say they still follow every tip. If you have information, contact the FBI at tips dot f b i dot gov, or Scottsdale police.
cases.summary: On the morning of April 10, 2001, a ranch house near Scottsdale and McDowell roads in Scottsdale exploded and burned. Firefighters found the bodies of Mary Fisher and her children Brittney, 12, and Bobby, 10. Police say the victims' throats had been cut and Mary had also been shot, and that a gas line had been severed and rigged to explode. Robert Fisher, then 40, and the family dog, Blue, were missing. The evening before, ATM surveillance showed Fisher withdrawing $280 while driving Mary's Toyota 4Runner — the last documented sighting. On April 20, 2001, investigators found the 4Runner near Payson in the Tonto National Forest with Blue beneath it. The FBI wants Fisher for unlawful flight to avoid prosecution on charges of first-degree murder (three counts) and arson of an occupied structure; he was on the FBI's Ten Most Wanted list for years (removed in 2021 per Wikipedia/FBI advisory, Not Yet Verified here). He has never been found or tried; Scottsdale police say they continue to pursue leads. Tips: Scottsdale Police non-emergency line 480-312-5000, or the FBI at 1-800-CALL-FBI / tips.fbi.gov (ABC15).

cases.audioScript: In March 1963, an eighteen-year-old movie theater worker in Phoenix, Arizona, was grabbed on her way home from work, forced into a car, driven into the desert and raped. Her description of the car led police to a twenty-three-year-old man named Ernesto Miranda. On March thirteenth, officers arrested him and questioned him for about two hours. He signed a written confession, and a jury convicted him of kidnapping and rape. But no one had told Miranda he had the right to stay silent or to have a lawyer. His appeal reached the United States Supreme Court, and on June thirteenth, 1966, in a five-to-four decision, the Court threw out his conviction. Chief Justice Earl Warren wrote that police must warn suspects of their rights before questioning them in custody. That is why officers today read the Miranda warning: you have the right to remain silent. Arizona retried Miranda in 1967 without the confession, using other evidence, and he was convicted again. He was later paroled, and in 1976 he was stabbed to death in a Phoenix bar fight. The woman he attacked has never been publicly named here, and her privacy is respected.
cases.summary: In the early hours of March 3, 1963, an 18-year-old Phoenix movie-theater worker was accosted on her way home, forced into a car, driven to the desert and raped (Encyclopedia.com account). Police traced a car to Ernesto Miranda, 23, who was arrested at his home on March 13, 1963, identified by the complaining witness, and interrogated for two hours, producing a signed written confession that was admitted at his trial; he was convicted of kidnapping and rape. On June 13, 1966, the U.S. Supreme Court (Miranda v. Arizona, 384 U.S. 436, 5-4, opinion by Chief Justice Warren) reversed, holding that statements from custodial interrogation are inadmissible unless the suspect is first warned of the right to remain silent and to counsel. Arizona retried Miranda in 1967 without the confession; testimony from his former partner about his admissions led to another conviction and a 20-to-30-year sentence. He was paroled and was stabbed to death in a Phoenix bar fight on Jan. 31, 1976.
cases.solvedHow: Solved by police tracing a car described by the victim, a lineup identification and a confession; after the Supreme Court excluded the confession, the 1967 retrial convicted him on other evidence.

cases.audioScript: On June twenty-fifth, 1995, the body of a woman was found in an off-roading area of Standard Wash, near Lake Havasu City, Arizona. She had been shot to death. At first she was a Jane Doe, but investigators later identified her as forty-eight-year-old Jean Andrae Brady. Detectives interviewed several people, including her ex-husband, but no suspect was ever identified. More than thirty years later, in September 2026, the Mohave County Sheriff's Office asked for new leads. They want to hear from anyone who knew Jean, or her associates in Lake Havasu City in 1995, or anyone who knows who might have had cause to harm her. Detectives also hope to find her relatives, so they can return boxes of personal belongings recovered from a storage unit she rented. Her parents died decades ago, and investigators believe her extended family may live in Missouri or Kansas. If you can help, call the Mohave County Sheriff's Office Special Investigations Unit at 928-753-0753, extension 4408.

cases.audioScript: In June 2008, thirty-year-old Travis Alexander was found dead in the shower of his home here in Mesa, Arizona. He had been stabbed many times and shot. At trial she claimed self-defense, saying Travis attacked her. Prosecutors said she killed him in a jealous rage. She was arrested and charged with first-degree murder, and the case went to trial in Phoenix. The televised trial in Phoenix drew a national audience, and on May eighth, 2013, a jury found her guilty of first-degree murder. But that jury could not agree on death or life, and in 2015 a second jury deadlocked too, with a single holdout. So the decision went to the judge. On April thirteenth, 2015, Judge Sherry Stephens sentenced Arias to natural life in prison, with no chance of parole, calling the crime especially cruel and noting she destroyed evidence and went to great lengths to hide her involvement. Travis's sisters told the court how hard it is to remember him alive.
cases.summary: Travis Alexander, 30, was found dead in the shower of his Mesa, Arizona, home in June 2008; he had been shot in the head and his throat was slashed. His former girlfriend Jodi Arias admitted stabbing and shooting him but claimed self-defense; prosecutors said she killed him in a jealous rage. A Maricopa County jury found Arias guilty of first-degree murder on May 8, 2013, but deadlocked on the penalty, and a second penalty jury deadlocked in March 2015 with one holdout against death. On April 13, 2015, Judge Sherry Stephens sentenced Arias to natural life without parole, saying the crime involved substantial planning, that Arias did not render aid, destroyed evidence and went to great lengths to conceal her involvement.

cases.audioScript: On Valentine's Day 2007, thirty-nine-year-old Jodine Serrin was at home in her condominium in Carlsbad, California. Jodine lived on her own and was active in local support groups, including the National Alliance for the Mentally Ill. That night, her parents could not reach her by phone, so around ten o'clock they let themselves in. A man was in their daughter's bedroom. Her father told him to get out, and the man fled. Jodine had been beaten, raped and strangled. She died of blunt force head injuries. For ten years the case stayed open. In 2017, investigators released a DNA-based composite from Parabon NanoLabs and announced a reward of fifty-two thousand dollars. Then DNA matching through the suspect's relatives pointed to a transient named David Mabrito. Oceanside police had kept an unprocessed DNA sample from a traffic stop, and it matched the crime scene evidence. Mabrito had died by suicide in 2011, so he was never charged. In November 2018, Carlsbad police said they had identified the person responsible. The chief said they never forgot Jodine.
cases.summary: Jodine Elizabeth Serrin, 39, was found murdered in her ground-level condominium in the 1900 block of Swallow Lane, Carlsbad, on Feb. 14, 2007. Her parents, unable to reach her by phone, let themselves in around 10 p.m.; her father encountered a man in the bedroom and told him to leave, then discovered she had been beaten, raped and strangled (NBC News; Times of San Diego). An autopsy found she died of blunt-force head injuries (Times of San Diego). On the 10th anniversary in 2017, Carlsbad police and the San Diego County DA released a Parabon Snapshot DNA-phenotype composite and announced a $52,000 combined reward. On Nov. 13, 2018, police announced that DNA comparisons and genealogical work identified David Mabrito, a transient who was 38 in 2007 and who died by suicide in 2011; an unprocessed DNA sample taken by Oceanside police during a traffic stop was matched to the crime-scene evidence (NBC 7 San Diego). Because he is dead, he was never charged; he is recorded as identified by police, never charged/convicted.

cases.audioScript: On Christmas Eve, 2002, twenty-seven-year-old Laci Peterson vanished from her home in Modesto, California. She was eight months pregnant with a son the family had named Conner. Her disappearance set off one of the most-watched searches in the country. In April 2003, the remains of Laci and her unborn son washed up along the shore of San Francisco Bay, found by a woman walking her dog, near where her husband, Scott Peterson, had told police he was fishing the day she disappeared. Four days later, he was arrested. In 2004, after a six-month trial, a jury found Scott Peterson guilty of first-degree murder in Laci's death and second-degree murder in Conner's. He was sentenced to death. In 2020, the California Supreme Court overturned that death sentence over jury selection, and in 2021 he was resentenced to life without parole. His conviction still stands. In April 2026, a San Mateo County judge denied his third habeas petition in its entirety; his lawyers say they will appeal. Laci is remembered by her family as a mother-to-be who was days away from welcoming her son.
cases.summary: Laci Peterson, 27 and eight months pregnant, disappeared from the couple's Modesto, California, home on Christmas Eve 2002. In April 2003 her remains and those of her unborn son, Conner, were found washed up on the San Francisco Bay shoreline, near where Scott Peterson told police he had been fishing when she disappeared. Peterson was arrested four days after the remains were found. After a six-month trial in 2004 (moved to San Mateo County), a jury convicted him of first-degree murder for Laci and second-degree murder for Conner, and he was sentenced to death. In 2020 the California Supreme Court overturned the death sentence because the jury had been improperly screened for bias against the death penalty, while leaving the convictions in place; he was resentenced to life without parole the next year. The Los Angeles Innocence Project took up his case in 2024 and filed a third habeas petition in August 2025; on April 27, 2026, San Mateo County Superior Court Judge Elizabeth Hill denied all 14 claims. The Stanislaus County DA said the 2004 conviction has been upheld through two decades of litigation. LAIP said it would appeal. As of the DA's May 12, 2026 update, his separate appeal on the Juror No. 7 bias claim remained pending before the California Supreme Court (Stanislaus County DA).
cases.solvedHow: Convicted by jury in 2004 on circumstantial evidence (see evidence list). Conviction upheld on appeal (2020) and in habeas proceedings through April 2026.

cases.audioScript: In April 2016, San Francisco park workers found a woman buried in John McLaren Park. She was identified as Nicole Fitts. Days earlier, her family had reported both Nicole and her two-and-a-half-year-old daughter, Arianna, missing. But police soon learned that Arianna had not been seen since January or February of that year, in Oakland. Investigators say Arianna was last in the care of a babysitter and the babysitter's husband, and that Nicole was lured to meet the babysitter around the time she vanished. The FBI says it does not believe Arianna was with her mother when Nicole was killed. Nobody has been charged in Nicole's murder, and Arianna has never been found. Today, San Francisco police offer a reward of up to two hundred and fifty thousand dollars for information leading to an arrest and conviction. An SFPD sketch artist has released age progressions showing what Arianna may look like now. She was born in September 2013. If you have seen Arianna Fitts, or know what happened to her mother, call the San Francisco Police tip line at four one five, five seven five, four four four four.
cases.summary: Nicole Fitts and her daughter Arianna, then about 2 1/2, were reported missing to the San Francisco Police Department on April 5, 2016. On April 8, 2016, at about 10:30 a.m., San Francisco Recreation and Parks staff found Nicole buried in John McLaren Park; the medical examiner identified her, and SFPD investigated her death as a homicide. Investigators determined Arianna had not been seen since late February 2016 (FBI: January or February, in Oakland) and that she was last in the care of her babysitter and the babysitter's husband; SFPD says Nicole was lured to meet the babysitter around the time of her disappearance. The FBI says it believes Arianna was not with her mother when she was killed. SFPD announced a $100,000 reward and an age-progression sketch in 2020; its current case page lists a $250,000 reward. No one has been charged and Arianna remains missing. Tips: SFPD 24-hour tip line 1-415-575-4444, or text a tip to TIP411 (San Francisco Police Department).

cases.audioScript: In late August 2013, nineteen-year-old Bryce Laspisa left Sierra College in Rocklin, California, and set out on a long drive home to his family in Laguna Niguel. He was driving his mother's Toyota Highlander. Along the way he stopped in Kern County, and his family grew worried as the hours passed. At about 2:08 in the morning on August thirtieth, Bryce called his mother to say he was tired and had pulled off the road to rest. It was the last time anyone heard from him. A few hours later, around 5:30 a.m., the SUV was found near Castaic Lake in northern Los Angeles County. Bryce was not with it. Days of searching around the lake turned up no trace of him. A body found burning near the lake that September was confirmed not to be Bryce. More than a decade later, he is still missing. He was nineteen, five foot eleven, with red hair and blue eyes. If you have information about Bryce Laspisa, please call the Los Angeles County Sheriff's Department at 323-890-5500.
cases.summary: Bryce Laspisa, 19, a Sierra College student, left Rocklin on Aug. 28, 2013, drove to Chico, and then began the roughly 500-mile drive to his family's home in Laguna Niguel in his mother's Toyota Highlander. On Aug. 29 he called for roadside assistance in Buttonwillow (Kern County) after running out of fuel and was later checked on by a Kern County officer, who reported he seemed fine (NBC, from his mother's account). At about 2:08 a.m. on Aug. 30 he called his mother to say he had pulled off to rest; that is the last known contact (LASD release). The 2003 Highlander was found later that morning in the Castaic Lake area of Los Angeles County — described by LASD as off Lake Hughes Road and by the LA Times as on the Main Ramp Road near the lake at about 5:30 a.m. A burned body found near the lake in September 2013 was confirmed not to be him. He remains missing; LASD asks for tips. Tips: Los Angeles County Sheriff's Department 323-890-5500, or anonymously through Crime Stoppers at 800-222-TIPS (8477) (LASD release).
cases.solvedHow: Unsolved. Techniques: searches of the Castaic Lake area, phone pings, public appeals by LASD (2019), and an age-progression image (Charley Project).

cases.audioScript: Just before three in the morning on April fifteenth, 2017, Humboldt State University sophomore David Josiah Lawson was at an off-campus house party on Spear Avenue in Arcata, California. As his group was leaving, a confrontation broke out in front of the house, and a fight followed. In the chaos, Josiah was stabbed. He died of his wounds. A man was arrested that morning and charged with murder, but weeks later a judge dismissed the charges, saying the evidence was not enough to go to trial, and in March 2019 prosecutors announced that a grand jury had declined to indict. No one has been convicted. Josiah's mother, Charmaine Lawson, has spent years pushing for answers, and the case drew national attention on campus and beyond. The Arcata Police Department says the murder remains an open case. Investigators believe witnesses who were at that party may finally be willing to talk, and that their accounts are crucial to bringing the case back to court. A reward of up to fifty-five thousand dollars has been offered. If you were there that night, call the Arcata Police confidential tip line at seven oh seven, eight two five, twenty-five ninety.

A fight broke out in front of the house as his group was leaving. A man was arrested and charged, but on May 5, 2017, a judge dismissed the charges for insufficient evidence; a criminal grand jury empanelled in February 2019 declined to indict, as the DA announced on March 13, 2019 (North Coast Journal; NBC News). Arcata police describe the case as an open murder investigation and continue to appeal for witnesses. A reward of $55,000 has been publicized for information leading to an arrest (NBC News, 2021). No one has been convicted. Tips: Arcata Police Department confidential tip line (707) 825-2590, or APD Dispatch (707) 822-2424 (Arcata PD release, April 2024).

cases.audioScript: In 1979, twelve-year-old Robin Samsoe of Huntington Beach, California, disappeared. She was later found murdered. The man convicted of killing her was Rodney James Alcala, a photographer who a year earlier had appeared as a contestant on the television show The Dating Game. Alcala was sentenced to death for Robin's murder in 1980, but that verdict was overturned. So was a second death sentence. While he waited for a third trial, DNA evidence connected him to the killings of four women in the Los Angeles area in the late 1970s: Jill Barcomb, Georgia Wixted, Charlotte Lamb and Jill Parenteau. In 2010, an Orange County jury convicted Alcala of all five murders, and a judge sentenced him to death. That same year, investigators released more than a hundred photographs found in his storage locker, asking the public to help identify the women and children in them. In 2012, he pleaded guilty in New York to murdering two more young women there in the 1970s, Cornelia Crilley and Ellen Hover. Alcala died of natural causes on California's death row in July 2021, at seventy-seven. Investigators believe there may be other victims who were never identified.
cases.summary: Rodney James Alcala was convicted in Santa Ana on February 25, 2010, of five counts of first-degree murder: the 1979 kidnapping and murder of 12-year-old Robin Samsoe of Huntington Beach and the killings of four Los Angeles-area women, Jill Barcomb (18, 1977), Georgia Wixted (27, 1977), Charlotte Lamb (32, 1978) and Jill Parenteau (21, 1979). On March 30, 2010, Judge Francisco Briseno followed the jury's recommendation and sentenced him to death (Daily Pilot/Los Angeles Times). Alcala had twice before been sentenced to death for Samsoe's murder, in 1980 and 1986; both judgments were overturned on appeal. DNA evidence linking him to the Los Angeles cases was found after the second reversal. In March 2010 the Orange County DA and Huntington Beach police released more than 100 photographs found in his Seattle storage locker and asked the public to help identify the people pictured (OCDA). On December 14, 2012, in Manhattan, Alcala pleaded guilty to the 1971 murder of Cornelia Crilley and the 1977 murder of Ellen Hover, both 23 (Los Angeles Times; DNAinfo), and was later sentenced to 25 years to life. He was known as the "Dating Game Killer" because he appeared on The Dating Game in 1978. He died of natural causes at a hospital near Corcoran, California, on July 24, 2021, aged 77 (NBC News; CBS News; BBC).
cases.solvedHow: The Samsoe case was prosecuted three times; DNA testing later tied Alcala to four Los Angeles-area murders, which were joined to the 2010 retrial. New York cold-case investigators reopened two 1970s murders and obtained guilty pleas in 2012.

cases.audioScript: In May 2010, Sam Herr's father went to check on his twenty-six-year-old son's apartment in Costa Mesa, California. Inside, he found the body of Sam's friend, twenty-three-year-old Julie Kibuishi, who had been shot. Sam was missing, and at first it looked as if he might be the killer. But withdrawals from Sam's bank account led detectives to a neighbor, a community theater actor named Daniel Wozniak. Prosecutors said Wozniak, desperate for money for his upcoming wedding, rent and debts, lured Sam, an Army veteran with about sixty-two thousand dollars saved from his service in Afghanistan, to a theater in Los Alamitos and shot him. Then he used Sam's phone to lure Julie to the apartment, killed her, and staged the scene to frame Sam. Wozniak later confessed. In December 2015, an Orange County jury convicted him of two counts of special-circumstances murder, including murder for financial gain, and in January 2016 the jury recommended the death penalty, and he was sentenced to death that September. In November 2026, California's governor announced a plan to commute all death sentences to life without parole; that move is being challenged. Sam's father said in court that the verdict confirmed what the family had always known. Sam Herr and Julie Kibuishi are remembered by their families and friends.
cases.summary: On May 21, 2010, Daniel Wozniak shot Army veteran Sam Herr, 26, in a Los Alamitos theater where Wozniak performed, then used Herr's phone to lure Juri 'Julie' Kibuishi, 23, to Herr's Costa Mesa apartment, where he shot her and staged the scene to make it appear Herr had attacked her and fled (LA Times). Herr's father found Kibuishi's body on May 22, 2010 (ABC News). Withdrawals from Herr's bank account led Costa Mesa police to Wozniak, who confessed. Prosecutors said he wanted money for his wedding, rent and debts and targeted Herr's roughly $62,000 in savings. On Dec. 16, 2015, a jury convicted Wozniak of two felony counts of special-circumstances murder (multiple murders; murder for financial gain), and on Jan. 11, 2016, recommended death (Orange County DA). The court sentenced him to death on Sept. 23, 2016 (Judge John Conley), and the case is on automatic appeal (Orange County DA). On Nov. 5, 2026, Gov. Gavin Newsom announced a plan to change all California death sentences to life without the possibility of parole; the Habeas Corpus Resource Center said sentences had not yet been formally commuted, and on Nov. 19, 2026 a coalition of prosecutors asked the California Supreme Court to halt the effort (LA Times). His exact status is therefore unsettled as of Nov. 21, 2026.
cases.solvedHow: Solved through financial records (withdrawals from Herr's account), interrogation leading to a confession, and recovery of the handgun; jury conviction in 2015.
cases.techniques: Financial records; Interrogation/confession; Firearm evidence; Jury trial

cases.audioScript: On January thirtieth, 1989, thirteen-year-old Ilene Misheloff was walking home alone from Wells Middle School in Dublin, California. At about three in the afternoon, witnesses saw her walking on Amador Valley Boulevard near Village Parkway, and she was not seen again. Her key fob was later found near the entrance to John Mape Park, along the route she usually took home. She was wearing a charcoal gray Esprit polo sweater, a pink and charcoal striped skirt, and black low-top Keds, and she had braces and freckles. For more than thirty years, the community held a candlelight vigil and walk on the anniversary. After Ilene's mother, Maddi, died in 2020, the walk ended, but the investigation did not. On the thirty-fifth anniversary, Dublin's police chief said the department will continue to follow every tip and will not rest until the case is brought to a conclusion. Police have offered a ninety-five-thousand-dollar reward for information leading to an arrest and conviction. If you know anything, call Dublin Police Services at 925-833-6670.
cases.summary: On Jan. 30, 1989, 13-year-old Ilene Misheloff was abducted while walking home from Wells Middle School in Dublin, California. She was last seen at about 3 p.m., walking alone on Amador Valley Boulevard near Village Parkway. Her key fob was later found near the entrance to John Mape Park, along the route she normally took home. She was last seen wearing a charcoal gray Esprit polo sweater, a pink and charcoal gray horizontally striped skirt and black low-top Keds; she had braces, pierced ears, freckles and a small lump on the inside of her left ankle. For more than 30 years a community vigil and walk marked the anniversary; it ended after her mother, Maddi Misheloff, died in April 2020. On the 35th anniversary in January 2024, Dublin Police Chief Nate Schmidt said the department would continue to follow every tip, and Patch reported a $95,000 reward for information leading to the arrest and conviction of the person responsible. Dublin Police asks anyone with information to contact Sgt. Craig Evans at 925-833-6670; the FBI San Francisco office also accepts tips.

cases.audioScript: On Memorial Day weekend, 1996, nineteen-year-old Kristin Smart, a student here at Cal Poly San Luis Obispo, went to a party near campus. Around two in the morning, she was seen on a lawn next door, and she set off to walk back to her dorm. She never made it. For decades, there was no arrest, and she was declared legally dead in 2002. Her family kept billboards up along Highway 101 so no one would forget. Then, in April 2021, San Luis Obispo County sheriff's officials arrested a former classmate, Paul Flores, who had long been called a prime suspect. Prosecutors said he killed Kristin during an attempted rape. In October 2022, a jury in Salinas convicted him of first-degree murder, and in March 2023 he was sentenced to twenty-five years to life. But Kristin's body has never been found, and investigators were still serving search warrants in 2026. If you know where she is, contact the San Luis Obispo County Sheriff's Office.
cases.summary: Kristin Smart, 19, of Stockton, a Cal Poly San Luis Obispo student, disappeared on Memorial Day weekend 1996 after an off-campus party; a party host told investigators he saw her on a neighboring lawn around 2 a.m. She was declared legally dead in 2002. Paul Flores, a Cal Poly classmate long described as a prime suspect, was arrested by San Luis Obispo County sheriff's officials on April 13, 2021. A Monterey County jury convicted him of first-degree murder in October 2022; prosecutors said Smart was killed during an attempted rape. He was sentenced on March 10, 2023 to 25 years to life. Her body has never been found; authorities served a new search warrant in May 2026.
cases.solvedHow: Solved without a body: decades of searches and warrants, renewed public attention, and a 2021 arrest led to a jury conviction on circumstantial and witness evidence.

cases.audioScript: On February twenty-fourth, 1986, twenty-nine-year-old nurse Sherri Rasmussen was beaten and shot to death in the Van Nuys condo she shared with her husband of three months. Detectives first believed two burglars who had attacked another woman nearby were responsible. The case went cold for more than twenty years. Then a Los Angeles police cold case team tested a bite mark on Sherri's arm, and the DNA showed the killer was a woman. Investigators began looking at one of their own: Stephanie Lazarus, a veteran LAPD art-theft detective and her husband's ex-girlfriend. Lazarus was arrested in June 2009. In March 2012, a jury convicted her of first-degree murder, with the prosecutor calling it a case of a bite, a bullet, a gun barrel and a broken heart. She was sentenced to twenty-seven years to life. Only in 2023, at a parole hearing, did she admit that she took Sherri's life. Parole was denied again in 2025.
cases.summary: Sherri Rasmussen, 29, director of nursing at Glendale Adventist Medical Center, was bludgeoned and shot to death on Feb. 24, 1986, in the Van Nuys condo she shared with her husband of three months. Detectives initially believed two robbers who had attacked another woman in the area were responsible. More than two decades later, an LAPD cold case team using DNA from a bite mark on her arm determined the killer was a woman, and suspicion turned to LAPD detective Stephanie Lazarus, her husband's former girlfriend. Lazarus was arrested in June 2009 at LAPD headquarters, convicted of first-degree murder on March 8, 2012, and sentenced on May 11, 2012 to 27 years to life. At a 2023 parole hearing she admitted the killing; a parole grant was rescinded after Gov. Gavin Newsom raised concerns, and parole was denied again in February 2025.
cases.solvedHow: Solved by an LAPD cold case unit that tested preserved bite-mark DNA more than 20 years later; the female profile redirected the investigation to the victim's husband's ex-girlfriend, an LAPD detective, whose DNA matched.

cases.audioScript: In the 1980s, Dorothea Puente ran a boardinghouse on F Street in downtown Sacramento. To many, she seemed like a kindly grandmother. Prosecutors said she took in elderly, ill and alcoholic tenants, and then killed them for their government benefit checks. In 1988, a social worker came looking for a tenant named Bert Montoya. Puente gave her different stories, including that he had gone to Mexico. Acting on a tip from another tenant, police began to dig in the yard. In November 1988, they found seven bodies. Officers searched for Puente after the bodies were found, and she was arrested in Los Angeles. Tests found traces of a prescription sedative she often refilled in all of the bodies buried in the garden. In 1993, after a record twenty-four days of deliberation, a jury convicted her of murdering three tenants: Dorothy Miller, Benjamin Fink and Leona Carpenter. The jury could not agree on six other murder counts. She was sentenced to life in prison without parole, and she died in prison in 2011, at eighty-two.
cases.summary: Dorothea Montalvo Puente operated a boardinghouse on F Street in Sacramento in the 1980s; prosecutors said she preyed on elderly, ill and alcoholic tenants and killed them for their disability and Social Security checks. She had earlier served three years of a five-year prison term for drugging elderly people and stealing their benefit checks, and was on parole while running the boardinghouse. In 1988, a social worker checking on tenant Bert Montoya was given shifting explanations for his absence; acting on a tip from another tenant, police dug in the yard and in November 1988 found seven bodies, including Montoya's. Puente was located and arrested in Los Angeles and flown back to Sacramento on Nov. 18, 1988. Toxicology tests found Dalmane, a prescription drug Puente frequently refilled, in all of the bodies buried in the garden, and a note listing initials and dollar amounts was found in the house. She was tried on nine murder counts; the trial was held in Monterey before Judge Michael J. Virga. On Aug. 26, 1993, after 24 days of deliberation, the jury convicted her of first-degree murder of Dorothy Miller and Benjamin Fink and second-degree murder of Leona Carpenter, and deadlocked on six other counts. She was sentenced to life without parole and died in prison of natural causes on March 27, 2011, at age 82.

cases.audioScript: Between 1972 and 1973, young women hitchhiking around Santa Cruz County, California, began disappearing. They were high school and college students, ages fifteen to twenty-three. Their killer was a six-foot-nine former construction worker named Edmund Kemper. He buried some victims in the Santa Cruz mountains near Summit Road and at his home in Aptos. In 1973 he killed his own mother and her friend. Then he did something few killers do: he called Santa Cruz police from a pay phone and confessed. Kemper was convicted of eight murders and given eight concurrent life sentences. As a teenager, he had already been accused of shooting his grandparents. He has been denied parole many times since 1979. On July ninth, 2024, the board denied him again, for seven years. At that 2024 hearing, he did not attend, and the parole board found he still posed a high risk to reoffend, citing an incident in prison as recently as 2022. He will not be eligible again until 2031, when he will be eighty-two.
cases.summary: Edmund Kemper killed seven women and one girl in Santa Cruz County in 1972-1973, including female high school and college students aged 15-23, his mother and her friend. The eight murder counts at his April 30, 1973 arraignment named Mary Ann Pesce, Anita Luchessa, Aiko Koo, Cindy Schall, Rosalind Thorpe, Allison Liu, his mother Clarnell Strandberg and her friend Sally Hallett. Years earlier, at 15, he had killed his paternal grandparents. After killing his mother and her friend, he called Santa Cruz police from a phone booth in Pueblo, Colorado, confessed, and turned himself in. He was convicted in 1973 and received eight concurrent life sentences. He was denied parole on July 9, 2024 for seven years; next eligibility is 2031.

cases.audioScript: In February 2010, the McStay family of Fallbrook, California vanished. Joseph and Summer McStay and their little boys, four-year-old Gianni and three-year-old Joseph Junior, were simply gone. Investigators found no signs of a struggle at the home. Food had been left out, and the family dogs were still there. For more than three years, nobody knew what had happened to them. Then in November 2013, an off-road motorcyclist came across their remains in shallow graves in the Mojave Desert, north of Victorville. They had died of blunt-force trauma. In 2014, police arrested Joseph's former business associate, Charles Chase Merritt. Prosecutors said he bludgeoned the family with a sledgehammer. On June tenth, 2019, a jury found him guilty of four counts of first-degree murder, and in January 2020 a judge sentenced him to death. At his sentencing, Judge Michael Smith upheld the jury's recommendation of death after a two-day hearing. Merritt told the court, I did not do this thing, and he still maintains his innocence.
cases.summary: Joseph McStay, 40, and Summer McStay, 43, and their sons Gianni, 4, and Joseph Jr., 3, disappeared from their Fallbrook home in February 2010. Their remains were found by an off-road motorcyclist in shallow graves north of Victorville in November 2013, along with a rusty sledgehammer; they died of blunt-force trauma. Joseph's former business associate Charles "Chase" Merritt was arrested in November 2014, convicted June 10, 2019 of four counts of first-degree murder, and sentenced to death Jan. 21, 2020. Authorities said Merritt killed the family after Joseph tried to cut him out of their custom water-feature business.

cases.audioScript: Between October 1977 and February 1978, Los Angeles was terrorized by a killer the press called the Hillside Strangler. At least ten young women and girls, ages twelve to twenty-eight, were killed and left where they would be found. It was actually two men: cousins Angelo Buono, a Glendale upholsterer, and Kenneth Bianchi. They posed as vice officers, flashing fake badges to lure victims back to Buono's house. In January 1979, Bianchi was arrested in Bellingham, Washington, for murdering two Western Washington University students. To avoid the death penalty, he pleaded guilty and agreed to testify against his cousin. Buono's trial became one of the longest in American history, running seven hundred twenty-nine days. In November 1983 the jury returned nine guilty verdicts. Buono was sentenced to life without parole and died in prison in 2002. Bianchi is still in prison in Washington state. In July 2025, he was denied parole again and will not be eligible for another decade.
cases.summary: Between October 1977 and February 1978, cousins Angelo Buono Jr. and Kenneth Bianchi killed at least 10 young women and girls, ages 12 to 28, in Los Angeles County, often posing as police officers to lure victims. Bianchi was arrested in Bellingham, Wash., on Jan. 12, 1979 for two more murders, then pleaded guilty and testified against Buono. Buono was convicted of nine murders in November 1983 and died in Calipatria State Prison in 2002 at 67; Bianchi was denied parole in July 2025. The nine murders Buono was convicted of were those of Judith Lynn Miller, Elissa Kastin, Jane Evelyn King, Dolores Cepeda, Sonja Johnson, Kristina Weckler, Lauren Rae Wagner, Kimberly Diane Martin and Cindy Lee Hudspeth; Yolanda Washington, 19, was the first victim.
cases.solvedHow: Solved after Bianchi's January 1979 arrest in Bellingham, Wash.; he pleaded guilty and testified against Buono, who was convicted after a 729-day trial.

cases.audioScript: On the night of August eighth into the ninth, 1969, followers of Charles Manson broke into the Benedict Canyon home of actress Sharon Tate here in Los Angeles. Tate, who was pregnant, and four others were killed: Jay Sebring, Abigail Folger, Wojciech Frykowski and Steven Parent. The next night, the killers struck again, murdering grocery executive Leno LaBianca and his wife, Rosemary. His followers carried out the killings under his orders; he believed the murders could start a race war. Five people were tried: Manson, Tex Watson, Susan Atkins, Patricia Krenwinkel and Leslie Van Houten. All were sentenced to death. When California struck down the death penalty in 1972, their sentences became life in prison. Manson and Atkins died in custody. Watson is still in prison. Van Houten was paroled in 2023. And in October 2026, a parole panel again recommended Krenwinkel for release, a decision that still needs review by the full board and the governor.
cases.summary: On Aug. 9, 1969, followers of Charles Manson killed actress Sharon Tate, who was pregnant, along with Jay Sebring, Abigail Folger, Wojciech Frykowski and Steven Parent at the Benedict Canyon home Tate shared with her husband, Roman Polanski. The following night, grocery executive Leno LaBianca and his wife, Rosemary, were killed. The followers killed the seven victims under orders from Manson, who believed the murders could start a race war. Manson, Charles "Tex" Watson, Susan Atkins, Patricia Krenwinkel and Leslie Van Houten were tried and sentenced to death; Krenwinkel was convicted in 1971 of seven counts of first-degree murder. Their death sentences were commuted to life in prison after the California Supreme Court invalidated death sentences in 1972. Manson died in custody in November 2017 and Atkins also died in custody, and Watson remains in prison; Van Houten was released on parole in 2023. Krenwinkel, held at the California Institution for Women in Corona, was preliminarily granted parole at her 18th suitability hearing on Oct. 6, 2026; Gov. Gavin Newsom had reversed earlier grants, most recently in October 2025. The decision becomes final only after a 120-day Board of Parole Hearings review and a further 30-day review by the governor.

cases.audioScript: On December twenty-third, 2000, writer Susan Berman was shot at point-blank range in the back of the head inside her home in Los Angeles's Benedict Canyon. She was a longtime friend and confidante of New York real estate heir Robert Durst. Prosecutors said that before her death, Berman had been scheduled to speak to police about a fake alibi she allegedly gave Durst when his wife, Kathie, disappeared in New York in 1982. In a 2015 HBO documentary series, The Jinx, Durst appeared to confess to the killings while wearing a live microphone. In September 2021, a Los Angeles jury convicted him of first-degree murder, and he was sentenced to life without parole. Durst died in custody in January 2022 at seventy-eight, of natural causes, while serving that sentence. Because his appeal was still pending, California law required his conviction to be vacated. The prosecutor said that technical rule does not change what the jury found.

cases.audioScript: Between October twelfth, 1972 and February thirteenth, 1973, thirteen people were killed in and around Santa Cruz County, California. The victims ranged in age from four to seventy-three, and one was a priest killed in a church confessional in Los Gatos. On February thirteenth, 1973, Santa Cruz man Fred Perez was killed, and Herbert Mullin was arrested that day. At his trial that summer, Mullin said he heard messages telling him to commit human sacrifices to prevent huge earthquakes on the San Andreas Fault. He was convicted of ten murders and sentenced in September 1973 to life in prison. He was later convicted of another murder, and prosecutors said he confessed to two more that were never charged. In the same era, Santa Cruz County also prosecuted two other multiple killers, Edmund Kemper and John Linley Frazier. Mullin was denied parole in March 2021. He died of natural causes at the California Health Care Facility in Stockton on August eighteenth, 2022, at age seventy-five.
cases.summary: Herbert Mullin killed 13 people in Santa Cruz County and Los Gatos between Oct. 12, 1972 and Feb. 13, 1973, saying voices told him human sacrifices would prevent earthquakes. He was arrested Feb. 13, 1973 after the killing of Fred Perez and convicted of 10 murders, then an 11th. He was denied parole in 2021 and died in prison Aug. 18, 2022. The victims were Lawrence White, Mary Guilfoyle, Father Henri Tomei, Jim and Joan Gianera, Kathy Francis and her sons Daemon Francis and David Hughes, campers David Oliker, Robert Spector, Brian Card and Mark Dreibelbis, and Fred Perez.

cases.audioScript: Around one in the morning on May fourteenth, 1983, two California Highway Patrol officers saw a car weaving on Interstate five in south Orange County. They arrested the driver, computer consultant Randy Kraft, for drunk driving. In the front passenger seat was the body of twenty-five-year-old Terry Gambrel, a Marine stationed at El Toro. In the trunk, investigators found a coded list that prosecutors called his scorecard of victims. Prosecutors tied Kraft to the deaths of young men dumped along Southern California freeways for more than a decade. Six of the victims were Marines. In May 1989, after a nine-month trial in Santa Ana, a jury convicted him of sixteen murders. That November, a judge sentenced him to death. Kraft told the court he had not murdered anyone. The California Supreme Court upheld the judgment in 2000. In 2023, Orange County sheriff's investigators used genetic genealogy to identify a young man found dead in 1974 as seventeen-year-old Michael Ray Schlicht, and reopened his homicide case.
cases.summary: Randy Kraft was arrested May 14, 1983 on I-5 in south Orange County with the body of Marine Terry Gambrel, 25, in his car; a coded list in the trunk was called his scorecard. He was convicted of 16 Orange County murders of young men (1972-1983) on May 12, 1989 and sentenced to death Nov. 29, 1989; the California Supreme Court affirmed in 2000. In 2023 the OC Sheriff identified a 1974 John Doe as Michael Ray Schlicht and reopened that homicide.

cases.audioScript: On the morning of July eighteenth, 1989, twenty-one-year-old actress Rebecca Schaeffer answered the door of her Los Angeles apartment building and was shot in the chest. She had co-starred in the sitcom My Sister Sam. Her killer, nineteen-year-old Robert Bardo of Tucson, Arizona, had been obsessed with her for years, writing letters and once trying to see her at a studio lot. He got her home address through a private investigator, who obtained it from the state Department of Motor Vehicles. The next day, police in Tucson found him running in freeway traffic, and he said he had shot someone. In October 1991, after a non-jury trial prosecuted by Marcia Clark, a judge found him guilty of first-degree murder and ruled he lay in wait. In December he was sentenced to life without parole. Her killing led California to pass the nation's first laws making stalking a crime, prompted the LAPD to start a threat assessment unit, and led to limits on public access to DMV records.
