Obsessed fan Robert John Bardo, who found her address through a private investigator using DMV records, was convicted of first-degree murder with lying in wait in Oct. 1991 and sentenced to life without parole. The case led to the nation's first anti-stalking laws and DMV privacy limits.

cases.audioScript: In June 2014, nineteen-year-old Erin Corwin, the wife of a Marine stationed at Twentynine Palms, California, did not come home from a trip toward Joshua Tree National Park. Her husband reported her missing on June 28. Investigators said she and her next-door neighbor on the base, Marine Christopher Brandon Lee, were having an affair, and she was pregnant with his child. Friends said Lee had told her he was taking her into the desert for a surprise, and she thought he might propose. For nearly two months people searched, and prosecutors said Lee told detectives he had no idea where she was. On August 16, 2014, searchers found her body in an abandoned mine shaft outside Twentynine Palms. A day later Lee was arrested in Alaska, where his family had moved after his discharge. At trial in 2016, Lee admitted strangling her and putting her body in the shaft. A jury convicted him of first-degree murder with a lying-in-wait enhancement, and he was sentenced to life without parole.

Her body was found in an abandoned desert mine shaft on Aug. 16, 2014; neighbor and Marine Christopher Brandon Lee, with whom she was having an affair, was arrested in Alaska the next day. Lee admitted the strangling at trial, was convicted of first-degree murder with lying in wait, and was sentenced to life without parole on Nov. 29, 2016.

cases.audioScript: In May 2004, fifty-three-year-old Oakey Albert Kite Junior, known as Al, was living alone in his townhouse in Aurora, Colorado. That month he rented a room to a man who called himself Robert Cooper. The man said he was from the East Coast and worked for Wells Fargo Bank. On May twenty-fourth, 2004, Al was found dead in the basement of his home. He had been bound, beaten, tortured and stabbed. His wallet and cell phone were missing. Afterward, an unidentified man tried to use Al's debit card at an ATM. Investigators learned that the name, identification and contact information on the renter's application were false. The man who called himself Robert Cooper is the primary suspect, and he has never been identified. Witnesses described him as a white man, about five foot ten, around one hundred seventy to one hundred eighty pounds, with brown or black hair, and possibly an Eastern European accent. No one has been charged. If you rented a room to, worked with, or knew a man using the name Robert Cooper in 2004, contact Aurora police or the FBI.

An unidentified man attempted to use his debit card at an ATM afterward. A man who rented a room from Kite shortly before the murder, identifying himself as "Robert Cooper," claimed to be from the East Coast and to work for Wells Fargo Bank, and gave false identification and contact information on his rental application; he is the primary suspect. Witnesses described him as a white male, about 5'10", 170-180 lbs, brown or black hair, possibly with an Eastern European accent. The FBI ViCAP bulletin gives the discovery date as May 25, 2004; the CBI listing and Oxygen give May 24, which is used here. The case is listed by the Colorado Bureau of Investigation and remains unsolved. "Robert Cooper" is an alias of an unidentified person, not a real person's name, which is why it is recorded. cases.audioScript: On December twentieth, 1984, twelve-year-old Jonelle Matthews sang in a Christmas concert with her middle school honor choir in Greeley, Colorado. A friend's father dropped her off at home around eight that night. She was never seen alive again. For thirty-four years, Jonelle's disappearance haunted Greeley. Then, in July 2019, a pipeline crew digging in a field in rural Weld County found human remains. The coroner identified them as Jonelle. A forensic pathologist ruled her death a homicide. Police named a man who had lived about two miles from her, Steven Pankey, as a person of interest. In October 2020, a grand jury indicted him. His first trial ended with a hung jury on the main counts. At his second trial, in October 2022, a jury found him guilty of felony murder and kidnapping. A judge sentenced him to life in prison, with the possibility of parole after twenty years, under the law in place in 1984. Jonelle's parents and sister spoke in court. After almost thirty-eight years, they finally had answers about the girl who never came home from her Christmas concert.
cases.summary: Jonelle Matthews, 12, disappeared on Dec. 20, 1984, after performing in a Christmas concert with the Franklin Middle School Honor Choir in Greeley, Colorado. She was last seen about 8 p.m. when a friend and the friend's father dropped her off at home (Greeley Tribune). On July 23, 2019, a pipeline excavation crew found human remains near Weld County Roads 49 and 34 1/2; the Weld County Coroner identified them as Jonelle and a forensic pathologist determined she was a homicide victim (Greeley PD). Steven Dana Pankey was identified as a person of interest and then a suspect. A Weld County grand jury indicted him on Oct. 9, 2020, and he was arrested (Greeley PD; Greeley Tribune). His first trial in 2021 ended in a mistrial on most counts, though he was convicted of false reporting (Denver7). On Oct. 31, 2022, a jury found him guilty of felony murder and second-degree kidnapping; it found him not guilty of first-degree (after deliberation) murder. Judge Timothy G. Kerns sentenced him to life in prison with the possibility of parole after 20 years, under the statute in effect at the time of the crime (Denver7).
cases.solvedHow: Remains recovered by chance during 2019 pipeline excavation reopened the case as a homicide; Greeley PD and the Weld DA took evidence to a grand jury, which indicted Pankey. Convicted at a second trial.

cases.audioScript: In March 2023, forty-three-year-old Angela Craig, a mother of six here in Aurora, kept getting sick. Dizziness, vomiting, fainting, and doctors could not figure out why. She went to the hospital again and again. On March eighteenth, she died. Toxicology showed lethal levels of cyanide and tetrahydrozoline, the active ingredient in some eye drops, in her system. Prosecutors said her husband, dentist James Craig, had been poisoning her workout smoothies, and gave her a final dose of cyanide after she was already in the hospital. Investigators found searches for poisons and orders placed from a computer at his dental practice. He was arrested days after her death. From jail, prosecutors said, he offered another inmate money to kill the lead detective. His defense said Angela took her own life. The jury rejected that. On July thirtieth, 2025, James Craig was convicted of first-degree murder and sentenced to life without parole, plus thirty-three years. Two of Angela's children spoke in court. Her family said she was, most of all, a mother who loved her kids.
cases.summary: Angela Craig, 43, of Aurora, Colorado, a mother of six, suffered days of unexplained illness in March 2023, including dizziness, vomiting and fainting, and was in and out of the hospital. She died March 18, 2023; her cause of death was lethal doses of cyanide and tetrahydrozoline, the active ingredient in some eye drops, and prosecutors said arsenic was also used. Prosecutors said her husband, Aurora dentist James Craig, poisoned her through workout smoothies and gave her a final fatal dose of cyanide after she had been admitted to the hospital on March 15. Evidence at trial included toxicology results, more than 1,000 hours of surveillance video, searches for poisons and orders placed through a computer at his dental practice, and a note on his phone that prosecutors said staged a false suicide narrative. Prosecutors cited a struggling dental practice, about $4 million in life insurance with him as sole beneficiary, and extramarital affairs as motive. Craig was arrested shortly after her death; while jailed, he offered an inmate $20,000 to kill the lead investigator, Aurora police Det. Bobbi Olson, and offered money for false testimony that his wife planned suicide. On July 30, 2025, after more than 10 days of testimony and 48 witnesses at the Arapahoe County Courthouse, a jury convicted him of first-degree murder and solicitation charges, rejecting the defense claim that he helped her die by suicide. Judge Shay Whitaker sentenced him the same day to life in prison without parole, plus 33 consecutive years on the other counts.

cases.audioScript: Just after noon on October thirteenth, 2021, letter carrier Jason Schaefer was delivering mail at a row of mailboxes here in Longmont. He was thirty-three, a father, and well loved by his family and co-workers. A woman walked up and shot him three times. Prosecutors say it was his ex-girlfriend, Devan Schreiner, the mother of his child. Two days earlier, Jason had filed court papers asking for primary custody of their child. Postal inspectors and Longmont police tracked Schreiner's movements and arrested her the same day. In March 2023, a Boulder County jury found her guilty of first-degree murder, and she was sentenced to life without parole. Prosecutors said her boyfriend, a federal corrections officer named Andrew Ritchie, helped plan the killing and tracked Jason's route. A jury convicted him too, but in October 2026 an appeals court threw out that conviction and ordered a new trial. Ritchie is charged, his retrial is pending, and he is presumed innocent.
cases.summary: Jason Schaefer, 33, a U.S. Postal Service letter carrier, was shot three times at about 12:30 p.m. on Oct. 13, 2021, while delivering mail near Heatherhill Street and Renaissance Drive in Longmont, Colorado. Postal inspectors learned he and his ex-girlfriend Devan Schreiner, the mother of his child, were in a custody dispute, and that two days earlier he had filed for primary custody. The investigation placed Schreiner near the scene, and postal inspectors and Longmont police arrested her later that day. According to an affidavit, Schreiner had been fired from the Longmont post office two weeks earlier after a dispute with Schaefer, and USPS GPS tracking of her and her postal vehicle stopped during the time of the shooting. In March 2023, a Boulder County jury convicted Schreiner, then 27, of first-degree murder after about eight hours of deliberation, and Judge Patrick Butler sentenced her immediately to life without parole. Prosecutors alleged that her boyfriend, Andrew "AJ" Ritchie, a federal correctional officer, helped plan the killing and tracked Schaefer's route; a September 2023 jury verdict against him was later overturned. On Oct. 22, 2026, a three-judge Colorado Court of Appeals panel overturned that verdict because a juror who had said she could not be fair was allowed to stay on the jury, and ordered a new trial. Ritchie is charged, his retrial is pending, and he is presumed innocent.

cases.audioScript: Early on December twenty-sixth, 1996, in Boulder, Colorado, Patsy Ramsey found a ransom note saying her six-year-old daughter, JonBenet, had been kidnapped. She called nine one one, and Boulder police arrived within minutes. The note demanded one hundred eighteen thousand dollars. Hours later, JonBenet was found dead in the basement of the family's home. An autopsy found she had been strangled, and she had suffered a blow to the head. In 2008, touch DNA testing found an unknown male's DNA on her clothing, matching DNA found earlier, and it did not belong to any member of the Ramsey family. Investigators have pursued a number of potential suspects, persons of interest and theories over the years, but no one has ever been convicted. Police say detectives have followed more than twenty-one thousand tips, and in 2026 investigators began retesting old evidence with newer DNA technology. If you know anything, call the Boulder Police tip line at 303-441-1974.

cases.audioScript: Early on February eleventh, 1987, a bicyclist found thirty-seven-year-old Peggy Hettrick in an open field on Landings Drive in Fort Collins, Colorado. She had been stabbed in the upper back and mutilated, and investigators believe she was killed early that morning. According to the state's cold case file, she was born on March first, 1949, and had blue eyes and red, auburn hair. In 1999, authorities arrested a man for her murder, and he was convicted and sent to prison. But in 2008, DNA testing overturned that conviction and pointed to another, unknown suspect, and he was freed. No one else has ever been charged. Her case remains unsolved, and the Colorado Attorney General's Office says the investigation continues. The Larimer County Coroner still lists her death among the county's open, unsolved homicides. If you know anything about the murder of Peggy Hettrick, call the Colorado Attorney General's tip line at 303-866-5479.

The case remains unsolved and open with the Colorado Attorney General's Office.

cases.audioScript: On the morning of May twenty-fourth, 2019, Jennifer Dulos, a fifty-year-old mother of five here in New Canaan, Connecticut, dropped her children off at school. It was the last time anyone heard from her. She and her estranged husband, Fotis Dulos, were in a bitter divorce and custody battle. Investigators later found clothing and sponges with Jennifer's blood in trash cans in Hartford, where cameras recorded a man appearing to be Fotis dumping bags. In January 2020, Connecticut State Police charged Fotis Dulos with murder and kidnapping, and charged his girlfriend, Michelle Troconis, with conspiracy. Weeks later, Fotis Dulos died after a suicide attempt, before he could stand trial. In 2024, a jury convicted Michelle Troconis of conspiracy to commit murder, and she was sentenced to fourteen and a half years in prison. Jennifer's body has never been found. Her case led Connecticut to expand its legal definition of domestic violence. Anyone with information about where Jennifer is can contact Connecticut State Police.
cases.summary: Jennifer Farber Dulos, 50, a New Canaan mother of five, vanished on May 24, 2019; police said she was last heard from while dropping her children at school. She and her estranged husband, Fotis Dulos, were in a contentious divorce and custody battle. Court documents described clothes and sponges with her blood found in Hartford trash cans, where surveillance cameras captured a man appearing to be Fotis Dulos disposing of bags. On Jan. 7, 2020, Connecticut State Police charged Fotis Dulos with capital murder, murder and kidnapping; his girlfriend Michelle Troconis and his friend, attorney Kent Mawhinney, were charged with conspiracy to commit murder. Fotis Dulos died on Jan. 30, 2020, two days after a suicide attempt, before trial. Troconis was convicted in 2024 on six counts including conspiracy to commit murder and on May 31, 2024 was sentenced to 14 1/2 years to serve. In June 2025 prosecutors dropped the conspiracy charge against Mawhinney; he pleaded guilty to misdemeanor interfering with an officer, with time served. Jennifer Dulos's body has never been found.

cases.audioScript: On the night of October thirtieth, 1975, fifteen-year-old Martha Moxley was out with friends in her Greenwich, Connecticut neighborhood. It was Mischief Night, the night before Halloween, when kids roam the neighborhood pulling pranks. The next day, October thirty-first, she was found dead beneath a tree in the backyard of her family's home. She had been beaten to death with a golf club. The case set off a national media frenzy and a stalled police investigation. In 2002, a man was convicted of her murder. But a judge later ruled he had been denied a fair trial, and in 2018 the Connecticut Supreme Court vacated the conviction. In 2020, the state dropped the case, saying it could not prove it beyond a reasonable doubt. Fifty years later, there is still no definitive answer to who killed Martha Moxley. No one stands convicted of her death today, and the case remains unsolved.

cases.audioScript: On June first, 2012, nineteen-year-old Natanalie Perez, known to her family as Naty, was last seen at a motel on Southwest Eighth Street in Miami, where she was believed to be living. She had grown up and graduated from high school in Sebring, Florida, and moved to South Florida to live with a friend. Her family says she had stopped calling and texting the way she used to, and her phone went straight to voicemail. In the fall of 2012, Miami police told reporters she may have been seen at the Dolphin Mall as recently as August, and her mother and aunt handed out flyers alongside a Miami police detective. That lead did not bring her home. Her family has said they believe she was being exploited by people who controlled her, but no one has been charged. The National Center for Missing and Exploited Children has released an age-progressed photo, and notes she may be with a man. Naty has a tattoo on her left wrist. If you have seen Natanalie Marie Perez, call the Miami Police Department at three oh five, six oh three, sixty-three hundred, or NCMEC at one eight hundred, the lost.

cases.audioScript: In January 2006, twenty-four-year-old Jennifer Kesse was living in a condo off south Orlando in Orlando, Florida. On Tuesday, January twenty-fourth, she did not show up for work, and she was reported missing. Her car, a black 2004 Chevy Malibu, was found days later, abandoned about a mile away at another complex. Surveillance video showed a person parking her car and walking away, but the camera captured only one frame every three seconds, and a fence post blocked the person's face. For years, that grainy image was the only significant lead. Her family sued Orlando police for access to the case file. In 2022, the Florida Department of Law Enforcement took over the investigation. Agents have conducted more than one hundred fifteen interviews, reviewed tens of thousands of documents, and re-examined evidence, and her father says DNA is being retested with modern methods. No one has ever been arrested. If you have information, call the FDLE Orlando office at 407-245-0888, or email O R O C Cold Case Tips at fdle dot state dot f l dot u s.
cases.summary: Jennifer Kesse, 24, of Orlando, did not show up for work on Jan. 24, 2006, and was reported missing; Solve the Case reports her last phone contact was the night before. She was last seen leaving her apartment in south Orlando. Her black 2004 Chevrolet Malibu was found days later at another complex about a mile away. Surveillance video recorded an unidentified person parking the car and walking away; the camera took one frame every three seconds and a fence post blocked the face in every image. Her family sued the Orlando Police Department for the investigative records. FDLE assumed the case in 2022 and reports more than 115 interviews and tens of thousands of documents reviewed. No arrests have been made.

cases.audioScript: On Friday, February nineteenth, 1993, twelve-year-old Jennifer Renee Odom stepped off her school bus around three in the afternoon in rural Pasco County, Florida, near the town of Dade City. She waved goodbye to friends and started walking the short two hundred yards toward home. Children still on the bus later told investigators they saw a faded blue pickup truck slowly following her. Jennifer never made it home. For six days, officers and volunteers searched about sixty square miles of groves and woods. On February twenty-fifth, a man and a woman found her body in an abandoned orange grove in southeast Hernando County. Her book bag and clarinet case turned up nearly two years later, on January fifth, 1995, in western Hernando County. The case stayed open for more than thirty years. In 2015, a familial DNA search in a related 1992 Pasco County case led investigators to Jeffrey Norman Crum, already serving life sentences in that earlier case. He was indicted in July 2023 for Jennifer's murder, kidnapping and sexual battery. On August twentieth, 2026, a Hernando County jury found him guilty of those charges after a four-day trial. Five days later, on what would have been Jennifer's forty-sixth birthday, the same jury unanimously recommended the death penalty. A judge was still to impose sentence.
cases.summary: Jennifer Renee Odom, 12, born Aug. 25, 1980, disappeared on Friday, Feb. 19, 1993, after stepping off her school bus around 3 p.m. in a rural area of Pasco County near Dade City and starting a roughly 200-yard walk home. Children on the bus reported a faded blue pickup truck slowly following her; she never arrived home. Law enforcement and volunteers searched about 60 square miles of groves, pastures and woods around Dade City. On Feb. 25, 1993, a man and a woman found her body in an abandoned orange grove in southeast Hernando County. Her clothing, including a red sweater and a Hooters jacket, was not found. On Jan. 5, 1995, a couple hunting for scrap metal found her book bag and clarinet case in western Hernando County. The investigation remained open for more than three decades as investigators pursued hundreds of leads and applied new forensic methods. Investigators identified similarities between Jennifer's case and a January 1992 attack on another teenage girl in Pasco County. Jeffrey Norman Crum was later convicted in that earlier case, sentenced to life in prison in 2019, and was serving two life sentences. The living survivor of the 1992 case is not named here. A DNA breakthrough in the 1992 Pasco County case in 2015, including a familial DNA search, helped investigators identify a member of Crum's family and ultimately led them to Crum in the Hernando County case, along with evidence about his ownership of a blue truck and familiarity with the area where Jennifer was taken and found. A Hernando County grand jury indicted Crum on July 24, 2023, on first-degree murder, kidnapping and sexual battery; State Attorney Bill Gladson announced the indictment on July 27, 2023. After a four-day trial, a Hernando County jury on Aug. 20, 2026, found Crum guilty of kidnapping, sexual battery and murder. Jurors deliberated about five hours. On Aug. 25, 2026, which would have been Jennifer's 46th birthday, the same jury unanimously recommended the death penalty (FOX 13 reported a 12-0 vote after about two hours and 15 minutes). The State Attorney's Office said a Spencer hearing was scheduled for Oct. 21, 2026, and that the recommendation is not the final sentence. No official release confirming a final sentence was found in sources checked Nov. 26, 2026.
cases.solvedHow: Solved by conviction in August 2026. Investigators spent more than three decades pursuing leads and retesting evidence. They identified similarities to a January 1992 attack on another teenage girl in Pasco County. A 2015 familial DNA search in that Pasco case led investigators to Jeffrey Norman Crum, who was later convicted in the earlier case and was serving two life sentences. Investigators developed additional evidence tying him to Jennifer's disappearance, including his ownership of a blue truck and familiarity with the area. He was indicted on July 24, 2023, and a Hernando County jury convicted him on Aug. 20, 2026, after a four-day trial.

A 17-year-old girl is attacked in Pasco County in a case the State Attorney later described as having very similar facts to Jennifer's. (The living survivor is not named in this file.)

About 3 p.m.: Jennifer steps off her school bus in rural Pasco County near Dade City, waves goodbye to friends, and starts walking about 200 yards toward home. Children on the bus report a faded blue pickup slowly following her. She does not arrive home.
A search begins, involving law enforcement, police dogs and community volunteers across about 60 square miles of rural Pasco and Hernando counties around Dade City.
A man and a woman find Jennifer's body in an abandoned orange grove in southeast Hernando County. Her clothing is not found with her.
A couple hunting for scrap metal find Jennifer's missing book bag and clarinet case in western Hernando County.
A familial DNA search in the 1992 Pasco County case helps investigators identify a member of Crum's family and ultimately leads them to Crum in the Hernando County investigation.
Crum is convicted in Pasco County and sentenced to life in prison in the January 1992 sexual-battery case; he was serving two life sentences by the time of the 2023 indictment.
A Hernando County grand jury indicts Jeffrey Norman Crum on one count each of first-degree murder, kidnapping and sexual battery of Jennifer Odom.
State Attorney Bill Gladson announces the indictment. The Hernando County Sheriff's Office releases a 1993 photograph of Crum and asks the public for information through Detective George Loydgren.

After a four-day trial, a Hernando County jury finds Crum guilty of kidnapping, sexual battery and murder. The State Attorney's Office publishes a verdict release the same day (WUSF, published Aug. 21, says jurors deliberated about five hours).

The same jury unanimously recommends the death penalty, on what would have been Jennifer's 46th birthday. The State Attorney schedules a Spencer hearing for Oct. 21, 2026, and notes that the recommendation is not the final sentence.

A Spencer hearing for Crum was scheduled at 8:30 a.m. (State Attorney, Aug. 25, 2026). No official Fifth Circuit release confirming that the hearing was held or that a final sentence was imposed was found in sources checked Nov. 26, 2026.

cases.audioScript: In the early hours of January fifteenth, 1978, a man slipped into the Chi Omega sorority house near Florida State University in Tallahassee. Within minutes, two members, twenty-year-old Lisa Levy and twenty-one-year-old Margaret Bowman, had been beaten and strangled in their beds. Two other women in the house were badly hurt but survived, and blocks away another student was attacked in her apartment that same night and survived. Less than a month later, a Pensacola police officer stopped a stolen Volkswagen and, after a struggle, arrested the driver. Days later, the man revealed his true identity: Ted Bundy, a fugitive who had escaped jail in Colorado. One of the key pieces of evidence at trial was a bite mark on Lisa Levy, which a forensic dentist matched to Bundy's distinctive teeth. The trial was held in Miami, and on July twenty-fourth, 1979, the jury found him guilty of both murders. He was sentenced to death, and in 1980 was also convicted of murdering twelve-year-old Kimberly Leach. Bundy was executed in Florida's electric chair on January twenty-fourth, 1989, after confessing to killings in several states.
cases.summary: On Jan. 15, 1978, Ted Bundy entered the Chi Omega sorority house near Florida State University and killed Lisa Levy, 20, and Margaret Bowman, 21; two other residents were injured and survived. Shortly afterward he broke into a nearby apartment and attacked another FSU student, who survived. He was arrested by Pensacola police on Feb. 15, 1978 driving a stolen car and later revealed his identity. Bite-mark evidence matched to his teeth was key at trial; a Miami jury convicted him on July 24, 1979. He was executed Jan. 24, 1989.
cases.solvedHow: Solved after a Pensacola traffic stop of a stolen Volkswagen on Feb. 15, 1978 led to Bundy's arrest and identification; forensic bite-mark comparison and eyewitness testimony supported the 1979 conviction.

cases.audioScript: In December 2000, Mike Williams of Tallahassee, Florida, went duck hunting on Lake Seminole and never came home. For years it looked like a tragic hunting accident. Then in 2016, the case broke open, when his widow's next husband was arrested for kidnapping her. That man was sentenced to twenty years in prison, and in October 2017, in exchange for immunity, he confessed. He told investigators he had lured Mike on the hunting trip and shot and drowned him, and that he and Mike's wife Denise had been having an affair. He said they planned to make it look like an accident, so they could be together and collect on Mike's life insurance. A jury convicted Denise Williams of conspiracy, first-degree murder and accessory after the fact. In November 2020, an appeals court threw out the murder conviction, but the conspiracy conviction stood. On September ninth, 2021, a judge resentenced her to thirty years in prison for conspiring to murder her first husband.
cases.summary: Mike Williams disappeared in December 2000 on a duck-hunting trip at Lake Seminole; it was initially treated as an accident. In October 2017, a man who had married Williams' widow confessed under an immunity agreement that he lured Williams on the trip and shot and drowned him; he said he and Denise Williams planned it to be together and collect life insurance. Denise Williams was convicted of conspiracy, first-degree murder and accessory; the murder conviction was reversed in Nov. 2020, and on Sept. 9, 2021 she was resentenced to 30 years for conspiracy.

cases.audioScript: In 2006, Abraham Shakespeare of Lakeland, Florida, won a thirty-million-dollar lottery prize and took a seventeen-million-dollar lump sum. He gave away much of the money to people who simply asked for it. Dorice DeeDee Moore befriended him and agreed to manage what was left, but prosecutors said she stole his winnings instead. She formed a company in his name and gave herself control of its funds. Shakespeare, forty-seven, was shot twice in the chest with a thirty-eight caliber pistol sometime in April 2009. He was not reported missing until November. Authorities said Moore used his cellphone to send texts that seemed to come from him, and offered someone a house to report a false sighting. In January 2010 his body was found under a concrete slab behind a home in the Plant City area. Jurors also saw Walmart video of Moore buying gloves, duct tape and plastic sheeting, items detectives later found near the burial site. On December tenth, 2012, a jury convicted her of first-degree murder after about three hours of deliberation, and she was sentenced to life without parole. A judge later denied her request for a new trial.
cases.summary: Abraham Shakespeare, 47, of Lakeland, Florida, who won a $30 million lottery prize in 2006, was shot twice in the chest in April 2009. His body was found in January 2010 under a concrete slab at a home in the Plant City (Turkey Creek) area. Dorice "DeeDee" Moore, who had taken control of his money, was convicted of first-degree murder on Dec. 10, 2012 and sentenced to life without parole.
cases.solvedHow: Detective work and trial: Polk County detectives traced false contacts made in the victim's name, recovered his body under a concrete slab, and tied Moore to it through financial evidence, witnesses and store video; a jury convicted her in 2012.

cases.audioScript: On the evening of October 14, 1965, twenty-five-year-old Mary Shotwell Little, a secretary at Citizens and Southern Bank in Atlanta and a newlywed of six weeks, met a coworker for dinner and shopping at Lenox Square in Buckhead. They parted around 8 p.m. She never arrived at work the next day. Police found her 1965 Mercury Comet in the mall parking lot with blood specks on the interior and exterior, a coating of red dust, and some of her clothing. The odometer showed about forty miles that could not be accounted for. About a month later, investigators said her gasoline credit card had been used at stations in Charlotte and, later that day, in Raleigh, North Carolina. The Atlanta Police Department, the FBI, and the Georgia Bureau of Investigation all worked the case. An Atlanta police spokesman said a 2009-2010 review, and another review in January 2014, found no progress. A 2025 news report marked sixty years with the case still unsolved. No one has been charged. Mary Shotwell Little has never been found.
cases.summary: Mary Shotwell Little, 25, a secretary at Citizens and Southern (C&S) Bank in Atlanta, vanished on October 14, 1965, after dinner and shopping with a coworker at Lenox Square in the Buckhead district. She had married in September 1965, about six weeks earlier, and was originally from the Charlotte, North Carolina, area; the Charlotte Observer identified her as a Myers Park High School graduate. Atlanta News First and the DeKalb History Center report that the two women parted at the mall around 8 p.m. She did not show up for work the next morning. Police were called, and officers found her 1965 Mercury Comet in the Lenox Square parking lot. News accounts of what was found in and on the car agree on bloodstains or blood specks, including on the interior and, in some reports, the exterior or door area; the Charlotte Observer also reported a set of women's undergarments inside, and Atlanta News First described undergarments covered in blood and some kind of red dust on the car. Atlanta News First, consistent with a 2023 DeKalb History Center account, reported about 40 unaccounted-for miles on the odometer. The DeKalb History Center, citing period reporting, also wrote that groceries from the previous evening were still in the back seat and that security rounds had not seen the car in that section of the lot earlier that morning; those two details are not independently repeated in the other news pages fetched for this file and are treated cautiously. In November 1965, investigators announced that her signature was on gasoline credit-card receipts from a purchase in Charlotte early on October 15 and another later that afternoon in Raleigh. WSB-TV reported in 2015, at the 50-year mark, that the case had been investigated by the FBI, the GBI, and Atlanta homicide detectives, and that it remained unsolved; her car had been found the next day with her blood inside it and on the door knob, and she had not been seen since. WSB-TV also reported that many case files had been lost over the years; that a retired detective, Ray Pate, who was not assigned to the case in 1965, later compiled FBI materials; and that the GBI had executed a search warrant in Forsyth County about 20 years before that 2015 report, after a tip, and found nothing. The Charlotte Observer quoted an Atlanta Police Department spokesman in 2014 as saying that an investigator had reviewed the file as recently as January of that year and validated her as an official missing person, and that a missing-persons investigator in the homicide unit had done a full review in 2009-2010, 'unfortunately, no progress in the case was made.' The same 2014 article and the 2015 WSB-TV report discussed unofficial theories, including a possible connection to the later murder of Diane Shields, another C&S Bank employee, and a 1966 prison inmate's account involving a location in Mount Holly, North Carolina; the Observer reported that FBI agents concluded the inmate's story was not credible. Those theories have not produced charges and are not treated as facts here. A DeKalb History Center essay published in October 2023 said there had been no new leads in decades. On October 14, 2025, Atlanta News First reported on the 60th anniversary and on a documentary about the still-unsolved disappearance. No one has been charged. Mary Shotwell Little has never been found.

cases.audioScript: Between 1979 and 1981, here in Atlanta, some twenty-nine young Black children, teens and young adults were killed, and the city lived in fear. By the spring of 1981, investigators noticed bodies being left in the Chattahoochee River, so a task force staked out the bridges across it. Before dawn on May twenty-second, a stakeout team heard a loud splash and stopped a car coming off the bridge. The driver was twenty-three-year-old Wayne Williams. Two days later, the body of Nathaniel Cater was found downstream. Williams was arrested in June 1981, and charged with murdering two adults, Nathaniel Cater and Jimmy Ray Payne. In February 1982, after testimony about hair and fiber evidence, a jury found him guilty of both murders, and he received two life sentences. Williams was never charged in any of the children's deaths. The FBI says a task force concluded the evidence linked him to twenty more of the cases, but he has always said he is innocent. In 2019, Atlanta reopened the evidence, hoping to give the children's families answers.
cases.summary: From July 1979 to the spring of 1981, some 29 young African Americans, most of them children, were killed in Atlanta, a series the FBI code-named ATKID and that became known as the Atlanta child murders. A task force of the Atlanta Police Department, the Georgia Bureau of Investigation and the FBI staked out the 14 bridges across the Chattahoochee River after bodies began appearing in the river. At about 2:52 a.m. on May 22, 1981, a surveillance team heard a loud splash and stopped a car crossing the bridge; the driver, 23-year-old Wayne Williams, was let go for lack of probable cause. Two days later, the body of Nathaniel Cater was found downstream. Williams was arrested June 21, 1981, and charged with the murders of Cater and Jimmy Ray Payne, both adults found in the Chattahoochee River. On Feb. 27, 1982, a jury found him guilty of both murders after hair and fiber evidence, including fibers linked to his home and car and dog hairs, and witness testimony; he received two consecutive life sentences. The Supreme Court of Georgia affirmed the convictions in 1983, noting the state had introduced evidence of ten other alleged murders to help establish identity. Williams was never charged in any of the child killings; the FBI says the task force concluded evidence linked him to 20 other deaths, but he maintains his innocence, and in 2019 Atlanta officials began re-examining the evidence to give the families answers.

cases.audioScript: On New Year's Day 2008, twenty-four-year-old Meredith Emerson went hiking with her black Lab, Ella, in the north Georgia mountains near Blood Mountain. She never came home. A sixty-one-year-old drifter named Gary Michael Hilton had abducted her on the trail, intending to drain her bank accounts. Prosecutors said Meredith fought him physically, and then fought with her wits, feeding him wrong PIN numbers for her cards to buy time. Hilton was the last person seen with her on the trail, and he had tried to use her credit card, according to his arrest warrant. On January fourth he killed her, and her body was found nearly fifty miles from where she vanished. On January thirty-first, 2008, Hilton pleaded guilty in Dawson County and was sentenced to life without parole. As part of the plea he led authorities to her remains, and in exchange prosecutors did not seek the death penalty. At the time, investigators in North Carolina and Florida were also looking at him in other killings.
cases.summary: Meredith Emerson, 24, was abducted on Jan. 1, 2008 while hiking with her dog near Blood Mountain in north Georgia. Gary Michael Hilton held her for days trying to get money from her accounts; she gave him wrong PIN numbers. He killed her on Jan. 4. Hilton was the last person seen with her and had tried to use her credit card. He pleaded guilty Jan. 31, 2008 in Dawson County Superior Court and was sentenced to life without parole; the plea spared him the death penalty. In April 2011 he was convicted and sentenced to death in Leon County, Florida, for the murder of Cheryl Dunlap. In March 2012 he pleaded guilty in federal court in North Carolina to the October 2007 kidnapping and murders of John and Irene Bryant, and on April 25, 2013 he received four federal life sentences, to be served consecutively with his Georgia and Florida sentences.

cases.audioScript: Early on the morning of June twenty-seventh, 1995, twenty-seven-year-old Jodi Huisentruit overslept for the first time. She was the morning anchor at KIMT-TV in Mason City, Iowa. When her producer called around four a.m., Jodi said she'd be right in. She never arrived. When police went to check on her, they found her car in the parking lot of her apartment building, and her things scattered around it: red high heels, a hair dryer, hair spray, earrings, and her car key, bent. Neighbors later said they had heard a scream. There were no cameras and no witnesses. Jodi has not been seen since. She was declared legally dead in 2001. Mason City police and the Iowa Division of Criminal Investigation say the case is anything but cold. Tips still come in, sometimes every day, and detectives travel to follow them. No one has been charged. If you know something, call Mason City police at 641-421-3636.
cases.summary: Jodi Huisentruit, 27, a morning anchor at KIMT-TV in Mason City, Iowa, vanished early on June 27, 1995. Her producer called her at about 4 a.m. when she had not arrived; she said she had overslept and would be right in (CNN; Charley Project). When she still had not arrived, police were asked to check on her. At her apartment complex parking lot they found her car and her belongings scattered around it, including red shoes, a hair dryer, hair spray, earrings and a bent car key (CNN; KCRG; Charley Project). Neighbors reported hearing a scream (Charley Project). She was declared legally dead in May 2001 (Charley Project). The Mason City Police Department and Iowa DCI continue to investigate; in 2026 the lead investigator said tips arrive weekly or even daily and that he had followed leads in about five states in the past year (KGLO). In 2025 a judge unsealed a 2017 search warrant concerning a person of interest who has since died; police said nothing useful came from it (KCRG). No one has been charged.

cases.audioScript: On the night of June ninth, 1912, in the small southwestern Iowa town of Villisca, eight people were killed with an axe inside a private home. The dead were Josiah Moore, his wife Sarah, their four children — Herman, Mary Katherine, Arthur Boyd, and Paul — and two young guests, sisters Ina and Lena Stillinger. They were found the next day. The crime has never been solved, and no one has ever been convicted. A traveling minister, Reverend George Kelly, was later charged, tried twice, and acquitted. More than a century later, the axe itself is kept by the Montgomery County History Center in nearby Red Oak, where it has been placed on public exhibit. Villisca still lives with the question of who walked through that house in the dark and killed eight neighbors, six of them children, and why. More than a hundred years later, it remains one of the most famous unsolved murders in Iowa history.
cases.summary: Between the evening of June 9, 1912, and the early morning of June 10, eight people were killed with an axe in a private residence in Villisca, Montgomery County, Iowa. The victims were Josiah B. Moore, his wife Sarah, their four children, and two child guests, Ina and Lena Stillinger. A 2015 Iowa Legislature historical compilation and a 2024 Red Oak Express report quoting the Montgomery County History Center curator identify the children as Herman (Herman Montgomery), Mary (Mary Katherine), Arthur (Arthur Boyd), and Paul (Paul Vernon). The crime remains unsolved, and no one has been convicted. According to the 2015 official compilation, Reverend George Kelly was arrested in 1917, confessed after a long interrogation, recanted, was tried twice, and was acquitted. In 2024, the Red Oak Express reported that the Montgomery County History Center in Red Oak unveiled an exhibit of the axe used in the murders; the Freeman Journal reported in August 2026 that the axe is held by the Montgomery County Historical Society in Red Oak.
cases.solvedHow: Unsolved. No one has been convicted. Historical techniques reported in the sources used here include a local search of the residence, a lengthy investigation over the following years, grand-jury and courtroom proceedings, and two murder trials of Reverend George Kelly that ended without a conviction (hung jury, then acquittal), according to a 2015 Iowa Legislature historical compilation. Local news in 2024–2026 reports that the axe itself is now held and exhibited by the Montgomery County History Center in Red Oak. This build found no published current tip line or reward and no official report of modern DNA testing.
cases.techniques: Local scene response and search of the residence (historical); Multi-year investigation and courtroom proceedings; Murder trials (1917) ending in acquittal; Preservation and public exhibit of the axe

timeline.event: Between the evening of June 9 and the early morning of June 10, 1912, eight people were killed with an axe in a private residence in Villisca, Iowa: Josiah and Sarah Moore, their four children, and two child guests, Ina and Lena Stillinger.

The eight victims were found bludgeoned in the residence. The 2015 official compilation states they were discovered that morning after a neighbor and Josiah Moore’s brother could not raise the household, and that Villisca’s primary peace officer then searched the house.
The 2015 official compilation states that funeral services were held in Villisca’s town square and that the eight were buried at Villisca Cemetery; the cortege was described as 50 carriages long.

According to the 2015 official compilation, traveling minister Reverend George Kelly was arrested for the murders in 1917, gave a confession after many hours of interrogation, later recanted, was tried twice, and was acquitted after a first trial ended in a hung jury.

The Red Oak Express reports that the Montgomery County History Center in Red Oak unveiled an exhibit of the axe used in the murders, still described as Iowa’s most famous unsolved murder. The curator lists the eight victims by full name.
The Freeman Journal reports that the murders have never been solved, that eight people were killed, and that the axe is held by the Montgomery County Historical Society in Red Oak.

evidence.item: Eight people were killed with an axe inside a private residence in Villisca; the crime remains unsolved and no one has been convicted.

The murder weapon, an axe, has been preserved and, as of 2024–2026, is exhibited or held by the Montgomery County History Center / Historical Society in Red Oak. The Freeman Journal, quoting researcher Edgar Epperly, said the axe had been in police hands.

The 2015 official compilation states that the axe belonged to Josiah Moore and was found in the guest room, and it describes wound patterns in graphic terms that are not repeated in this file out of respect for the victims.

cases.audioScript: On December nineteenth, 1979, eighteen-year-old Kennedy High School senior Michelle Martinko went to Westdale Mall in Cedar Rapids, Iowa, after a choir banquet. She left the mall alone that night. Early the next morning, police found her body in her parents' Buick in the parking lot. She had been stabbed twenty-nine times and had defensive wounds on her hands. Glove prints inside the car suggested the killer had driven it afterward. The case went cold for decades. In 2005, the state crime lab developed a partial male DNA profile from a bloodstain on her dress. In 2018, genetic genealogy pointed police to a family of brothers from Manchester, Iowa. Police retrieved a straw one of them, Jerry Burns, left at a Pizza Ranch, and its DNA matched the dress. Burns was arrested on December nineteenth, 2018, the anniversary of her death. A jury convicted him of first-degree murder in 2020, and he was sentenced to life without parole. In 2023 the Iowa Supreme Court upheld the conviction, ruling he had abandoned the straw.
cases.summary: Michelle Martinko, 18, was stabbed to death in her parents' car at Westdale Mall in Cedar Rapids on Dec. 19, 1979. In 2018 genetic genealogy and DNA from a discarded straw matched Jerry Burns to blood on her dress; he was arrested Dec. 19, 2018. He was convicted of first-degree murder in 2020 and sentenced to life without parole; the Iowa Supreme Court affirmed in 2023.
cases.solvedHow: Genetic genealogy and abandoned DNA: Parabon genealogy narrowed the suspect pool to one family; DNA from a straw Burns discarded at a restaurant matched the dress, confirmed by a warrant swab; a jury convicted him in 2020.

cases.audioScript: In the late 1970s and early 1980s, the valley where Lewiston, Idaho, meets Clarkston and Asotin, Washington, lost four young people. On April twenty-eighth, 1979, twelve-year-old Christina White vanished in Asotin during the county fair. She had called her mother that afternoon to say she felt sick from the heat. Neither Christina nor her new white ten-speed bicycle was ever found. Then, on September twelfth, 1982, stepsisters Kristina Nelson, twenty-one, and Brandy Miller, eighteen, left Kristina's Lewiston apartment to walk to a grocery store. That same night, thirty-five-year-old Steven Pearsall was dropped off at the Lewiston Civic Theatre, where he worked, to do laundry and practice his clarinet. Police later found the clarinet. None of the three came home. In March 1984, the remains of Kristina and Brandy were found down a hillside off Highway 3, about forty miles from Lewiston. Steven has never been found. In 1995, Lewiston police said they believed one man was responsible, but no one has ever been charged, and no suspect is named here. If you remember anything about the fair in 1979 or the theater in 1982, police still want to hear from you.
cases.summary: Investigators in the Lewis-Clark Valley have long linked four cases. Christina Lee White, 12, vanished in Asotin, Washington, on April 28, 1979, during the Asotin County Fair; a source on Solve the Case (Asotin County Sheriff's case 1979-18) says she called her mother at about 2:30 p.m. from a friend's house to say she felt sick from the heat. She and her bicycle were never found. On Sept. 12, 1982, stepsisters Kristina Nelson, 21, and Jacqueline "Brandy" Miller, 18, walked toward a Lewiston grocery store and disappeared; the same night Steven Pearsall, 35, a janitor at the Lewiston Civic Theatre, was dropped off there around midnight and vanished. His clarinet was found at the theater. On March 19, 1984, the remains of Nelson and Miller were found down a hillside off Highway 3 near Kendrick, about 40 miles from Lewiston; the coroner ruled the deaths homicides. Pearsall has never been found. In January 1995, Lewiston police told The Spokesman-Review they were '99 percent certain' who was responsible for the four cases, but no one has been charged. That person is living as far as public sources show and is not named here. Kristin David's 1981 murder is often compared to these cases but is filed separately (US-ID-002). Tips: Asotin County Sheriff's Office, 509-243-4717, or the FBI at 1-800-CALL-FBI / tips.fbi.gov (People magazine).
cases.solvedHow: Unsolved. Police publicly described a single suspect in 1995 but said they lacked the evidence to charge; no arrest has been made.
cases.techniques: Interviews and polygraph requests (reported 1995); Public appeals and anniversary coverage

cases.audioScript: On the morning of Friday, June twenty-sixth, 1981, twenty-two-year-old Kristin David set out on her blue ten-speed bicycle from Moscow, Idaho. She was a senior at the University of Idaho, studying broadcast journalism and political science, and she planned to ride south on Highway 95 to Lewiston. Witnesses later told investigators they saw a woman matching her description being approached by a man in a brown van just outside the town of Genesee. On July fourth, her remains began to be found in and along the Snake River, about six miles west of Clarkston, Washington. They had been hidden in black plastic bags, and some were wrapped in pages from April 1981 editions of the local newspaper. Her bicycle and clothing were never found. The FBI describes the man in the van as white, about thirty, around five foot ten, stocky, with a beard, driving a well-kept brown van with yellow plates. In 2021, the FBI said evidence was being retested and that the case is not cold. No one has been charged. If you saw that van on Highway 95, contact the FBI at tips dot F B I dot gov.
cases.summary: Kristin Noel David, 22, a University of Idaho senior, left Moscow, Idaho, on her blue 10-speed bicycle on June 26, 1981, heading south on U.S. Highway 95 toward Lewiston. The FBI says multiple travelers that day saw a female cyclist matching her description being approached by a man driving a brown van on the southbound side of the highway just outside Genesee. On July 4, 1981, her dismembered remains began to be found in and along the Snake River about six miles west of Clarkston, Washington, just west of Silcott Island; more were found downriver the next day. The remains were in black plastic bags, and some were wrapped in pages from April 1981 editions of the local newspaper (Fox News identifies it as the Lewiston Morning Tribune). Her bicycle, clothing and personal items were never recovered. In June 2021 the FBI Salt Lake City office released a description of the suspect (white male, about 30, about 5'10", about 180 lbs, stocky, bearded) and his van (well-kept brown van with yellow plates with dark lettering), said evidence was being retested, and said the case was not considered cold. The investigation is joint with the Asotin County Sheriff's Office and Lewiston Police. Her case is often compared to the Lewis-Clark Valley cases (US-ID-001), but investigators have not publicly linked them. No one has been charged. Tips: FBI at tips.fbi.gov or 1-800-CALL-FBI (FBI Salt Lake City); the Whitman County Gazette also lists the Whitman County Sheriff's Office, 509-397-6266.

cases.audioScript: In June 2017, investigators in Canyon County, Idaho, found the bodies of three people hidden in a shed on a rural property near Caldwell that Mike Bullinger had recently bought. They were Cheryl Baker, fifty-six, Nadja Medley, forty-eight, and Nadja's fourteen-year-old daughter, Payton, all from Ogden, Utah. Each had been killed by a single gunshot. Cheryl was married to the property's owner, Gerald Michael Bullinger, known as Mike. According to news reports, Nadja believed she was engaged to him. Bullinger was gone. A car connected to him was later found abandoned at the Pacific Creek Campground in Wyoming, near Grand Teton National Park, and he was reported entering the park on June eleventh. In August 2017, after DNA confirmed the identities of Nadja and Payton, Canyon County charged Bullinger with three counts of first-degree murder. A massive search followed, but he has never been found. In 2018, the sheriff said he believed Bullinger was probably dead. He has not been convicted of any crime, and the case remains open. If you have information about Mike Bullinger, contact the Canyon County Sheriff's Office.
cases.summary: On June 19, 2017, three bodies were found in a shed on a recently purchased rural property near Caldwell, Idaho, belonging to Gerald Michael "Mike" Bullinger (Jackson Hole News&Guide). The coroner identified Cheryl Baker, 56 (some reports say 57), of Ogden, Utah, through dental records on June 30, and Nadja Medley, 48, and her daughter Payton Medley, 14, also of Ogden, through DNA; each was killed by a single gunshot (Idaho News 6; KUTV). Baker was married to Gerald Michael "Mike" Bullinger; Medley was reportedly engaged to him. A car connected to Bullinger was found abandoned at the Pacific Creek Campground in Teton County, Wyoming, and police said he was seen entering Grand Teton National Park on June 11 (Jackson Hole News&Guide). In August 2017, after the DNA results, Bullinger was charged with three counts of first-degree murder. He has never been located; in June 2018, Canyon County Sheriff Kieran Donahue said he was probably dead (Salt Lake Tribune). He has not been tried or convicted. Tips: Canyon County Sheriff's Office, 208-454-7510 (main line); if Bullinger is seen, do not approach and call 911 (Canyon County Sheriff's Office; EastIdahoNews).

cases.audioScript: On May twenty-ninth, 1984, thirty-one-year-old Linda Hatfield worked her shift at the Hunt Club in Garden City, Idaho. When she finished at one a.m., a bouncer walked her to her car and watched her drive off toward her home in Middleton. That was the last confirmed sighting of Linda. About an hour later, witnesses in Middleton reported seeing her T-Bird and another vehicle parked in the street, and they heard what sounded like a man and a woman arguing. At eight-thirty that morning, her car was found in a parking lot on South Curtis Road in Boise. By June fourth, investigators had found enough evidence to change her case from a missing person to a homicide. That November, her wallet and credit cards were found in the drained New York Canal. Linda's remains have never been found, and no one has been charged. In 2025, Ada County Sheriff's detectives said they were reanalyzing important evidence, and they want to know more about her missing wedding ring set and the night she disappeared. If you know anything, call the Ada County Sheriff's Office at 208-577-3102.
cases.summary: On May 29, 1984, Linda Hatfield, 31, worked her shift at the Hunt Club in Garden City, Idaho; when she finished at 1 a.m., a bouncer walked her to her car and watched her drive toward her home in Middleton, the last confirmed sighting. At about 2 a.m., witnesses in Middleton reported seeing her T-Bird and another vehicle parked in the street and hearing what they believed was a man and a woman arguing. At 8:30 a.m., her car was found in a parking lot in the 2700 block of S. Curtis Road in Boise; because she had not yet been reported missing, it was left there. After her husband reported her missing to the Canyon County Sheriff's Office on June 1, the Ada County Sheriff's Office and Boise Police processed the car, and by June 4, 1984, the case had been changed from a missing person case to a homicide. In November 1984, her wallet and credit cards were found in the recently drained New York Canal, and in June 1987 a court ruled there was clear and convincing evidence she was deceased. In 1988 a man told investigators she may have been set up to be robbed; the Ada County Sheriff's Office names Cary Burgess, who was known to frequent the Hunt Club, as a primary suspect (identified by police, never charged/convicted in this case); he arrived at a family member's house between 2 and 3 a.m. that night covered in mud, with a woman's wedding ring set, and appearing manic. Burgess was convicted of a separate July 6, 1984 abduction and rape in Boise and died in prison in 2001. Her remains have never been found. In April 2025, Ada County detectives said they were reanalyzing important items of evidence and asked for information about her missing wedding ring set, the location of her remains and the night she disappeared.
cases.solvedHow: Unsolved. Techniques so far: vehicle processing (1984); canal recovery of personal items; 1987 court finding of death; follow-up of a 1988 tip; 2025 reanalysis of evidence; public appeal through the sheriff's Cold Case Files podcast.

cases.audioScript: In the early morning hours of November thirteenth, 2022, four University of Idaho students were stabbed to death in an off-campus house here in Moscow. They were Madison Mogen and Kaylee Goncalves, both twenty-one, and Xana Kernodle and Ethan Chapin, both twenty. Two roommates survived. One later told police she saw a masked figure dressed in black walk past her and leave the house. For weeks there was no suspect, and fear spread across the campus and the town. Then investigators focused on a white Hyundai Elantra seen circling the neighborhood that night, and on a tan leather knife sheath left on one of the beds. DNA from that sheath eventually led investigators to a criminal justice graduate student at Washington State University, just across the state line in Pullman. On December thirtieth, 2022, Bryan Kohberger was arrested at his parents' home in Pennsylvania. In July 2025, to avoid the death penalty, he pleaded guilty to all four murders. He was sentenced to four consecutive life terms without parole, and he declined to say a word in court. Their families say the four are remembered for how they lived.
cases.summary: Madison Mogen, 21, Kaylee Goncalves, 21, Xana Kernodle, 20, and Ethan Chapin, 20, all University of Idaho students, were stabbed to death at an off-campus home in Moscow, Idaho, in the early morning of Nov. 13, 2022. Moscow police said an edged weapon such as a knife was used and there was no sign of forced entry. A surviving roommate told investigators she saw a masked figure in black walk past her and leave the home, and surveillance footage showed a white Hyundai Elantra circling the home several times between 3:29 a.m. and 4:04 a.m. A tan leather knife sheath was found on one victim's bed; the Idaho State Lab reported on Dec. 28, 2022, that a DNA profile from trash collected by investigators identified a male who could not be excluded as the biological father of the person whose DNA was on the sheath. Bryan Kohberger, 28, a criminal justice graduate student at Washington State University in Pullman, was arrested in Pennsylvania on Dec. 30, 2022, and charged with four counts of first-degree murder and felony burglary. A grand jury indicted him in May 2023, and a judge entered not-guilty pleas on his behalf. In July 2025 he pleaded guilty to all four murders under a plea deal that spared him the death penalty, and on July 23, 2025, at the Ada County Courthouse in Boise, he was sentenced to four life terms without parole. Prosecutors said that at trial they would have used DNA, his online purchase history, surveillance video of his car and cellphone data.
cases.solvedHow: Solved by investigative genetic genealogy on touch DNA from the knife sheath, confirmed by DNA from family trash, plus car surveillance and phone records; ended in a guilty plea (no trial).

cases.audioScript: In September 2019, two children from Rexburg, Idaho, simply stopped being seen. Sixteen-year-old Tylee Ryan and her seven-year-old brother, Joshua, known as JJ, were the children of Lori Vallow. That November, worried relatives asked Rexburg police to check on JJ, and officers could not find him. By then, Lori had married Chad Daybell, an author who wrote books about the end times. His first wife, Tammy, had died in October 2019, at first believed to have died in her sleep, and the couple married on a Hawaii beach weeks later. In June 2020, after months of searching, investigators found the children's remains buried on Chad Daybell's property near Salem. Prosecutors said the killings were fueled by power, sex, money and apocalyptic beliefs. In May 2023, a jury convicted Lori Vallow Daybell, and she was sentenced to life without parole. A year later, a jury convicted Chad Daybell of all three murders, and on June first, 2024, he was sentenced to death. Tylee's brother asked that the children be remembered for who they were, not as a headline.
cases.summary: Tylee Ryan, 16, and Joshua "JJ" Vallow, 7, the children of Lori Vallow Daybell, were last seen on different days in September 2019; in late November 2019 relatives asked Rexburg police for a welfare check on JJ, and police did not find him at the family's home. Chad Daybell's first wife, Tammy Daybell, died on Oct. 19, 2019, initially believed to have died in her sleep, and Chad and Lori married in Hawaii less than three weeks later. The children's remains were found on Chad Daybell's Idaho property in June 2020 after a monthslong search. A jury convicted Lori Vallow Daybell in May 2023 of two counts of first-degree murder and three counts of conspiracy, and on July 31, 2023 she was sentenced to life in prison without parole. Chad Daybell was convicted on May 30, 2024 of first-degree murder in all three deaths, conspiracy and insurance fraud, and on June 1, 2024 Judge Steven Boyce sentenced him to death on the jury's finding. Prosecutors described the case as driven by power, sex, money and apocalyptic spiritual beliefs.

cases.audioScript: On the night of September twenty-second, 2006, sixteen-year-old Cassie Jo Stoddart was house-sitting at a relative's home in Pocatello, Idaho. Two classmates, Brian Draper and Torey Adamcik, came over to hang out with her. Later that night, two masked intruders stabbed her about thirty times and left her to die. Her young cousin found her. Investigators found what the killers had buried in Black Rock Canyon near Pocatello: black clothing, three knives, two masks and a homemade videotape. On the tape, Draper and Adamcik planned and discussed the murder the day before, the day of and right after the killing. Both boys were sixteen. In April 2007, Draper was convicted of first-degree murder and sentenced to life in prison. That June, a jury convicted Adamcik of first-degree murder and conspiracy, and he received a fixed life sentence. The Idaho Supreme Court has since upheld both murder convictions. Both men remain in prison.

Both received life sentences. The Idaho Supreme Court affirmed Draper's murder conviction (2011, conspiracy count overturned) and upheld Adamcik's conviction and sentence.

cases.audioScript: On February first, 2010, Navy Seaman Kyle Antonacci was found dead in his barracks room at Naval Station Great Lakes, north of Chicago. He was twenty-two, an explosive ordnance disposal trainee from Long Island, New York. Months earlier, Kyle had been a key witness in a rape case against another sailor. He later admitted he had not told investigators everything about that night, and he became the subject of a perjury investigation. According to the Defense Department's Inspector General, Kyle was found about three hours after he walked out of an interview with the Naval Criminal Investigative Service. The Armed Forces Medical Examiner ruled his death a suicide, by hanging. His family never accepted that. They told reporters he had injuries, including a broken nose, and that the Navy first gave them a different explanation of how he died. A former Lake County coroner later said he believed Kyle was killed. In 2014, the Inspector General found that NCIS had not fully met its own standards in the rape, perjury and death investigations, but found no evidence of a conspiracy and did not overturn the suicide ruling. Officially, the case is closed. For Kyle's family, the questions remain.
cases.summary: Seaman Kyle Antonacci, 22, an explosive ordnance disposal trainee from Long Island, N.Y., was found hanging in his barracks room at Naval Station Great Lakes, Illinois, on February 1, 2010. He had been a prosecution witness in a court-martial rape case arising from a May 2009 barracks party, later admitted he had not disclosed that he also had sex with the woman that night, and was the subject of an NCIS perjury investigation at the time of his death (Navy Times; Los Angeles Times). The DoD Inspector General's evaluation (DODIG-2015-007, Nov. 3, 2014) says he was found deceased about three hours after leaving the NCIS office following a February 1, 2010 interrogation, and that the case agent did not document releasing him to his command. The Armed Forces Medical Examiner's opinion was that the manner of death was suicide. The Inspector General found that the rape, perjury and death investigations were not conducted in full compliance with NCIS standards and that a threat Antonacci reported was not thoroughly investigated, but concluded the death-investigation deficiencies did not materially affect the suicide opinion and found nothing to suggest a conspiracy. His family disputes the ruling; ABC News (2011) reported they said the Navy first told them he died in a car crash and did not tell them about injuries including a broken nose. The Los Angeles Times (2013) reported that the former Lake County coroner said he was denied access to key evidence, was pressured to call it a suicide, and believed Antonacci was murdered. No one has been charged in connection with his death. Other people involved in the underlying 2009 rape case are not named here.
cases.solvedHow: Officially resolved as a suicide by the Armed Forces Medical Examiner. Review steps: NCIS death investigation, AFME autopsy and opinion, and a DoD Inspector General evaluation in 2014.

cases.audioScript: On July fifth, 1996, Everett Thompson was at work at the restaurant he owned on Chicago's South Side when his wife, Lydia, called him, frantic. She said her brother, Kenneth White, who had moved in with the family months earlier after his release from prison, had chased her around the house with an ax, and she had locked herself in a bedroom. Everett left work to go home. He, Lydia, and their sons, eleven-year-old Everett Junior and eight-year-old Andrew, were never seen again. Kenneth White told people the family had gone on vacation. Investigators later learned he had forged documents to sell the family's home, and that the house had been altered after their disappearance. In December 1997, while White was held on a federal bank fraud charge, a prosecutor told a judge the government believed he had killed the family. He was never charged with murder. On Christmas Day, 1997, White died by suicide in custody. Chicago police called him their top suspect. The Thompsons have never been found. If you have any information about Everett, Lydia, Everett Junior or Andrew, contact Chicago police.
cases.summary: Everett Thompson Sr., 40, owned a restaurant in Chicago's Park Manor neighborhood; he and his wife Lydia, 43, lived with their sons Everett Jr., 11, and Andrew, 8, in the 8100 block of South Rhodes Avenue in Chatham (Charley Project; Chicago Tribune). Lydia's brother Kenneth White had moved in after his release from prison. On July 5, 1996, Lydia called Everett at work, frantic, saying White had chased her with an ax; Everett left and the family was not seen again (Charley Project, citing Chicago police and NWI Times). White told various stories about a family vacation, forged documents to sell the house, and the house was found altered. In December 1997, while White was detained on a federal bank-fraud complaint, Assistant U.S. Attorney Jacqueline Ross told a magistrate judge that the circumstances showed he had killed the family; the judge noted he was not charged with murder (Chicago Tribune, Dec. 24, 1997). White died by suicide in federal custody on Dec. 25, 1997 (Chicago Tribune), and Chicago police described him as their top suspect (Chicago Tribune, Jan. 8, 1998). He is recorded as identified by police, never charged/convicted. The family has never been found; the Cook County Sheriff lists all four as missing. Tips: Cook County Sheriff's Office secure online form on the family's missing-person page (cookcountysheriffil.gov).

cases.audioScript: Two days after Christmas in 1956, fifteen-year-old Barbara Grimes and her younger sister Patricia, twelve or thirteen, left home on Chicago's South Side to see Elvis Presley in Love Me Tender at the Brighton Theater. Their older sister and a brother were to meet them at a bus stop after the film. The girls never showed up. What followed became one of the largest missing person searches in Cook County history. Hundreds of officers searched. Elvis himself asked the girls to go home. On January twenty-second, 1957, a motorist spotted their bodies beside a rural road near Willow Springs, southwest of the city. Investigators questioned many people over the years. A man who confessed later took it back, and no case against anyone ever held. No one has been convicted. Almost seventy years later, the Cook County Sheriff's Office still lists the Grimes sisters as an open case. If you know anything, the Sheriff's Office takes tips online.
cases.summary: On December 28, 1956, Barbara Grimes, 15, and her sister Patricia, 12 or 13 (sources differ), left their family's McKinley Park home to see the Elvis Presley film 'Love Me Tender' at the Brighton Theater. They did not come home, and they were reported missing to Chicago Police (Cook County Sheriff; NBC News; A&E). The search became one of the most labor-intensive missing person cases in Cook County history, with hundreds of officers involved and an appeal from Elvis Presley (NBC News). On January 22, 1957, their bodies were found beside a rural road near Willow Springs; the Sheriff lists the location as German Church Road and County Line Road (Cook County Sheriff; CBS Chicago; A&E). Several people were questioned. A man who signed a confession in January 1957 later recanted, saying it was coerced, and was released; accounts differ on whether he was ever formally charged (A&E says charges filed in the case were dropped for lack of proof; NBC News says he was never formally charged). The Sheriff's Office continues to accept tips. No one has been convicted.
cases.solvedHow: Unsolved. 1950s techniques: mass door-to-door canvass, dredging of canals and rivers, flyers, public appeals, and polygraph-era interrogations. The Cook County Sheriff's cold case unit continues to review tips.

cases.audioScript: In December 1978, fifteen-year-old Robert Piest of Des Plaines, Illinois, disappeared, and witnesses said he was last seen talking with a local building contractor named John Wayne Gacy. Gacy was known in his community for performing as a clown at parties. Police obtained a search warrant for his home in unincorporated Norwood Park Township, just outside Chicago. Under the house, in the crawl space, investigators found the remains of victim after victim. In all, Gacy killed thirty-three teenage boys and young men between 1972 and 1978. In March 1980 a jury convicted him of thirty-three murders, and on May tenth, 1994, he was executed. Decades later, the Cook County Sheriff reopened the case to put names to the unidentified. Using genetic genealogy, in 2021 they identified one victim as Francis Wayne Alexander. Five victims still have no names. If a male relative of yours went missing in the 1970s, the Cook County Sheriff's Office is asking for a DNA sample.
cases.summary: John Wayne Gacy killed 33 teenage boys and young men in the Chicago area from 1972 to 1978; most remains were found in the crawl space of his unincorporated Norwood Park Township home. The investigation began after 15-year-old Robert Piest of Des Plaines disappeared on Dec. 11, 1978, and witnesses reported last seeing him with Gacy. Gacy was convicted of 33 murders in March 1980 and executed on May 10, 1994. In 2011 the Cook County Sheriff reopened efforts to identify eight unnamed victims; three have since been identified, including Francis Wayne Alexander in 2021 through genetic genealogy with the DNA Doe Project. Five victims remain unidentified, and the Sheriff has DNA profiles from all five for comparison with relatives.
cases.solvedHow: Solved in December 1978 when the Robert Piest missing-person investigation focused on Gacy; surveillance and search warrants uncovered remains under his house. Since 2011, DNA and genetic genealogy have been used to name unidentified victims.
cases.techniques: Missing-person investigation; Surveillance; Search warrants and excavation; Jury trial; DNA and investigative genetic genealogy (victim ID)

cases.audioScript: On the night of July thirteenth, 1966, a man broke into a townhouse in Chicago's Jeffery Manor neighborhood that housed student nurses from South Chicago Community Hospital. Over several hours, he killed eight young women. They were Gloria Davy, Patricia Matusek, Nina Jo Schmale, Pamela Wilkening, Suzanne Farris, Mary Ann Jordan, Merlita Gargullo and Valentina Pasion. All were in their early twenties. A ninth student nurse hid under a bed and survived. She later gave police a description of the killer, and at trial she pointed him out to the jury. Two days later, a doctor at Cook County Hospital treating a man after a failed suicide attempt noticed a tattoo reading Born to Raise Hell, which matched a newspaper description, and alerted police. The man was Richard Speck. Fingerprints at the scene matched his. In April 1967, a jury convicted him and recommended death. His death sentence was later overturned, and he died in prison custody in 1991.
cases.summary: On the night of July 13-14, 1966, Richard Speck broke into a townhouse in Chicago's Jeffery Manor neighborhood that housed student nurses of South Chicago Community Hospital and killed eight women in their early twenties. A ninth woman survived by hiding under a bed; a Cook County Hospital physician recognized Speck's 'Born to Raise Hell' tattoo two days later. Her testimony and fingerprints at the scene convicted him on April 15, 1967. His death sentence was reversed; he served a prison term at Stateville and died Dec. 5, 1991.
cases.solvedHow: Survivor description and public tip: a Cook County Hospital physician recognized Speck's 'Born to Raise Hell' tattoo from a newspaper description; fingerprints and the survivor's testimony convicted him.

cases.audioScript: On February 23, 2023, Rebecca Bliefnick, known as Becky, was shot to death inside her home in Quincy, Illinois. She and her husband, Timothy Bliefnick, were going through a divorce. Prosecutors said he rode a recently bought bicycle to her house, broke in through a window, and opened fire, leaving her to die in a bathroom. The judge said he shot her fourteen times, some while she lay on the floor, while the couple's children slept at his house. Prosecutors pointed to searches on his password-protected laptop, and the judge said he researched, planned and practiced the murder. A former contestant on television's Family Feud, he was convicted on May 31 of two counts of first-degree murder and home invasion. In August 2023, Adams County Judge Robert Adrian sentenced him to natural life in prison, Illinois' equivalent of life without parole. An assistant state's attorney said in twenty-two years he had never seen a murder so planned.

cases.audioScript: On June 9, 2017, Yingying Zhang, a visiting scholar from China, missed a bus to an appointment on the University of Illinois campus. She was last seen getting into a black Saturn Astra driven by Brendt Christensen, a former doctoral candidate. The two had never met before, and her remains have never been recovered. Christensen's then-girlfriend was secretly cooperating with the FBI and wearing a wire when he described killing Zhang to her as they attended a memorial vigil. FBI investigators testified they found Zhang's blood and DNA in his Champaign apartment. At his 2019 federal trial, his own lawyers admitted in opening statements that he killed her. A jury convicted him of kidnapping resulting in death and lying to the FBI. Prosecutors sought the death penalty, but the jury could not agree unanimously, so Judge James Shadid sentenced him to life without release. Her family pleaded with him to say where she is.

A wire worn by his cooperating girlfriend and Zhang's blood and DNA in his apartment led to a federal kidnapping-resulting-in-death conviction. The jury split on death and he was sentenced July 18, 2019 to life without release.
