timeline.event: The official 2021 Berkshire DA release says her family reported the then 18-year-old missing earlier in the month of the Nov. 16 discovery (i.e., earlier in November). In a Nov. 17, 2021 WAMC interview, DA Andrea Harrington said she was reported missing in October 1974 and that there were sightings in the North Adams area between October and mid-November 1974. iBerkshires, published the same week, says she was last seen on Friday, Nov. 1, and that a hunter found her body two weeks after she was reported missing, which is consistent with a report in early November. The October-versus-early-November wording is noted and not forced into a single date.

iBerkshires reports that more than 50 people were interviewed in the weeks after the discovery and that a traveling offender investigators had considered was ruled out after he was placed in Georgia at the time; he was never charged in this case and died in December 1974. This elimination is reported by a single news outlet.

iBerkshires reports that on Friday night, Nov. 1, 1974, Benoit left the former Sons of Italy in North Adams, a public social club, after a dance; friends later told police she had spilled something on her clothes and was leaving to change. She had been staying at a friend's apartment (not pinned). A Berkshire Eagle column quoting Berkshire District Attorney Andrea Harrington also states she was last seen on Nov. 1, 1974, a Friday.

Her body was discovered down an embankment alongside the Deerfield River in Florida, Massachusetts, on Saturday, Nov. 16, 1974, the 47th anniversary date used in the official Berkshire DA release. iBerkshires reports a hunter found her in the Hoosac Tunnel area of Florida. WAMC, interviewing the DA, also gives Saturday, Nov. 16, along the river in Florida.

The official 2021 DA release, and iBerkshires quoting the DA's office, describe renewed investigative efforts in the early 2000s based on a lead of moderate to significant value, without enough then to bring charges.

On the 47th anniversary of the discovery, the Berkshire District Attorney's Office issued an official release offering $10,000 for information leading to an arrest and conviction; the family offered an additional $5,000, for a $15,000 total. The office said it was exploring new technology and forensic resources and had added a contract investigator. Tips: 413-499-1112 or North Adams Police at 413-664-4944. No one has been charged.

DA Harrington told WAMC there is no statute of limitations on homicide, that people in the North Adams community may know what happened, and that the $15,000 reward was being offered to encourage them to come forward.

A Berkshire Eagle column quotes Berkshire District Attorney Andrea Harrington as saying the death certificate lists the manner as homicide and the cause as asphyxia by strangulation, and that narcotics did not play a role. The official 2021 DA release does not itself state the cause.

cases.audioScript: In June 2013, semi-professional football player Odin Lloyd was shot and killed in North Attleborough, Massachusetts. Former New England Patriots tight end Aaron Hernandez was charged with his murder and tried in Bristol Superior Court in Fall River. In 2015, a Bristol County jury convicted Hernandez of first-degree murder, and he was sentenced to life in prison with no chance of parole. Two years later, Hernandez was found dead in his prison cell, while his appeal was still pending. Under an old legal rule called abatement ab initio, a judge then erased his conviction, as if he had never been found guilty. Bristol County prosecutors appealed, arguing the old rule was outdated and unfair to victims, and that his estate could pursue the appeal if it wished. On March thirteenth, 2019, the Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court unanimously reinstated the conviction and threw out that rule, calling it outdated. The court record now notes that his conviction was neither affirmed nor reversed, because he died before his appeal was heard.
cases.summary: Semi-professional football player Odin Lloyd was found shot to death in a North Attleborough, Mass., industrial park on June 17, 2013. Former Patriots tight end Aaron Hernandez was convicted of first-degree murder in Bristol Superior Court in 2015 and sentenced to life without parole. After Hernandez died in prison in 2017, a judge vacated the conviction under abatement ab initio; on March 13, 2019, the SJC abolished that doctrine and reinstated the conviction. Two co-defendants were convicted as accessories after the fact: Ernest Wallace (acquitted of murder, May 2016) and Carlos Ortiz (guilty plea, June 2016); each received 4 1/2 to 7 years.

cases.audioScript: On New Year's Day 2023, thirty-nine-year-old Ana Walshe, a real estate manager and the mother of three young sons, vanished from her home in Cohasset, Massachusetts. She was not reported missing until January fourth, when her husband, Brian Walshe, called her employer in Washington, D.C., where she worked and lived part time. He told investigators she had left early that morning to handle a work emergency. Prosecutors said that in fact he killed her in the predawn hours of January first, hours after the family rang in the new year, dismembered her body and left her remains in dumpsters in the area. Investigators found internet searches on his devices about disposing of a body and cleaning up blood. Her body has never been found. Before trial, he pleaded guilty to misleading police and illegally disposing of her body. In December 2025, a jury convicted him of first-degree murder, and he was sentenced to life in prison without parole.

He pleaded guilty to misleading police and conveying a body, was convicted of first-degree murder Dec. 15, 2025, and was sentenced Dec. 18, 2025 to life without parole plus consecutive terms.

cases.audioScript: On the morning of June 27, 2000, 16-year-old Molly Bish went to her summer job as a lifeguard at Comins Pond, a public swimming area in Warren, Massachusetts. She was dropped off by her mother. She never made it through her shift, and she was not seen again. Searchers spent days in the air and on the ground. Nearly three years later, in June 2003, her remains were found in a wooded area of neighboring Palmer, in a place known as Whiskey Hill, and were identified as hers. The case became a murder investigation. No one has ever been charged. In 2021, the Worcester County district attorney named a man who had died in 2016 as a person of interest and asked the public for information about him. That man was never charged or convicted. Officials say the investigation remains active, and they continue to ask anyone who knows something to come forward. If you have information, call the State Police detectives at the Worcester County district attorney's office at 508-453-7575, or email WorcesterDAunresolved@mass.gov.
cases.summary: Molly Bish, a 16-year-old lifeguard from Warren, Massachusetts, disappeared on June 27, 2000, from her post at Comins Pond, a public recreational area in the town. The official Town of Warren page says her mother dropped her off that morning and later recalled seeing a man in a white sedan parked in the area that morning and the day before; that person has not been publicly named as a charged suspect. An extensive ground and air search followed. The Town of Warren official page says a hunter in Palmer in late fall 2002 noticed fabric similar to her bathing suit, that the observation was reported to police in May 2003, and that a large search of the Whiskey Hill area began on May 12, 2003. Remains were found there on June 3, 2003, and were positively identified as Molly Bish on June 9, 2003, after which the case was investigated as a murder. The Worcester County District Attorney's Office likewise says her remains were found three years later in a wooded area of Palmer. No one has been charged. On June 3, 2021, District Attorney Joseph D. Early Jr. named Francis "Frank" P. Sumner Sr., who died in 2016, a person of interest after investigators received new information. He was identified by police, never charged/convicted. Boston.com reported the announcement the same day. The official DA case page, dated July 24, 2023, still lists the case as unresolved and asks anyone with information to call Massachusetts State Police detectives at 508-453-7575 or email WorcesterDAunresolved@mass.gov.
cases.solvedHow: Unsolved. Techniques reported publicly include a large 2000 ground and air search, a 2003 organized search of the Whiskey Hill area in Palmer after a hunter reported possible clothing, forensic identification of remains, later investigative follow-up including a 2021 official person-of-interest announcement (the named person was never charged and is deceased), and an ongoing tip line. The Town of Warren page also notes that investigators have questioned persons of interest in Florida; those people are not named here.

That man has not been publicly identified by name as a charged suspect. An extensive ground and air search followed. Boston.com, citing prosecutors, also places the disappearance on the morning of June 27, 2000, at the pond.
The Town of Warren official page says that in late fall 2002 a hunter in Palmer noticed a piece of fabric similar to the bathing suit Molly had been wearing.

The Town of Warren official page says that in May 2003 the hunter's earlier observation was relayed to another person who notified police, and that a massive search of the Whiskey Hill area of Palmer began on May 12, 2003, with more than 200 searchers. Boston.com, in a shorter account, dates the bathing-suit find to May 2003.

The Town of Warren official page says remains were found on June 3, 2003, in the Whiskey Hill area of Palmer and were thought to be Molly's. cases.audioScript: On Sunday, January sixth, 2002, forty-six-year-old fashion writer Christa Worthington was found stabbed to death in her home in Truro, on Cape Cod. Her two-and-a-half-year-old daughter was found unharmed beside her. Worthington had written for Women's Wear Daily, The New York Times and Elle before moving to Truro in 1997. Police looked hard at the men in her life, and cleared them. A year later, crime lab DNA from her body matched none of the suspects, and the district attorney took the unusual step of asking every man in Truro for a DNA sample. In April 2005, police found the DNA matched Christopher McCowen, the garbage collector on her route, who had given a sample. He had twice told police he did not know her. In November 2006 a jury convicted him of first-degree murder, aggravated rape and armed burglary, and he was sentenced to life without parole. Massachusetts' highest court rejected his appeal in 2010, and all four of his motions for a new trial have been denied.

After a town-wide DNA appeal, her garbage collector Christopher McCowen's DNA matched and he was arrested in April 2005. He was convicted in Nov. 2006 of first-degree murder, aggravated rape and armed burglary and sentenced to life without parole; appeals and new-trial motions have failed.

cases.audioScript: Just after Christmas in 2010, sixteen-year-old Phylicia Barnes, an honors student from Monroe, North Carolina, was visiting her older half-sister in northwest Baltimore. On December twenty-eighth, she exchanged texts with her sister around midday, and was seen at the apartment in the early afternoon. By evening, she was gone. Her disappearance set off months of intense searches. On April twentieth, 2011, people spotted a body in the Susquehanna River near the Conowingo Dam, about forty miles away. Dental records confirmed it was Phylicia, and the medical examiner ruled her death a homicide. In 2012, police arrested a man and charged him with murder. But over three trials, the case fell apart: a conviction was thrown out, a retrial ended in a mistrial, and in 2018 a judge acquitted him. No one else has been charged, and no one stands convicted of killing Phylicia Barnes. Her family is still waiting for justice. If you know anything about what happened to Phylicia between December twenty-eighth and April of 2011, contact the Baltimore Police Department or Metro Crime Stoppers of Maryland.
cases.summary: Phylicia Simone Barnes, 16, of Monroe, North Carolina, disappeared on Dec. 28, 2010, while visiting her older half-sister at an apartment in northwest Baltimore near Reisterstown Road Plaza. Her body was found on the morning of April 20, 2011, in the Susquehanna River near the Conowingo Dam; she was identified through dental records, and the Office of the Chief Medical Examiner ruled her death a homicide. In April 2012 Baltimore police arrested a man, who was charged with first-degree murder. He was convicted of second-degree murder in February 2013, but the conviction was vacated in 2013 over undisclosed evidence; a 2014 retrial ended in a mistrial; and on March 30, 2018, a Baltimore judge granted a judgment of acquittal in a third trial. No one has been convicted.

cases.audioScript: In January 1999, eighteen-year-old Hae Min Lee, a senior at Woodlawn High School outside Baltimore, disappeared after school. Weeks later, her body was found buried in Baltimore's Leakin Park. Her former boyfriend, Adnan Syed, then seventeen, was charged. In 2000, a jury convicted him of first-degree murder, and he was sentenced to life in prison. Years later, the case became one of the most debated in the country. In September 2022, Baltimore prosecutors moved to vacate his conviction over problems with the evidence. A judge agreed, and Syed walked free after more than twenty years. But Hae's brother appealed, saying the family hadn't been given proper notice of that hearing, and in 2023 the appellate court reinstated the conviction. In March 2025, a judge reduced his sentence to time served under a Maryland law for people convicted as juveniles. Syed remains free, and his murder conviction still stands. Through all of it, Hae Min Lee's family has asked that she be remembered.
cases.summary: Hae Min Lee, 18, a Woodlawn High School student, disappeared Jan. 13, 1999; her body was found in Baltimore's Leakin Park on Feb. 9, 1999 (exact dates per Wikipedia). Her former boyfriend Adnan Syed, then 17, was convicted in February 2000 of first-degree murder, kidnapping, robbery and false imprisonment and sentenced to life plus 30 years. In September 2022, Baltimore prosecutors moved to vacate the conviction over unreliable evidence; a judge granted the motion and Syed was released after nearly 24 years in prison. In March 2023 the Appellate Court of Maryland reinstated the conviction, finding the circuit court violated the rights of Lee's brother, Young Lee, to notice of the hearing; Maryland's Supreme Court held in 2024 (Syed v. Lee, 488 Md. 527) that Young Lee was denied reasonable notice of the vacatur hearing and remanded; the State had entered a nolle prosequi in October 2022 before the reinstatement. On March 6, 2025, Baltimore Circuit Judge Jennifer Schiffer ruled under the Juvenile Restoration Act that Syed should serve no more time, and on March 14, 2025, she formally resentenced him to time served plus five years' supervised probation. His conviction stands.

cases.audioScript: On the evening of October second, 2002, a fifty-five-year-old man was shot dead in a grocery store parking lot in Wheaton, Maryland. By ten the next morning, five more people were dead. One was cutting grass. One was a taxi driver at a gas station. One was vacuuming her van. They were shot at random, from a distance. For three weeks, the shootings terrorized the Washington region. The victims ranged in age from twenty-five to seventy-two. One was an FBI intelligence analyst, killed outside a home improvement store with her husband beside her. Montgomery County Police Chief Charles Moose led the hunt, with the FBI and many other agencies. The break came when a caller linked the shootings to a robbery in Montgomery, Alabama. A fingerprint from that scene matched a teenager named Lee Boyd Malvo. That led to John Allen Muhammad, and to a blue Chevy Caprice. On October twenty-fourth, police found the two asleep in the car at a Maryland rest stop. The rifle was in the trunk. Ten people were killed. Muhammad was executed in Virginia in 2009. Malvo was sentenced to life in prison.
cases.summary: Between Oct. 2 and Oct. 22, 2002, snipers killed 10 people and critically wounded three in Maryland, Virginia and Washington, D.C. (FBI). The first victim, James D. Martin, 55, was killed in a Wheaton, Md., grocery store parking lot on Oct. 2; five more were killed in Montgomery County and Washington the next day (AP via CBS). The Montgomery County Police Department, led by Chief Charles Moose, ran the investigation with the FBI, ATF and other agencies. A caller claiming to be the sniper linked the shootings to a robbery in Montgomery, Alabama; a fingerprint on a magazine from that scene matched Lee Boyd Malvo, which led investigators to John Allen Muhammad and a 1990 Chevrolet Caprice registered in New Jersey (FBI). Early on Oct. 24, 2002, Maryland State Police, Montgomery County SWAT and the FBI Hostage Rescue Team arrested both men asleep in the car at a rest stop off I-70 in Maryland; a Bushmaster .223 rifle was in the trunk (FBI). The Justice Department sent Muhammad to Prince William County, Va., for capital murder prosecution (DOJ). He was executed by lethal injection at Greensville Correctional Center on Nov. 10, 2009, for the killing of Dean Harold Meyers; Malvo was sentenced to life in prison (AP via Spokesman-Review; NBC4; ABC News).
cases.solvedHow: A caller claiming to be the sniper linked the spree to an Alabama robbery-murder; fingerprint evidence there identified Malvo, leading to Muhammad and the car, which was spotted at a Maryland rest stop.

cases.audioScript: In March 2011, inside the Lululemon Athletica store at Bethesda Row in Maryland, thirty-year-old employee Jayna Murray was killed. Jayna was a former Johns Hopkins student who worked at the store. The woman responsible was her own co-worker, Brittany Norwood. Norwood stabbed Jayna more than three hundred times, in one of the most brutal murders Montgomery County had seen. Then Norwood told police a story: masked men had broken in and attacked them both. That story quickly fell apart under mounting forensic evidence. In November 2011, a Montgomery County jury found Norwood guilty of first-degree murder. On January twenty-seventh, 2012, Judge Robert Greenberg sentenced her to life in prison without the possibility of parole. The judge said that in his entire career, he could remember maybe two crimes that matched it in brutality. Jayna's family, eight members of whom spoke in court, called for her never to walk free again, and the judge agreed.
cases.summary: Jayna Murray, 30, was killed by co-worker Brittany Norwood inside the Lululemon Athletica store at Bethesda Row in March 2011. Norwood claimed masked men had attacked them; the story fell apart under forensic evidence. Investigators found the two women at the back of the store on March 12, and police later determined Norwood had not been assaulted. A medical examiner said Murray suffered more than 300 wounds. A Montgomery County jury convicted Norwood of first-degree murder in November 2011, and she was sentenced Jan. 27, 2012 to life without parole.
cases.solvedHow: Solved when forensic evidence at the scene contradicted Norwood's account of masked intruders, leading to her arrest and conviction.

cases.audioScript: On the evening of August 8, 1980, sixteen-year-old Joyce McLain left her home in East Millinocket, Maine, to go for a jog. Around 7:55 p.m., three people last saw her turn onto a dirt road behind a little league field beside Schenck High School. When she did not return, her mother searched the town through heavy thunderstorms. On the morning of August 10, a teenager found her body on the power-line corridor behind the soccer and little league fields. East Millinocket officers and Maine State Police responded. A medical examiner later concluded that she died from a blunt impact injury to the head. Heavy rain left no forensic evidence tying anyone to the scene. Philip S. Fournier, then nineteen, had been among people gathered at the high school that evening. In May 1981 he led investigators to where she was found and later told a pastor, his parents, and detectives that he had killed her; he was not arrested then. In 1989 he told a new supervisor that he had killed her. In March 2016 he was indicted for murder. After an eleven-day bench trial, a judge found him guilty on February 22, 2018, and imposed a forty-five-year prison sentence. On February 21, 2019, the Maine Supreme Judicial Court affirmed the conviction. The case is closed.
cases.summary: On August 8, 1980, 16-year-old Joyce McLain left her home in East Millinocket, Maine, to go for an evening jog. The Maine Supreme Judicial Court, reciting the trial court's findings, stated that at about 7:55 p.m. three people last saw her proceed down a dirt road behind the first-base dugout of a little league field adjacent to Schenck High School; that was the last reported sighting of her alive. When she did not return, her mother made phone calls and drove around town looking for her in heavy thunderstorms. Search efforts on August 9 were unsuccessful. At about 6:00 a.m. on August 10, a teenager who had joined the search found her body on the pole line behind the soccer and little league fields. East Millinocket police and Maine State Police responded and found a large wound on the back of her head; a rock with ceramic debris from an electric insulator was next to her head. A police dog later helped investigators locate articles of her clothing and a partially broken insulator that was collected as a potential murder weapon. Because of heavy rain on Friday and Saturday night, no biological material was found on the insulator, fragments, or rock, and overall no forensic evidence tied Fournier or anyone else to her death. Portland Press Herald reporting, later published by Central Maine, stated that her body was found behind the Schenck High School soccer fields in a wooded area near a row of power lines, and that at the time of her death she was a 16-year-old Schenck sophomore described as an honor student, cheerleader, musician and athlete. In the early morning of August 9, 1980, 19-year-old Philip S. Fournier, who had been among a group at the high school the previous evening, stole an oil truck and crashed it; he suffered severe head trauma and was in a coma for a period of time. Although he was identified as a suspect early, he was not questioned in the first months because of those injuries; after leaving the hospital he entered a substance-abuse program and did not return to East Millinocket until late December 1980. On May 5, 1981, Fournier met with investigators and led them down the path behind the soccer field to the pole line and to the area where the body had been found; he said that after dark on August 8 he had walked to the pole line alone and tripped over a dead body, and he accurately pointed out the area and described the state of the body. On May 12, 1981, he told a pastor that he had killed the victim by hitting her with a pole with a knob on it, then, at the pastor's request, told his mother and stepfather that he had killed her; the pastor drove him to the Bangor Police Department, where he was interviewed by two Maine State Police detectives and was not arrested. On May 15, 1981, he was interviewed again, described tripping over a female body at the pole line, and again was not arrested. In June 1989, on his first night as a janitor at Husson College, he told his supervisor, after being asked whether he knew about the murder, that he was the one who had killed the victim with a glass insulator and that he had 'beat' all of the interviews. The Portland Press Herald identified that supervisor as John DeRoche, then a janitorial supervisor at Husson University in Bangor, and reported that he came forward after Fournier's later arrest. In March 2016, Fournier was indicted for murder under 17-A M.R.S. § 201(1)(A); news coverage reported he had been arrested that month and held at the Penobscot County Jail. After an eleven-day jury-waived trial, the court (Penobscot County, Justice Ann Murray) found him guilty of murder in a judgment dated February 22, 2018, and imposed a 45-year sentence of incarceration. At trial, a former Maine chief medical examiner opined that the victim's death was caused by blunt impact injury to her head, with a contributing cause of neck injuries consistent with asphyxiation, and other autopsy testimony established details about the body that matched details Fournier had provided that had not been disclosed to the public. The Portland Press Herald reported that Justice Murray placed great credibility in DeRoche's testimony about the 1989 statement. Fournier appealed, challenging among other things the court's treatment of alternative-suspect evidence, the exclusion of a detective's opinion testimony, a finding that he had waived his religious privilege by repeating a significant part of his pastoral statement to his parents, and findings about his whereabouts that evening. On February 21, 2019, the Maine Supreme Judicial Court unanimously affirmed the conviction in 2019 ME 28 (docket Pen-18-170); a Bangor Daily News report published by WGME stated that he was serving the 45-year sentence at the Maine State Prison in Warren.
cases.solvedHow: Solved by a March 2016 murder indictment and a February 22, 2018 bench-trial conviction, affirmed on February 21, 2019. The trial court relied on Fournier's statements over many years, a 1981 walk-through in which he led investigators to the recovery area and described the scene, and other circumstantial evidence. No forensic evidence tied him, or anyone else, to the scene, in part because of heavy rain.

On his first night as a janitor at Husson College, Fournier tells his supervisor that he killed the victim with a glass insulator and had "beat" the interviews.
Fournier is indicted for murder (17-A M.R.S. § 201(1)(A)); news coverage reports his arrest in March 2016.
After an eleven-day jury-waived trial, Justice Ann Murray finds Fournier guilty of murder and later imposes a 45-year sentence (judgment dated February 22, 2018).
The Maine Supreme Judicial Court hears argument on Fournier's appeal.
The Maine Supreme Judicial Court unanimously affirms the conviction in 2019 ME 28.

evidence.item: Recovery on the pole line behind the Schenck High School soccer and little league fields on the morning of August 10, 1980, with a large wound to the back of the victim's head and a rock with ceramic insulator debris nearby.

A police dog helped locate clothing and a partially broken insulator later collected as a potential murder weapon. Heavy rain left no biological material on the insulator, fragments, or rock, and no forensic evidence tied Fournier or anyone else to the death.

Medical examiner opinion at trial: death caused by blunt impact injury to the head, with a contributing cause of neck injuries consistent with asphyxiation. Some autopsy details matched statements Fournier had made that had not been disclosed to the public.
May 1981 walk-through in which Fournier led police to the recovery area and described the scene, plus statements to a pastor, his parents, detectives, and, in 1989, a supervisor.

cases.audioScript: On the night of May ninth into May tenth, 1986, seventeen-year-old Kimberly Moreau left her family's home in Jay, Maine. Kim was a junior at Jay High School. She told her sister she would be back in about an hour. Instead, she spent the night riding around in a white sports car with a friend and two men she had just met. Later, she was dropped off in Jay, about half a mile from home. She never made it to her front door, and she has never been seen again. The Maine State Police suspect foul play. Over forty years, her family says there have been at least a hundred searches, including cadaver-dog searches of properties in Canton and Livermore. Nothing has been found. A state police detective has said a small group of people know what happened to Kim that night, and that now is the time for them to come forward. No one has ever been charged, and her remains have never been found. If you know anything about what happened to Kimberly Moreau, call the Maine State Police Major Crimes Unit at 207-624-7076, extension nine.
cases.summary: Kimberly Moreau, 17, was last seen in Jay, Maine, around midnight in May 1986; the Maine State Police listing says about midnight on May 9, while news reports give May 10. She was a junior at Jay High School. She told her sister she would return within about an hour and left to meet someone in a white Pontiac Trans Am. Police were told she and a friend rode around that night in a white sports car with two men they had just met. She was dropped off in Jay, about half a mile from her home, and has not been seen since. The Maine State Police suspect foul play and list the case as unsolved; extensive searches have been carried out throughout the region. Her father has said there have been at least 100 searches, including a 2015 cadaver-dog search of a property in Canton; a 2018 search of a Livermore property also produced nothing. The friend who was with her that night died in 2009. In 2024, Maine State Police Det. Cpl. Michael Chavez told WGME the case had never been closed and that people in the community know what happened. Her family runs an anonymous tip box, Kim's Justice, at P.O. Box 2 in Jay. No one has been charged and her remains have not been found.

cases.audioScript: On the afternoon of July 30, 1975, James Riddle Hoffa, known as Jimmy, was 62 years old and a former president of the International Brotherhood of Teamsters. He had an afternoon meeting planned at the Machus Red Fox restaurant, then a public restaurant in Bloomfield Township, in Oakland County, Michigan, a Detroit suburb. He was last seen at that restaurant's parking lot, and he has not been seen since. The last known photograph of him was taken in that parking lot, and police later found his 1974 Pontiac there. The FBI Detroit Field Office still calls the investigation active, one of the best-known missing-person cases in bureau history, and says it will follow every credible lead. Despite searches over the years, his remains have never been found. In 1982, a Michigan probate court declared him legally dead. No one has ever been arrested in connection with his death. On the 50th anniversary in 2025, the FBI asked the public for information at 1-800-CALL-FBI or tips.fbi.gov.
cases.summary: James Riddle "Jimmy" Hoffa, former president of the International Brotherhood of Teamsters, was last seen on July 30, 1975, at age 62. He had an afternoon meeting planned at the Machus Red Fox restaurant, a public restaurant in Bloomfield Township, Oakland County, Michigan; NPR and CBS report he was last known at that restaurant's parking lot and has not been seen since. CBS reports that the last known photograph of him was taken in that parking lot and that police found his 1974 Pontiac there. Hoffa had been sent to federal prison after convictions including jury tampering and fraud; President Richard Nixon commuted his sentence in 1971, with a condition that he stay out of union politics until 1980. After his release he sought to regain a role in the union. A Michigan probate court declared him legally dead in 1982; his remains have never been found, and FBI searches of various locations over the years have been empty-handed. The FBI Detroit Field Office said in a July 31, 2025, official release that the investigation remains active and asked anyone with information to call 1-800-CALL-FBI or submit a tip at tips.fbi.gov. No one has been arrested in connection with his death. CNN reported on October 27, 2025, citing two law-enforcement sources, that FBI employees were ordered to search for Hoffa-related records; that directive is not independently confirmed in the other sources used here.
cases.solvedHow: Unsolved. The FBI Detroit Field Office says the investigation remains active. Techniques reported publicly include following leads, searches of locations over the years (empty-handed), a 50th-anniversary public appeal and tip line in 2025, and (reported only by CNN) an October 2025 internal search for Hoffa-related records.

cases.audioScript: Shortly after midnight on May fourteenth, 2008, nineteen-year-old Brandon Swanson was driving home to Marshall, Minnesota, after celebrating the end of the semester with friends in Canby. His car slid into a ditch on a gravel road. He wasn't hurt. He called his parents, who drove out to find him while staying on the phone with him. Brandon thought he was near the small town of Lynd and started walking toward lights. Then Brandon shouted an expletive, and the line went silent. His parents called back again and again. No answer. Cell phone records later showed he wasn't near Lynd at all. His car was found about twenty miles away, near Taunton. Search dogs tracked his scent for miles, toward the Yellow Medicine River, and lost it there. Years of searches, including digs in the riverbed, have found nothing. His parents' fight led to Brandon's Law, which requires police in Minnesota to act quickly on missing adults. Brandon is still missing. If you know anything, call the Minnesota BCA at 651-793-7000.
cases.summary: In the early hours of May 14, 2008, Brandon Swanson, 19, was driving home to Marshall from Canby when his car went into a ditch. He called his parents at about 12:30 a.m.; they drove out to help but could not find him. He said he would walk toward the lights of Lynd and stayed on the phone; he swore and the call ended abruptly (BCA; Forum News Service). The Charley Project puts the end of the call shortly after 2:00 a.m.; Solve the Case says it went silent 47 minutes into the call. Using cell phone records, authorities found his car later that day off a gravel road near Taunton, about 20 miles from where he believed he was (BCA bulletin; Forum News Service; Charley Project). Search dogs tracked a scent about three miles to the Yellow Medicine River and lost it there. Searches of the river, including a 2021 excavation during drought, found nothing (Forum News Service). His parents lobbied for Brandon's Law (2009), which requires prompt investigation of missing adults (MPR News). Investigators continue to receive tips; Brandon has never been found.

cases.audioScript: On December sixteenth, 2004, twenty-three-year-old Bobbie Jo Stinnett was at home here in Skidmore, a town of about three hundred people. She was eight months pregnant. She bred rat terriers, and a woman had arranged to come see her puppies. That woman was Lisa Montgomery, who had driven from Melvern, Kansas, using a fake name. Montgomery strangled Bobbie Jo, cut the baby from her body, and drove away with the newborn. Bobbie Jo's mother found her that afternoon. Computer investigators traced the online messages to Montgomery's home, more than one hundred thirty miles away. The next day, police found her with the baby girl. The baby was alive, and she was returned to her father. Montgomery confessed. A federal jury convicted her of kidnapping resulting in death and recommended a death sentence. On January thirteenth, 2021, she became the first woman executed by the federal government in nearly seven decades. The crime shocked Skidmore. The county sheriff said nobody there could ever have imagined it.
cases.summary: Bobbie Jo Stinnett, 23, ran a rat terrier breeding business from her home in Skidmore, Missouri, and was eight months pregnant in December 2004. Lisa Montgomery, who lived in Melvern, Kansas, and had falsely claimed to be pregnant, contacted Stinnett on Dec. 15, 2004, under the alias Darlene Fischer about buying a puppy. On Dec. 16, Montgomery arrived at Stinnett's home around 12:30 p.m., strangled her, cut into her abdomen and removed the baby, and drove away with the infant. Stinnett's mother found her later that afternoon. Computer investigators traced the alias e-mail to Montgomery's home more than 130 miles away, and on Dec. 17 authorities found her with a newborn girl; she confessed to strangling Stinnett and taking the baby. The baby survived and was returned to her father. A federal jury convicted Montgomery of kidnapping resulting in death and recommended death; the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit affirmed on April 5, 2011. Montgomery was executed at the U.S. Penitentiary in Terre Haute, Indiana, on Jan. 13, 2021, the first woman executed by the federal government in nearly seven decades.

cases.audioScript: On the night of June sixth, 1992, nineteen-year-old Suzanne Suzie Streeter and her eighteen-year-old friend Stacy McCall were celebrating their high school graduation in Springfield, Missouri. They went to graduation parties, then returned to the home Suzie shared with her mother, forty-seven-year-old Sherrill Levitt. Between about two-fifteen and seven-thirty the next morning, all three women disappeared. When they were reported missing, the front door was open. The family dog was still there, along with their cars, keys, purses, money, and clothes. Police said there were no apparent signs of a struggle. Searchers looked in and around Springfield, including at Lake Springfield, and in other communities. Thirty-four years later, none of the three has been found, and no one has been charged. In 2012, Springfield police and the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children reviewed nearly twenty-five thousand pages of the file and presented the case to a panel of experts. The FBI still carries a ViCAP missing-persons alert, with age-progressed images issued in 2022. In 2023, Springfield police said the investigation was still active. If you know anything, call Springfield Crime Stoppers at 417-869-TIPS, or submit a tip at p3tips.com.
cases.summary: On June 7, 1992, Sherrill Elizabeth Levitt, 47, her daughter Suzanne “Suzie” Elizabeth Streeter, 19, and Streeter’s friend Stacy Kathleen McCall, 18, disappeared from a private residence in Springfield, Greene County, Missouri. The FBI’s ViCAP alert states that the three disappeared between 2:15 a.m. and 7:30 a.m., after Streeter and McCall returned to the residence to spend the night following graduation parties on the night of June 6, 1992. They have not been heard from or seen since, and their remains have never been found. When the women were reported missing, the front door was open, the family dog and the women’s cars, keys, purses, money, and clothing were left behind, and police said there were no apparent signs of a struggle. The Springfield Police Department (case 92-40169) leads the investigation, with assistance from the FBI and the Missouri State Highway Patrol. In 2012, Springfield Police partnered with the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children to review nearly 25,000 documents and physical evidence and to present the case to a 25-expert panel in Alexandria, Virginia; the department’s May 1, 2012, release said the case remained unsolved and asked the public for tips. On June 7, 2023, Springfield Police said in a statement that the investigation was still active and directed tips to Crime Stoppers at 417-869-TIPS or p3tips.com. A June 14, 2022, update to the FBI ViCAP alert includes 2022 age-progressed images and lists NamUs numbers 345, 3233, and 350. As of June 2026, KY3 reported that there had still been no positive leads as to why the women disappeared or where they are, and no one has been charged.
cases.solvedHow: Unsolved. No one has been charged, and the three women have never been found. Techniques reported: a multi-agency missing-persons investigation led by the Springfield Police Department with assistance from the FBI and the Missouri State Highway Patrol; collection and later review of physical evidence and nearly 25,000 documents; a 2012 case review with the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children, including a three-day presentation to a 25-expert panel; public appeals, flyer distribution, and geographic searches (including Lake Springfield); Crime Stoppers tip intake; and an FBI ViCAP missing-persons alert with 2022 age-progressed images.

cases.audioScript: On the night of April fourth, 1991, twenty-year-old Angela Hammond, known as Angie, was in Clinton, Missouri, after a date. About ten o’clock she dropped her boyfriend off at his home. At eleven-fifteen she called him from a pay phone in downtown Clinton. On that call, she told him an older two-tone green truck with a fishing mural in the back window kept circling the block. Then she said the truck had stopped, and a bearded man in coveralls was coming toward her in the phone booth. She screamed, and the line went dead. Her boyfriend later told police he drove to the scene and was passed by the same truck, and that she screamed his name as it left town. Angela has not been seen since. Thirty-five years later, the Clinton police chief said the case has never been forgotten, and her name was placed on Missouri’s 2026 cold-case playing cards. If you know something, call the Clinton Police Department at 660-885-2679, or the Missouri State Highway Patrol Missing Persons Clearinghouse at 1-800-877-3452.

cases.audioScript: Just before midnight on Friday, June fifteenth, 2018, security cameras in downtown Missoula, Montana, recorded twenty-three-year-old Jermain Charlo socializing outside a bar called The Badlander. Jermain was a mother of two and a member of the Confederated Salish and Kootenai Tribes. Shortly before midnight she walked away down the alley with a man she knew, and in the early morning hours of June sixteenth, she disappeared. She stopped posting on social media and stopped checking in with her grandmother, and her family knew something was wrong. On June twentieth, her aunt drove to Missoula to file a missing-person report in person. Missoula Police Detective Guy Baker led the investigation and said he had no doubt she was the victim of a criminal act. Searches came up empty, and police later released never-before-seen security video to CBS's 48 Hours, hoping someone would remember something. No one has been arrested, and police have not publicly named a suspect. If you were in downtown Missoula that night, or you know anything about what happened to Jermain, contact the Missoula Police Department.
cases.summary: Jermain Charlo, 23, a mother of two and a member of the Confederated Salish and Kootenai Tribes, disappeared in Missoula, Montana, in the early morning hours of June 16, 2018. Security video released by Missoula police shows her walking downtown and socializing outside The Badlander bar shortly before midnight on June 15, then leaving the area with a man she knew. In a June 21, 2018 appeal, Missoula police said she was last seen near Orange and South Fifth streets, wearing jeans, a white T-shirt, a brown Under Armour sweater and cowboy boots. The man first said he dropped her off at the Orange Street Food Farm, then told police it was a residential area about eight blocks west of the store; he has never been named a suspect and is not named here (CBS News). Her aunt filed a missing-person report in person with Missoula police on June 20, 2018. Lead detective Guy Baker said in 2020 that he had no doubt she was the victim of a criminal act, and NBC Montana reported an $11,000 reward at that time. Baker retired from the department in 2025 after taking part in dozens of searches for her. No one has been arrested and no suspects have been publicly named.

cases.audioScript: At about two-thirty in the morning on December ninth, 2001, novelist Michael Peterson called 911 from his home in Durham, North Carolina. Rescuers found his wife, forty-eight-year-old Nortel executive Kathleen Peterson, dead at the bottom of a back staircase. He told authorities she had fallen. Eleven days later he was indicted for first-degree murder. At his 2003 trial, prosecutors argued a missing fireplace blow poke was the likely weapon, and a state crime lab agent testified the blood spatter showed a beating. In October 2003 the jury convicted him, and he was sentenced to life without parole. In 2011 a judge found that the agent had misled the court and jury, and granted a new trial. Peterson was released. In February 2017 he entered an Alford plea to voluntary manslaughter, acknowledging the state had enough evidence to convict him while maintaining his innocence. He was sentenced to time served and walked free. Kathleen's sisters said they still believed he was responsible for her death.
cases.summary: Kathleen Peterson, 48, was found dead at the bottom of a back staircase in her Durham home after a 2:30 a.m. 911 call on Dec. 9, 2001; her husband said she fell. Michael Peterson was convicted of first-degree murder in 2003, but a new trial was granted in 2011 after a judge found an SBI agent misled the jury. On Feb. 24, 2017 he entered an Alford plea to voluntary manslaughter and was sentenced to time served.
cases.solvedHow: Resolved by plea: after a 2003 murder conviction was vacated in 2011 over misleading crime-lab testimony, the case ended with a 2017 Alford plea to voluntary manslaughter.

cases.audioScript: On July twelfth, 2002, a young man from Wolf Point, Montana, named Russell Turcotte was at a gas station in Grand Forks, North Dakota, waiting for a money order so he could get home. His mother had planned to wire him the money in the morning, hoping he could make it back in time for a wedding. He never picked up the money, and he was not seen alive again. On November fifth, his remains were found in a tree row about ten miles west of Devils Lake, just off U.S. Highway 2. The death was ruled a homicide. Nearly two decades later, a sheriff told reporters his office still reviewed the file and hoped someone would come forward. The case is still listed among North Dakota’s official cold cases, and no one has been charged. If you know something, call the Ramsey County Sheriff’s Office at 701-662-0700, or the North Dakota Bureau of Criminal Investigation at 701-328-5500.
cases.summary: Russell Douglas Turcotte, a young man from Wolf Point, Montana, was last seen on July 12, 2002, at Simonson’s Gas Station in Grand Forks, North Dakota, where he was waiting for a money order to travel home. He never picked up the money order. On November 5, 2002, his remains were found in a tree row about 10 miles west of Devils Lake, about a half-mile north of U.S. Highway 2, in Ramsey County. The North Dakota Attorney General’s Office lists the case as a homicide. A March 16, 2021, Forum News Network report likewise said his death was ruled a homicide and remains unsolved. The official listing describes him as 20 years old; 2021 and 2022 news accounts say he was 19 when he went missing. In 2021, Ramsey County Sheriff Steve Nelson said the case remained under his department’s jurisdiction with assistance from the North Dakota Bureau of Criminal Investigation, that the file had been reviewed again in the previous few years, and that he hoped someone would come forward. Tips were directed to 701-662-0700. The official cold-case page still lists that number and also publishes a BCI tip line, 701-328-5500. No one has been charged.

cases.audioScript: In November 2017, twenty-four-year-old Sydney Loofe worked at a hardware store in Lincoln, Nebraska. On November fourteenth she went on a first date with a woman named Audrey whom she had met on a dating app. The next evening, she had a second date planned with Audrey. On November sixteenth, she didn't show up for work, and she was reported missing. A friend found Audrey's online profile and gave it to police. Investigators learned Audrey was really Bailey Boswell, who lived with Aubrey Trail in a basement apartment in Wilber. Cell-phone location data showed the pair driving slowly along county roads on November sixteenth. On December fourth and fifth, following that data, searchers found Sydney's remains in rural Clay County. Trail was convicted in 2019 and sentenced to death. Boswell was convicted in 2020 and sentenced to life. An autopsy found she was killed by homicidal violence, and investigators also recovered duct tape, tarps and gloves near the remains. The Nebraska Supreme Court has upheld both cases.
cases.summary: Sydney Loofe, 24, of Lincoln, Nebraska, was reported missing Nov. 16, 2017 after a second date with "Audrey," whom she met on a dating app. Police learned "Audrey" was Bailey Boswell, who lived with Aubrey Trail in a basement apartment in Wilber. Cell-site data led investigators to Clay County, where her dismembered remains were found Dec. 4-5, 2017. Trail was convicted in 2019 and sentenced to death; Boswell was convicted in 2020 and sentenced to life. The Nebraska Supreme Court affirmed both.

cases.audioScript: On February ninth, 2004, twenty-one-year-old Maura Murray, a nursing student at UMass Amherst, left campus without telling anyone she was driving to New Hampshire. At about seven thirty that night, her black Saturn sedan was involved in what appeared to be a single-car crash on Route 112 in Haverhill. A passerby spoke with a woman believed to be Maura at the scene. But when police arrived, she was gone, and she has not been seen or heard from since. Earlier that day, she had been captured on ATM surveillance footage wearing a dark jacket and jeans. Over the years, law enforcement and volunteers have searched the area around the crash many times, with no result. In 2024, on the twentieth anniversary, the New Hampshire Cold Case Unit released an FBI age-progression image of what Maura might look like today. In 2026, investigators said they were applying new technology to the evidence, and WMUR reported that included facial recognition and LiDAR. Her disappearance is treated as suspicious, and the Cold Case Unit says it works every day to pursue credible leads. If you have information, call the New Hampshire Cold Case Unit at 603-271-2663.
cases.summary: On Feb. 9, 2004, Maura Murray, 21, a UMass Amherst nursing student, left the college without telling others of her trip to New Hampshire, about 2.5 hours away. At approximately 7:30 p.m. her black Saturn four-door sedan was involved in what appeared to be a single-car accident on Route 112 (Wild Ammonoosuc Road) in Haverhill, N.H. A private citizen saw and spoke to a woman believed to be Murray at the scene, but she was gone when police arrived and has not been seen since. She had been recorded on ATM surveillance earlier that day wearing a dark jacket and jeans. Numerous searches of the area by authorities and private citizens found nothing. The NH Cold Case Unit treats the disappearance as suspicious and in February 2024 released an FBI age-progression image. In February 2026 the unit said it was applying advanced techniques to existing evidence; WMUR reported these include facial recognition and LiDAR.

cases.audioScript: On Sunday, August twenty-first, 1977, twenty-two-year-old Shari Roth left her home in North Conway, New Hampshire, alone, to go hiking. Shari was a social worker who had moved to North Conway after graduating from Syracuse University. She was headed for the Sawyer Brook Trail in Livermore, in the White Mountains between Bartlett and Lincoln. When she did not come home that evening, her friends reported her missing. Three days later, on August twenty-fourth, her body was found. An autopsy showed she had been strangled. Nearly fifty years on, no one has ever been charged. In August 2026, New Hampshire's Cold Case Unit released photos of Shari that had never been seen before. Investigators want to hear from anyone who hiked near Sawyer Pond or Mount Carrigain that week, anyone who kept a hiking log, and the owner of a red Volkswagen Beetle parked at the trail entrance that day, who is not a suspect but may have seen something. If you know anything about the murder of Shari Roth, call the New Hampshire Cold Case Unit at 603-271-2663.
cases.summary: Shari Lynn Roth, 22, left her North Conway home alone on Sunday, Aug. 21, 1977, to hike the Sawyer Brook Trail in Livermore, between Bartlett and Lincoln. Friends reported her missing that evening. Her body was found on Aug. 24, 1977, and an autopsy determined she had been strangled. According to her family, she was found off Route 302 near Sawyer Pond. cases.audioScript: On the evening of May first, 1990, twenty-four-year-old insurance salesman Gregg Smart arrived home to his condominium in Derry, New Hampshire. Teenagers waiting inside ambushed him, and he was shot in the head in a hallway, where his wife later found his body. The scene was staged to look like a break-in. His wife, Pamela Smart, a high school media director, had been having an affair with a fifteen-year-old student, Billy Flynn. Prosecutors said she coaxed Flynn into the killing with two teenage friends and was after a one-hundred-forty-thousand-dollar life insurance policy. She was arrested three months later. Flynn and his accomplices pleaded guilty to second-degree murder and testified against her. Jurors said secretly recorded tapes, in which she seemed to know about the murder beforehand, were the most damning evidence. In March 1991, in one of the first televised trials in the country, she was convicted as an accomplice to first-degree murder and sentenced to life without parole. In 2025, New Hampshire's governor refused to grant her a pardon hearing.
cases.summary: Gregg Smart, 24, was shot in the head at his Derry, New Hampshire condominium on May 1, 1990, by teenager Billy Flynn, who was having an affair with Smart's wife, Pamela. Flynn and two friends pleaded guilty to second-degree murder and testified against her; secret recordings were key evidence. Pamela Smart was convicted Mar. 22, 1991 of accomplice to first-degree murder, conspiracy and witness tampering and sentenced to life without parole; repeated clemency requests have been denied.

cases.audioScript: Just before Christmas in 1996, twelve-year-old Celina Mays went to bed at a family home on Crestview Drive in Willingboro, New Jersey, at about eleven at night. She was nine months pregnant, with her baby due around December twenty-ninth. The next morning, her bed held only pillows arranged under the blankets. Her purse and her prenatal vitamins were left behind. Celina has not been heard from since. Police say they have run down more than two hundred and fifty leads over the years. Investigators have said the family had close ties to a small church in nearby Mount Holly, the Gospel of Christ Ministries, which is now an abandoned building, and they are still looking for people who attended or worked there. The father of Celina's baby has never been identified. Willingboro police and the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children say they remain hopeful that Celina, and her child, may still be alive, perhaps living under another name. Today Celina would be in her forties. If you know anything about Celina Janette Mays, or about that church in the mid-1990s, call the Willingboro Township Police Department.
cases.summary: Celina Janette Mays, 12, of Willingboro, New Jersey, was nine months pregnant when she disappeared during the night of Dec. 15-16, 1996. Per the Charley Project and Solve the Case listings, she went to bed about 11 p.m. at her aunt's residence on Crestview Drive, where she lived with her father and other relatives; the next morning pillows were found under her blankets, and her prenatal vitamins, purse and other belongings had been left behind. CBS Philadelphia (2022) reported that Willingboro police had investigated more than 254 leads and that the family was closely tied to the Gospel of Christ Ministry church in Mount Holly, whose pastor (Celina's aunt) has since died. NCMEC (2024) reported that police have not identified the father of Celina's child and that the church building is now abandoned. Police have said she could be living under a different name. No one has been charged, and the case remains an open missing-person investigation.

cases.audioScript: On the evening of October 26, 1982, 15-year-old Sharon Thor was getting ready to leave her home in Franklin Township, New Jersey, for a weekly ballet lesson in nearby Bound Brook. It was about 5:30. The telephone rang. She seemed glad to hear from the caller, told her mother she would be right back, and went outside. A child playing nearby saw her get into a car with two men. She never came home. Three days later, on October 29, the day after she missed her 16th birthday, searchers found her body in a wooded area of the township. The prosecutor later said she had been killed the day she disappeared, and that the cause of death was multiple blunt-force trauma. No one has ever been charged. In 2009, the Somerset County prosecutor said the case was active again. In 2025, the Franklin Township police chief told NBC News that the investigation is still going on. If you have information, the contacts published by NBC News are the Somerset County Prosecutor's Office at 908-231-7100, the Franklin Township Police Department at 732-873-5533, or Somerset County Crime Stoppers at 1-888-577-8477.
cases.summary: Sharon Thor, 15, of Franklin Township, Somerset County, New Jersey, was last seen at about 5:30 p.m. on Oct. 26, 1982, after a phone call, when a child saw her get into a vehicle with two men as she was leaving for a ballet lesson in Bound Brook. She told her mother she would be right back and did not return. She was reported missing that evening. Searchers found her body on Oct. 29, 1982, in a wooded area in Franklin Township, the day after she missed her 16th birthday. The Star-Ledger, citing Somerset County Prosecutor Wayne Forrest in 2009, reported that an autopsy listed the cause of death as multiple blunt-force trauma, that she was killed the day she disappeared, and that someone tried to conceal her body. No one has been charged. The two men described by the witness have not been publicly named in the sources used here. In 2009, Forrest said the case was active again and that new leads suggested more than one person was involved, and that the two men were in their late teens or early 20s and lived in the area. In August 2025, Franklin Township Police Chief Francisco Roman Jr. told NBC News that the investigation remains ongoing by the Somerset County Prosecutor's Office and the Franklin Township Police Department. NBC News published tip contacts including the prosecutor's office at (908) 231-7100, township police at (732) 873-5533, the STOPit app (access code SOMERSETNJ), and Somerset County Crime Stoppers at 1-888-577-TIPS (8477). NBC News reports that a memorial play, "Remembering Sharon," was performed in 2023 at Villagers Theatre in Franklin Township. A theater-held reward fund of $1,975, described on the theater's production page, is listed in the rewards section; it is not an official police reward.

timeline.event: At about 5:30 p.m., 15-year-old Sharon Thor was preparing to leave her Franklin Township home for a weekly ballet lesson in Bound Brook when the telephone rang. She appeared pleased to hear from the caller, told her mother she would be right back, and went outside. A child who had been playing nearby saw her get into the passenger side of a vehicle that had pulled up; the Star-Ledger, citing then-Prosecutor Wayne Forrest, later said the two men seen with her were in their late teens or early 20s and lived in the area. She did not return. She was reported missing that evening. No one in the car has been identified in the sources used here, and no one has been charged.
She missed her 16th birthday, which NBC News reports was Oct. 28.

A team of searchers found her body in a wooded area in Franklin Township, described as about a quarter mile from her home (no street is given here). NBC, citing 1982 police comments to the Central New Jersey Home News, says about 50 members of the township police and fire departments and first-aid squads took part in the search that day. The Star-Ledger, citing Prosecutor Forrest, reports she was killed the day she disappeared, that someone tried to conceal her body, and that an autopsy listed the cause of death as multiple blunt-force trauma.

Somerset County Prosecutor Wayne Forrest said the case was active again. He said new leads suggested more than one person was involved and that the two men seen picking her up were in their late teens or early 20s and lived in the area. A news report that the prosecution wanted a DNA sample from a potential suspect was not confirmed by Forrest, and that person is not named here. No charges were announced.

NBC News reports that in March 2023, with help from her niece, Sharon's mother signed papers to allow investigators to exhume her body to be retested for DNA, and that the family said testing was still underway as of the August 2025 article. The prosecutor's office and police did not publicly detail that work in the sources used here.

NBC News reports that a play written in Sharon's memory by family friend Nicholas Pelino Jr., titled "Remembering Sharon," was performed in 2023 at Villagers Theatre in Franklin Township. The theater's production page (not entered as a schema source) states the staged reading was Aug. 26-27, 2023, and that 50 percent of proceeds, $1,975, would be held in a reward fund; that dollar figure is recorded in the rewards section and is not treated as an official police reward.

NBC News (Dateline Cold Case Spotlight) reported the case. Chief Francisco Roman Jr. said the investigation into the homicide remains ongoing by the Somerset County Prosecutor's Office and the Franklin Township Police Department and that the department could not comment on an ongoing investigation. NBC published tip contacts for the prosecutor's office, township police, a STOPit app code, and Somerset County Crime Stoppers.

cases.audioScript: In 1971, in a nineteen-room mansion in Westfield, New Jersey, John List killed his entire family. His wife Helen, forty-six. His mother Alma, eighty-four. His daughter Patricia, sixteen. And his sons John, fifteen, and Frederick, thirteen. He laid their bodies on sleeping bags in the living room, and then he vanished. For more than seventeen years, he lived under a new name. He dyed his hair, built new credit, set up a phony Social Security number and remarried in Colorado. But his new life looked a lot like his old one: a bespectacled accountant whose life centered on the Lutheran church. In May 1989, the TV show America's Most Wanted aired his case, and more than two hundred tipsters called. Tips from Richmond and Denver led to an accountant near Richmond, Virginia named Robert P. Clark. He was arrested on June first, 1989. In April 1990 a New Jersey jury convicted him of all five murders, and the judge gave him five consecutive life sentences.
cases.summary: On Nov. 9, 1971, John Emil List killed his wife Helen, 46, his mother Alma, 84, and his children Patricia, 16, John, 15, and Frederick, 13, in their Westfield, N.J., home, then disappeared. He lived under a new identity in Colorado and then Virginia as Robert P. Clark, an accountant. After America's Most Wanted aired the case in May 1989, tips led to his arrest in Richmond on June 1, 1989. He was convicted April 12, 1990 and sentenced to five consecutive life terms. cases.audioScript: Around 2 a.m. on December 3, 2016, police found an empty car on the Route 35 Bridge over the Shark River Inlet between Belmar and Neptune, New Jersey. It was registered to the grandmother of nineteen-year-old Sarah Stern of Neptune City, who was its missing driver. Divers, boats and helicopters searched the river, but her body was never found. About a month later, a friend of Liam McAtasney, who had been friends with Stern, went to authorities. He testified that McAtasney had described a plan to kill Stern and steal money left to her by her late mother. Police had him meet McAtasney, and a hidden camera in his car recorded McAtasney admitting he strangled her, took her safe and got rid of her body. Prosecutors said roughly eight thousand dollars was in her home. McAtasney's roommate, Preston Taylor, pleaded guilty to helping throw her body off the bridge and testified against him. In 2019 McAtasney was sentenced to life without parole plus ten years, and Taylor to eighteen years.
cases.summary: Sarah Stern, 19, of Neptune City disappeared Dec. 2, 2016; her empty car was found on the Route 35 Bridge early Dec. 3 and her body was never recovered. A cooperating friend secretly recorded Liam McAtasney confessing to strangling her and taking her safe; roommate Preston Taylor admitted helping dump her body from the bridge. McAtasney was sentenced in June 2019 to life without parole plus 10 years; Taylor to 18 years.

cases.audioScript: On February second, 2009, a woman walking her dog on Albuquerque's West Mesa noticed a bone sticking out of the dirt along the trail. It was human. Over the following weeks, detectives uncovered the skeletal remains of eleven women and one unborn child, buried in makeshift graves near 118th Street Southwest. Investigators have now identified all eleven victims. One of them, Jamie Barela, was fifteen years old. The others were Monica Candelaria, Victoria Chavez, Virginia Cloven, Syllannia Edwards, Cinnamon Elks, Doreen Marquez, Julie Nieto, Veronica Romero, Evelyn Salazar, and Michelle Valdez. Police say the case remains active and open. More than fifteen hundred tips have come in over the years, and every one has been followed up. No one has ever been charged. The Albuquerque Police Department is offering a reward of one hundred thousand dollars for information leading to an arrest and conviction. If you know anything, call the West Mesa task force at 505-768-2450, or Crime Stoppers at 505-843-STOP. These were daughters, sisters and mothers, and their families are still waiting.
cases.summary: On Feb. 2, 2009, a woman walking her dog on Albuquerque's west side found a bone protruding from an earthen trail. Over the following weeks detectives uncovered the skeletal remains of 11 women and one unborn child buried in makeshift graves near 118th Street SW on the West Mesa. All 11 victims have been identified: Jamie Barela (15), Monica Candelaria, Victoria Chavez, Virginia Cloven, Syllannia Edwards, Cinnamon Elks, Doreen Marquez, Julie Nieto, Veronica Romero, Evelyn Salazar and Michelle Valdez. APD says ten of the victims shared a common link; Jamie Barela had no known involvement in it. No one has been charged. In 2026 APD said the case remains an active and open investigation with persons of interest still being investigated, more than 1,500 tips received, and a $100,000 reward for information leading to an arrest and conviction.

cases.audioScript: At nine-thirty on the morning of September twentieth, 1988, nineteen-year-old Tara Calico left her home in Belen, New Mexico, for a bike ride, riding her mother's bicycle because her own was damaged. She rode the same thirty-six-mile route every day. At about eleven forty-five, she was last seen riding along Highway 47 in Valencia County, and she was never seen again. The only evidence found was a Boston cassette tape and a piece of her Walkman. For more than three decades, local, state and federal investigators worked the case. In June 2023, Valencia County Sheriff Denise Vigil said there was enough evidence to send the case to the district attorney for review of potential charges. The identities of the persons of interest are sealed by the court. As of September 2025, no charges had been filed, and the sheriff's office was setting insect traps in an abandoned mine shaft north of Belen in the search for her remains. Tara's parents have died, but her sisters and brothers are still waiting for answers. The FBI offers a reward of up to twenty thousand dollars. If you know anything, contact the Valencia County Sheriff's Office or the FBI's Albuquerque field office at tips dot F B I dot gov.
cases.summary: Tara Leigh Calico, 19, left her home in Belen, New Mexico, at 9:30 a.m. on Sept. 20, 1988, for a bike ride on her mother's bicycle, as her own was damaged. She was last seen riding along Highway 47 in Valencia County at about 11:45 a.m. on her routine 36-mile route and was never seen again. The only evidence found on a dirt road was a Boston cassette tape and a piece of her Walkman cassette player. She was a sophomore at the University of New Mexico-Valencia campus studying psychology; her mother, Patty Doel, died in May 2006. On June 13, 2023, Valencia County Sheriff Denise Vigil said the investigation was complete and there was sufficient evidence to submit it to the district attorney's office for review of potential charges; the identities of persons of interest are sealed by the court. In September 2025 the Albuquerque Journal reported that no charges had been filed and the DA had not declined the case, that the results of a 2021 search of a Valencia County residence (April per the Journal; fall per the News-Bulletin) were sealed by a district judge, and that Lt. Joseph Rowland was using insect traps in an abandoned mine shaft north of Belen. The FBI offers a reward of up to $20,000. A 1989 Polaroid found in Port St. Joe, Florida, was one of the most-publicized tips in the case; it has never been confirmed to show Calico.

cases.audioScript: In January 2025, Craig Thetford stopped being heard from here in Cloudcroft, a small village in the Sacramento Mountains. Months went by. In May, his family reported him missing, and deputies checked his home but found no sign of him. His wife, Deana Thetford, told different stories: that he had gone to Mexico with another woman, that he was at firefighter training in Albuquerque, that he was caring for his mother in Texas. Then an anonymous Crime Stoppers tip said she had shot him after a fight inside their home. Investigators found that he had been shot at least three times in the first week of January, and that she had spent more than five months hiding it. Prosecutors say she cleaned and repaired the scene, wrapped his remains, hid them in the carport, and sent messages pretending to be him. On June second, 2026, she pleaded guilty to second-degree murder, tampering with evidence and forgery, and was sentenced to eighteen years in prison.
cases.summary: Craig Thetford, a resident of Cloudcroft, New Mexico, was last seen in January 2025; after months without contact, his family reported him missing in May 2025, and an Otero County Sheriff's Office welfare check at the couple's home found no sign of him. His wife, Deana Thetford, gave conflicting explanations, saying he had left for Mexico with another woman, was at firefighter training in Albuquerque, was caring for his mother in Texas, and was working in Texas. In May 2025, an anonymous Crime Stoppers tip alleged she had shot and killed him after an altercation inside their home, prompting search warrants and analysis of forensic, financial, phone, credit card and GPS records across several states. Investigators determined she shot him during the first week of January 2025 and that he suffered at least three gunshot wounds. The DA's office said she cleaned the scene, repaired damage from the shooting, wrapped his remains in plastic and a rug, covered them with lime and stored them in the residence's carport, and later used a backhoe near the carport, where a freshly dug hole was found. She also sent fabricated texts and Facebook messages while impersonating him and forged records using his signature. On June 2, 2026, she pleaded guilty before Judge Stephen P. Ochoa to second-degree murder, tampering with evidence and forgery and was sentenced to 18 years in the New Mexico Department of Corrections.

cases.audioScript: On the afternoon of October thirteenth, 2024, a neighbor in Tijeras, in the mountains east of Albuquerque, heard gunshots from the house next door and called for help. Bernalillo County deputies arrived to find twenty-four-year-old Adlai Mestre leaving the home with a handgun. In a ravine near the house, deputies found the bodies of his father, Raymundo, his mother, Bertha, and his seventeen-year-old sister, Brielle. The family dog had also been shot. According to the criminal complaint, investigators found signs that someone had tried to clean up inside the home. Mestre was charged with murder. In June 2025, after questions about his mental state, a judge ruled his competency to stand trial restored, and a grand jury then indicted him on three counts of first-degree murder. In August 2026, a judge allowed him to pursue an insanity defense. He has not been convicted and is presumed innocent. No trial date has been set.

Inside were the bodies of three members of one family: twenty-four-year-old Killian Mayes, seventy-nine-year-old Mary Mouser and sixty-eight-year-old Victor Perea. Police say all three had been shot before the car was set on fire. The regional Major Crimes Unit traced a vehicle linked to the scene, with investigators traveling to Roswell and to Mississippi. Two people were charged with three counts of first-degree murder: Kane Mayes, a relative of the victims, and Cassandra Douglas. Douglas was arrested in Roswell and Mayes in Mississippi. In April 2026, Douglas took a plea deal and agreed to testify against Mayes. The Alamogordo News reported that his July 2026 trial ended in a mistrial, with a new trial tentatively set for February. cases.audioScript: In 1979, nineteen-year-old Gwenn Marie Story left the Cincinnati area with two male friends, hoping to find her biological father in California. Her family never heard from her again. On August fourteenth, 1979, a man walking through an open field near Sahara Avenue and Las Vegas Boulevard, where the El Rancho Vegas once stood, found the body of a young woman. The coroner ruled her death a homicide, and no one could identify her, so detectives called her Sahara Sue Doe. In the fall of 2022, Las Vegas police cold case detectives asked for forensic genetic genealogy, and the Texas lab Othram took on the case. On November fifteenth, 2023, forty-four years later, Othram told police she had been identified as Gwenn Marie Story. Her family says they were told the men left her in Las Vegas. Her name is known now, but her killer is not. Metro's Cold Case Section is still investigating, and asks anyone with information about Gwenn or the men she traveled with to call Crime Stoppers at 702-385-5555.
cases.summary: Gwenn Marie Story, 19, left the Cincinnati area in 1979 with two male friends to look for her biological father in California, and her family never heard from her again. On Aug. 14, 1979, a man walking through a field on the former El Rancho Vegas site, in the area of Sahara Avenue and Las Vegas Boulevard, found her body; the Clark County coroner ruled the death a homicide. News 3 reports investigators said she was stabbed to death. Unidentified, she became known as "Sahara Sue Doe." In fall 2022 LVMPD's cold case detectives requested forensic genetic genealogy and sent her remains to Othram in Texas, and on Nov. 15, 2023, Othram notified police she had been identified. LVMPD homicide Lt. Jason Johansson confirmed the identification and said the homicide remains unsolved. Her family told investigators they were told the men she traveled with left her in Las Vegas; the men are not named here. In May 2026, News 3 reported the search for her killer continues, with the Vegas Justice League supporting LVMPD's genealogy work.

cases.audioScript: Late on September seventh, 1996, Tupac Shakur was riding in a BMW with Death Row Records co-founder Marion Suge Knight in Las Vegas. At about eleven fifteen that night, while they were stopped at a red light at East Flamingo Road and Koval Lane, a white Cadillac pulled up beside them and someone in its back seat opened fire. Shakur was hit four times. He died six days later, on September thirteenth. For decades, no one was charged. Then Duane Davis, known as Keffe D, began saying publicly that he was in the Cadillac and had handed the gun to others in the back seat. In July 2023, Las Vegas police served a search warrant at a home in Henderson, and that September, Davis was arrested. Prosecutors said he arranged the shooting as retaliation for a fight earlier that night involving Shakur and Davis's nephew. A jury found Davis guilty of first-degree murder with a deadly weapon, and he was sentenced to forty years to life. He has appealed to the Nevada Supreme Court.

A jury convicted Davis of first-degree murder with a deadly weapon; he was sentenced to 40 years to life and has appealed to the Nevada Supreme Court.

cases.audioScript: In September 2022, sixty-nine-year-old Las Vegas Review-Journal investigative reporter Jeff German was found stabbed to death outside his home in Las Vegas. German had written a series of articles about Robert Telles, the elected Clark County public administrator. The stories described a hostile work environment in Telles' office, bullying, retaliation and an inappropriate relationship with a staffer, all of which Telles denied. ABC News reported that the coverage ended his political career and his marriage. Prosecutors said he lay in wait outside German's home. Days after the killing, Telles was taken into custody. Police said his DNA was found on German's hands and fingernails, and a straw hat and sneakers like those worn by the attacker in surveillance video were found cut up in his home. In August 2024 a jury found him guilty of murder. In October, a judge sentenced him to twenty-eight years to life in prison. He still says he did not kill German.
cases.summary: Las Vegas Review-Journal investigative reporter Jeff German, 69, was found stabbed to death outside his home in September 2022. Robert Telles, the Clark County public administrator German had written about, was arrested days later; DNA and cut-up clothing tied him to the attack. A jury convicted Telles of murder in Aug. 2024 and he was sentenced Oct. 16, 2024 to 28 years to life.
