cases.audioScript: On Thanksgiving night, November twenty-second, 1984, fourteen-year-old Wendy Jerome of Rochester, New York, left home to deliver a birthday card to a friend nearby. She never came home. When she missed her curfew, her mother, Marlene, called Wendy's friends and then the police. That night, Rochester police found Wendy's body on Webster Avenue near School Number Thirty-Three. She had been raped and murdered. Police preserved the scene, and for decades the case stayed open. As DNA technology improved, analysts tested Wendy's clothing and other evidence. Investigators turned to familial DNA testing, and in 2020, nearly thirty-six years later, they arrested Timothy Williams, who had lived in Wendy's neighborhood and was twenty at the time. His first trial ended in a mistrial. At a retrial in March 2024, a jury convicted him of three counts of second-degree murder, the first conviction in New York State built on familial DNA. In April 2024 he was sentenced to twenty-five years to life. Her mother said Wendy was the sweetest, most caring little girl in the whole world.
cases.summary: On Thanksgiving night, Nov. 22, 1984, Wendy Jerome, 14, went to deliver a birthday card to a nearby friend in Rochester and did not return. Her mother called friends and then police, and Rochester police found her body that night on Webster Avenue near School No. 33; she had been raped and murdered (Monroe County DA). The case went cold. As DNA methods improved, evidence including her clothing was tested, and familial DNA testing led investigators to Timothy Williams, who lived in the neighborhood and was 20 in 1984 (13WHAM). He was arrested in 2020. A first trial in late 2023 ended in a mistrial over alleged juror misconduct. On March 8, 2024, a jury convicted him of three counts of second-degree murder, which the DA called the first conviction using familial DNA in New York State. On April 17, 2024, Justice Alex Renzi sentenced him to three concurrent terms of 25 years to life. His defense said it would appeal; no appellate decision was found.

cases.audioScript: In 2010, police searching along Ocean Parkway near Gilgo Beach on Long Island found the remains of four young women, each wrapped in burlap. They became known as the Gilgo Four. More remains were found along the parkway in the months that followed, and for more than a decade the case went unsolved. In 2023, investigators arrested Rex Heuermann, an architect who lived in Massapequa Park. Prosecutors said burner phones used to contact the victims and DNA evidence tied him to the killings. Over the next two years, he was charged in the deaths of seven women. In April 2026, after years of insisting he was innocent, Heuermann pleaded guilty to murdering all seven: Melissa Barthelemy, Megan Waterman, Amber Costello, Maureen Brainard-Barnes, Jessica Taylor, Sandra Costilla and Valerie Mack. He also admitted killing an eighth woman, Karen Vergata. In June, he was sentenced to life in prison without parole, as victims' families faced him in court.
cases.summary: Beginning in December 2010, remains were found along Ocean Parkway near Gilgo Beach, including the "Gilgo Four" — Melissa Barthelemy, Megan Waterman, Amber Costello and Maureen Brainard-Barnes — bound with burlap. Rex Heuermann, a Massapequa Park architect, was arrested in July 2023 and initially charged in the deaths of Barthelemy, Waterman and Costello; Brainard-Barnes was added in 2024, followed by Jessica Taylor (disappeared 2003), Sandra Costilla (found in Southampton, 1993) and Valerie Mack (disappeared 2000). Investigators linked him through burner phones that pinged near his home and workplace, and DNA evidence. On April 8, 2026, he pleaded guilty to three counts of first-degree and four counts of second-degree murder and admitted killing Karen Vergata, for whom he was not charged. On June 17, 2026, in Riverhead, Judge Timothy Mazzei sentenced him to three consecutive life terms without parole (Barthelemy, Waterman, Costello) plus a consecutive 100 years to life (Brainard-Barnes, Taylor, Costilla, Mack). Other remains found along Ocean Parkway, and the 2010 death of Shannan Gilbert, are not attributed to him in these sources.
cases.solvedHow: Solved by a reconstituted task force using cellphone (burner phone) location data and DNA evidence, leading to a 2023 arrest and 2026 guilty plea.

cases.audioScript: On the night of March second, 1998, nineteen-year-old Suzanne Lyall, a student at the University at Albany, left her part-time job at Babbage's Software in Crossgates Mall at about nine twenty. She boarded a CDTA bus back to campus and got off at Collins Circle at about nine forty. She never returned to her dormitory on Colonial Quad. The next afternoon, just before four o'clock, her ATM card was used at a Stewart's Shop at Central Avenue and Manning Boulevard in Albany. Her father reported her missing on March fourth. A State Police investigator said in 2004 that almost from the start, the case had been treated as a homicide. That year, State Police released an image of what Suzanne might look like at twenty-five. Her parents, Doug and Mary Lyall, founded the Center for HOPE and pushed for change, including Suzanne's Law, signed in 2003, which removed waiting periods for missing-person reports for young adults aged eighteen to twenty-one. Suzanne has never been found. If you have information, call the New York State Police, Troop G, at 518-783-3211.

A NYSP senior investigator said in 2004 the case had been treated as a homicide almost from the start, and State Police released an age-progressed image that year. Her parents founded the Center for HOPE and advocated for Suzanne's Law (2003) and the Suzanne Lyall Campus Security Act (2007). She has not been found.

cases.audioScript: From the summer of 1976 to the summer of 1977, a gunman with a forty-four caliber revolver terrorized New York City, mostly in Queens, the Bronx and Brooklyn. He often targeted young couples sitting in parked cars. Six people were killed and seven were wounded. In letters to police and to a newspaper columnist, he called himself the Son of Sam. Women cut or dyed their long dark hair, and young people stayed home. The last killing came on July thirty-first, 1977, in Bath Beach, Brooklyn, when twenty-year-old Stacy Moskowitz was shot on a first date. That night, a parking ticket was written for a car near a fire hydrant nearby. It led police to an apartment in Yonkers. On August tenth, 1977, police arrested David Berkowitz, a postal worker, outside his building. He was carrying the revolver. He pleaded guilty, and was sentenced to six consecutive terms of twenty-five years to life. He has been denied parole again and again, and he remains in a New York prison. The victims are remembered, among them Donna Lauria, Christine Freund, Virginia Voskerichian, Valentina Suriani, Alexander Esau and Stacy Moskowitz.
cases.summary: Between July 29, 1976, and July 31, 1977, a gunman with a .44-caliber revolver killed six people and wounded seven in eight attacks across Queens, Brooklyn and the Bronx, often targeting young women and couples in parked cars. Those killed were Donna Lauria, 18; Christine Freund, 26; Virginia Voskerichian, 20; Valentina Suriani, 18; Alexander Esau, 20; and Stacy Moskowitz, 20. The killer left a note addressed to Capt. Joseph Borelli and wrote to Daily News columnist Jimmy Breslin, calling himself the "Son of Sam"; the case gripped the city with fear. After the July 31, 1977, shooting in Bath Beach, police traced a parking ticket issued to a Ford Galaxie parked near a fire hydrant to an apartment building in Yonkers. On Aug. 10, 1977, police arrested David Berkowitz, a postal worker, outside the building; he was carrying the .44-caliber revolver, and a loaded submachine gun was found in his car. Berkowitz first claimed demons spoke to him through a neighbor's dog, but later told Newsday he invented that story. He pleaded guilty on May 8, 1978, and on June 12, 1978, was sentenced to six consecutive terms of 25 years to life, one for each murder; New York later passed its "Son of Sam" law barring criminals from profiting from their crimes. Eligible for parole since 2002, he was denied for the 12th time in 2024 and skipped his 13th hearing in May 2026; he is held at Shawangunk Correctional Facility.
cases.solvedHow: A parking ticket written near the final shooting led police to Berkowitz's car and Yonkers apartment; he was arrested carrying the revolver and pleaded guilty.

cases.audioScript: Early on December fourth, 2024, UnitedHealthcare chief executive Brian Thompson was walking through midtown Manhattan toward his company's investor conference. Outside the midtown Hilton, a gunman ambushed him and shot him, then fled, setting off an interstate manhunt. Thompson was a Minnesota father of two. Five days later, in Altoona, Pennsylvania, a customer at a McDonald's recognized him from photos of the suspect, and an employee called police. That man was Luigi Mangione, a Maryland native. In August 2026, Mangione changed his plea and pleaded guilty in Manhattan federal court to two counts of stalking resulting in death. cases.audioScript: In 1928, an elderly man calling himself Frank Howard befriended the Budd family in New York City. He persuaded Grace's parents to let their ten-year-old daughter go with him to a birthday party. She never came home, and a huge search turned up no trace of her. Police found no record of a Frank Howard, and the case went cold for years. In November 1934, Grace's mother received an anonymous letter describing her daughter's murder. Detectives traced the monogrammed stationery to a Manhattan rooming house, and on December thirteenth they arrested sixty-six-year-old house painter Albert Fish. He admitted killing Grace and led police to her remains in Westchester County. At his 1935 trial, the defense argued insanity, but the jury convicted him. Nearly everyone, including the jury, agreed he was insane, yet he was still sentenced to die. He was executed in the electric chair at Sing Sing prison on January sixteenth, 1936. Authorities believed he may have killed other children as well.
cases.summary: In 1928, 10-year-old Grace Budd was lured from her Manhattan family by a man calling himself Frank Howard, who said he was taking her to a party; she never returned. In 1934 a letter to her mother was traced to Albert Fish, who was arrested Dec. 13, 1934, admitted the killing and led police to her remains in Westchester County. He was convicted in 1935 and executed at Sing Sing on Jan. 16, 1936.

cases.audioScript: On the last night of classes before spring break in 2006, twenty-seven-year-old Ohio State medical student Brian Shaffer went out with friends near campus in Columbus, Ohio. Early on Saturday, April first, the group rode an escalator up to the Ugly Tuna Saloona, a second-floor bar in the busy Gateway complex on North High Street. At about 1:55 a.m., a surveillance camera caught Brian outside the bar, talking with two young women. Then he walked out of the frame, apparently back toward the bar. His friends left around closing time. Cameras recorded them going. No camera ever recorded Brian leaving. He was supposed to fly to Florida with his girlfriend two days later. He never showed up, and he was reported missing that day. Police searched the building, the roof, and the riverbanks, and brought in cadaver dogs. More than a hundred people were interviewed. Nothing turned up. Twenty years on, the FBI and the Ohio Attorney General still list Brian as missing, and Columbus police say the case is active. If you were at the Gateway that night, or know anything about what happened to Brian Shaffer, call Columbus police.
cases.summary: Brian Randall Shaffer, 27, an Ohio State University medical student, disappeared early on April 1, 2006, after a night out with friends near campus in Columbus. The FBI's ViCAP bulletin says his last known contact was at 1:55 a.m. while he was having drinks with friends at a bar near the university; the Ohio Attorney General's listing says he was last seen about 2 a.m. at a bar in the 1500 block of N. High St. NBC News (Dateline, May 2006) reported that surveillance video showed Shaffer and companions riding the escalator to the second-floor Ugly Tuna Saloona at 1:15 a.m. and that at 1:55 a.m. he was recorded outside the bar talking with two young women before walking out of frame, apparently back into the bar. His companions later left; no camera recorded Shaffer leaving. He had been due to fly to Florida with his girlfriend on April 3 and was reported missing that day. Police searched the building and surrounding area, including the river, using cadaver dogs, without result. The FBI cites NamUs case MP#1709. In April 2026, Columbus police told The Columbus Dispatch the investigation remains active and that they had sought help from the Ohio Bureau of Criminal Investigation. No one has been charged, and no suspect has been named.

cases.audioScript: In the early morning of September thirteenth, 2016, a woman held captive in a vacant house in Ashland, Ohio, worked loose from her bindings and called 911. Police arrived within minutes and arrested the man who had held her for two nights: Shawn Grate. Inside the house, investigators found the bodies of two women, Stacey Stanley and Elizabeth Griffith. Over the following weeks, Grate gave police multiple confessions, and they led investigators to more victims in neighboring counties. In 2018, an Ashland County jury convicted him of the aggravated murders of Stacey and Elizabeth, and he was sentenced to death. The Ohio Supreme Court unanimously upheld those death sentences in December 2020. In 2019, Grate pleaded guilty in Richland County to the murders of Rebekah Leicy and Candice Cunningham, and he later admitted another killing in Marion County. The woman who escaped that morning is the reason all of these families finally got answers. He was also given life without parole in Richland and Marion counties. Remember Stacey, Elizabeth, Rebekah, Candice and Dana.
cases.summary: Shawn Grate moved from Richland County to Ashland County in June 2016 and began squatting in a vacant house in Ashland in July 2016. On Sept. 13, 2016, a woman he had held captive for two nights loosened her bindings around 6 a.m. and called 911; police arrested Grate and found the bodies of two women in the house. Between Sept. 13 and Oct. 17, 2016, he gave multiple confessions. An Ashland County jury convicted him of the aggravated murders of Stacey Stanley (Stacey Hicks) and Elizabeth Griffith and related counts, including the kidnapping and rape of the survivor; on June 1, 2018, he was sentenced to death plus 90 years to life. The Ohio Supreme Court unanimously affirmed on Dec. 10, 2020 (2020-Ohio-5584). On March 1, 2019, he pleaded guilty in Richland County to the aggravated murder of Rebekah Leicy and the murder of Candice Cunningham and was sentenced to life without parole plus consecutive terms. On Sept. 11, 2019, he pleaded guilty in Marion County to the 2006 aggravated murder of Dana Lowrey and received life without parole plus 16 years, consecutive (Cleveland 19; WBNS 10TV). The survivor is not named.
cases.solvedHow: Solved when a kidnapped woman escaped her bindings and called 911 on Sept. 13, 2016; Grate's subsequent confessions led to the other victims. Convicted by jury (Ashland) and guilty pleas (Richland, Marion).

cases.audioScript: On Friday, October twenty-seventh, 1989, ten-year-old Amy Mihaljevic walked from school to the Bay Square Shopping Center in Bay Village, Ohio, just west of Cleveland. Weeks earlier, a man had called her on the phone. He said her mother had been promoted, and he wanted Amy's help picking out a surprise gift. Witnesses saw Amy talking with a white man, thought to be in his thirties, and then walking with him through the parking lot. No vehicle was seen. Three and a half months later, on February eighth, 1990, a jogger found Amy's body in a farm field off County Road 1181 in rural Ashland County. She had been stabbed and struck in the head. Her boots, a denim backpack, a binder, and turquoise horse-head earrings were never found. Bay Village police and the FBI have never stopped working the case. Newer testing has found male DNA on Amy's sweatpants, though the sample is still too small to identify anyone. No one has been charged. The FBI offers up to twenty-five thousand dollars. If you know anything, call Bay Village police at 440-871-1234.
cases.summary: On October 27, 1989, 10-year-old Amy Mihaljevic was kidnapped from the Bay Square Shopping Center parking lot in Bay Village, Ohio. Weeks earlier an unknown man had telephoned her and arranged to meet after school on the pretext of buying a gift for her mother, who he said had been promoted. Eyewitnesses saw Amy speaking with a white male estimated to be in his 30s and walking through the parking lot with him; no vehicle was seen (Bay Village Police; Ohio Attorney General). On February 8, 1990, a jogger found her body in a farm field close to the road off County Road 1181 in Ruggles Township, rural Ashland County. The crime scene suggested her body was dumped shortly after the abduction. Cause of death was stab wounds to the neck and a blow to the head. Her boots, a denim backpack, a binder reading 'Buick, Best in Class', and turquoise horse-head earrings have never been located. The FBI offers up to $25,000. Police have asked the public to identify a blanket and a curtain linked to the case. Cleveland 19 reported in January 2026 that a lab had detected male DNA on Amy's sweatpants, but the sample was too small to identify anyone; in January 2026 police said hairs found on her clothing could not yield a profile. cases.audioScript: Early on the morning of July thirty-first, 2022, a Toyota Camry turned onto Progress Drive in an industrial park here in Strongsville. Behind the wheel was seventeen-year-old Mackenzie Shirilla. With her were her boyfriend, twenty-year-old Dominic Russo, and their friend, nineteen-year-old Davion Flanagan. Prosecutors say she had been driving at a controlled speed. Then, almost right after the turn, the car sped up. Prosecutors put the speed at about one hundred miles an hour; a TV report says the judge cited ninety-two from the vehicle data, so the sources differ. It went straight through a business sign and into a brick building. No one found the wreck for about forty-five minutes. Dominic and Davion died at the scene. The car's black box showed the gas pedal pushed all the way down and the brake never touched. Investigators found nothing wrong with the car. At a bench trial in August 2023, the judge watched video of the crash and called it a mission executed with precision. She found Shirilla guilty of murder, and sentenced her to fifteen years to life. Ohio prison records show she will not be eligible for parole until 2037. Two young men got into a car that morning, and never came home.
cases.summary: On July 31, 2022, at about 5:30 a.m., Mackenzie Shirilla, then 17, was driving her Toyota Camry with two passengers, Dominic Russo, 20, and Davion Flanagan, 19, in Strongsville, Ohio. According to the Cuyahoga County Prosecutor, she drove at a controlled speed down Progress Road, then, almost immediately after turning onto Progress Drive, accelerated to 100 mph (WKYC reports the judge cited 92 mph from vehicle data; the sources differ) and drove through a business sign into the Plidco Building at Progress Drive and Alameda Drive. A passerby found the crash about 45 minutes later and called police; both passengers were pronounced dead at the scene and Shirilla was hospitalized. The car's event data recorder showed the accelerator fully pressed and the brake never applied, and no vehicle defect contributed to the crash; psilocybin mushrooms and a digital scale were found on Shirilla. Russo was Shirilla's boyfriend and Flanagan was a friend. At a bench trial that began Aug. 7, 2023, prosecutors played video of the crash; on Aug. 14, 2023, Judge Nancy Margaret Russo found Shirilla guilty of four counts of murder, four counts of felonious assault, two counts of aggravated vehicular homicide, drug possession and possessing criminal tools. On Aug. 21, 2023, she was sentenced to 15 years to life, with the murder sentences running concurrently. Ohio Department of Rehabilitation and Correction records list her at the Ohio Reformatory for Women with a parole eligibility date of Oct. 29, 2037.

cases.audioScript: Early on the morning of December thirtieth, 1999, firefighters were called to a burning mobile home near Welch, in rural northeast Oklahoma. Inside, they found Danny and Kathy Freeman. Both had been shot. Their sixteen-year-old daughter, Ashley, and her best friend, Lauria Bible, who had stayed the night after a birthday celebration, were gone. For almost two decades, the case went unsolved. Then, leads in 2017 and 2018 pointed investigators to three men. Two of them had already died. The third, Ronnie Busick, was arrested in April 2018 and charged with murder, kidnapping and arson. Investigators believe the girls were held for days in a mobile home in Picher before they were killed. In 2020, Busick pleaded guilty to accessory to murder, and as part of the deal he was supposed to help find the girls' remains. Searches in Picher turned up nothing. He was sentenced to ten years in prison. Ashley and Lauria have still never been found. If you know anything, call the Craig County Sheriff's Office or the OSBI.
cases.summary: At about 5:30 a.m. on Dec. 30, 1999, the Welch Fire Department responded to the burning mobile home of Danny and Kathy Freeman near Welch, Craig County. Both were found shot; their daughter Ashley Freeman and her friend Lauria Bible, both 16, were missing and have never been found. Leads in 2017 and early 2018 indicated Ronnie Busick, Warren Phillip Welch II and David Pennington were involved; Welch (d. 2007) and Pennington (d. 2015) were deceased. The sheriff says the investigation indicates the girls were kidnapped, held in a mobile home in Picher for days, and strangled. Busick was arrested in April 2018 on four counts of first-degree murder, two of kidnapping and one of first-degree arson. In July 2020 he pleaded guilty to accessory to murder and agreed to help locate the remains; a root cellar in Picher was searched in August 2020 without success. On Aug. 31, 2020, Judge Shawn Taylor sentenced him to 15 years — 10 in prison and 5 suspended (CF-2018-56). The sheriff continues to list the case as Open and seeks tips.

cases.audioScript: At 9:02 on the morning of April 19, 1995, a truck bomb exploded at the north entrance of the Alfred P. Murrah Federal Building, right here in downtown Oklahoma City. The bomb, made from fertilizer and fuel oil, was packed into a rented Ryder truck. It killed 168 people, including 19 children, and injured hundreds more. More than 300 nearby buildings were damaged or destroyed. Just 90 minutes after the blast, an Oklahoma state trooper pulled over a car about 80 miles north of the city for a missing license plate. The driver, Timothy McVeigh, had a concealed weapon and was arrested. Meanwhile, the FBI traced the truck's axle to a body shop in Junction City, Kansas, and a composite sketch led agents to McVeigh's name, and to the discovery that he was already in jail. McVeigh was convicted on all counts in 1997 and executed in 2001. His friend Terry Nichols was convicted of conspiracy and manslaughter and sentenced to life without parole, and Michael Fortier, who knew of the plot, got 12 years. Today the site is the Oklahoma City National Memorial.
cases.summary: On April 19, 1995, at 9:02 a.m., an ammonium nitrate-fuel oil bomb in a rented Ryder truck exploded at the north entrance of the Alfred P. Murrah Federal Building in downtown Oklahoma City, killing 168 people, including 19 children, and injuring hundreds. About 90 minutes after the bombing, an Oklahoma state trooper stopped Timothy McVeigh roughly 80 miles north of the city for a missing license plate and arrested him for carrying a concealed weapon. The FBI traced the truck's rear axle to a Junction City, Kansas, body shop, and a composite sketch and hotel records identified McVeigh, who was found to be already in custody. McVeigh and Terry Nichols were indicted in federal court on Aug. 10, 1995; Michael Fortier, who knew of the plot, was also indicted. McVeigh was convicted on all counts on June 2, 1997, and executed on June 11, 2001; Nichols was convicted of conspiracy and manslaughter and sentenced to life without parole; Fortier was sentenced to 12 years. The FBI investigation included more than 28,000 interviews and 43,000 leads. In a separate Oklahoma state trial in McAlester, a jury convicted Nichols on 161 counts of first-degree murder (May 2004); on Aug. 9, 2004, Judge Steven Taylor sentenced him to 161 consecutive life terms without parole after jurors deadlocked on the death penalty.

cases.audioScript: In December 2001, a child's body was spotted floating in a coastal inlet near Waldport, Oregon. Three days later, a little girl was found in the same inlet. A tip led investigators to Michigan, where relatives identified the children as four-year-old Zachary and three-year-old Sadie Longo. Their family had moved to the Oregon coast just months earlier. Divers then searched a marina in nearby Newport and found the children's mother, thirty-four-year-old MaryJane, and their two-year-old sister, Madison. Their father, Christian Longo, was gone. He had flown to Cancun, and in January 2002 the FBI put him on its Ten Most Wanted list. Days later, after a tip from a tourist who recognized his photo, he was arrested at a beach camp in Tulum, Mexico. Longo admitted killing MaryJane and Madison but blamed his wife for the deaths of the older children. In April 2003, a jury rejected that claim and convicted him. He was sentenced to death. In 2022, Oregon's governor commuted every death sentence in the state to life without parole.
cases.summary: On Dec. 19, 2001, a child's body was found in a coastal inlet near Waldport, Oregon; a second child was found there three days later. On Christmas Eve, relatives in Michigan identified them as Zachary, 4, and Sadie Ann, 3. Divers then found their mother, MaryJane, 34, and sister Madison, 2, in a Newport marina. The family had moved to the Newport area from Ypsilanti, Michigan, about three months earlier. Christian Longo was charged with aggravated murder; he had flown from San Francisco to Cancun on Dec. 27. Added to the FBI's Ten Most Wanted list on Jan. 11, 2002, he was arrested in Tulum, Mexico, on Jan. 13, 2002, after a tourist recognized his photo. Longo admitted killing MaryJane and Madison but claimed his wife had drowned the older children. On April 7, 2003, a Lincoln County jury convicted him of aggravated murder in the deaths of Zachary and Sadie; on April 16, 2003, he was sentenced to death. On Dec. 13, 2022, Gov. Kate Brown commuted all 17 Oregon death sentences to life without parole.
cases.solvedHow: Solved by identification of the children through a tip, an FBI Ten Most Wanted manhunt, a public tip from a tourist in Mexico, and a jury trial.

cases.audioScript: On the morning of June fourth, 2010, seven-year-old Kyron Horman was at Skyline Elementary School in Portland, Oregon, where he was attending his school's science fair. He was wearing a black T-shirt with C-S-I in green letters, black cargo pants and black sneakers with orange trim, and he may have had his glasses on. At eight forty-five, according to the sheriff's timeline, his stepmother reported she last saw him walking down the hallway toward his classroom. At three-thirty that afternoon, Kyron did not come home on his school bus, and at three fifty-six a school employee called 911. The search grew into the largest single search effort in the state of Oregon, with local, county, state and federal partners, including the FBI. Kyron has not been seen or heard from since. In 2025 the Multnomah County Sheriff's Office finished digitizing the entire case, and it is now using new technology to analyze more than fifty-three hundred documents. District Attorney Nathan Vasquez says a lack of news on the case does not mean a lack of progress. Kyron has brown hair, blue eyes, and a distinct V-shaped strawberry birthmark on his forehead. A fifty-thousand-dollar reward is available, and the sheriff's tip line is 503-988-0560.
cases.summary: Kyron Horman, 7, was last seen on the morning of June 4, 2010, at Skyline Elementary School in Portland, Oregon, where he was attending his school's science fair. According to the sheriff's official timeline, his stepmother reported last seeing him at 8:45 a.m. walking down the hallway toward his classroom; he did not return home on his school bus at 3:30 p.m., and a Skyline Elementary employee called 911 at 3:56 p.m. Sheriff Dan Staton notified the FBI that evening, and the response grew into the largest single search effort in the state of Oregon, coordinated with the East County Major Crimes Team, the FBI, the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children and the district attorney. He remains missing. On June 4, 2026, the Multnomah County Sheriff's Office said it had finished digitizing the case in 2025, was applying new technology to more than 5,300 documents and over half a terabyte of data, and had increased staffing. A $50,000 reward is available for information leading to the resolution of his disappearance. In September 2026, KATU reported that a former prosecutor had sued the Multnomah County DA over redacted case records.

cases.audioScript: In 1983, near Springfield, Oregon, a young mother named Diane Downs drove her three children to a hospital. All three had been shot. Seven-year-old Cheryl Lynn died. Her two siblings survived. Downs, who had a bullet wound in her own forearm, told police a man had tried to carjack the family. Investigators came to believe there was no stranger. They said Downs shot the children herself, then shot her own arm. In 1984 she was convicted of murder, attempted murder and assault. The court sentenced her as a dangerous offender to life in prison, plus consecutive sentences. Decades later, she still says she did not shoot her children. In a virtual hearing in October 2025 she again maintained her innocence, and in December 2025 the Oregon Board of Parole denied her release, finding she continues to remain a danger. A federal court in 2023 also rejected her challenge to an earlier parole decision.
cases.summary: On May 19, 1983, Diane Downs shot her three children near Springfield, Oregon, killing 7-year-old Cheryl Lynn and wounding the other two; she shot herself in the forearm and blamed a carjacker, investigators said. She was arrested about nine months later, in February 1984. A jury convicted her on June 17, 1984, of murder, attempted murder and first-degree assault and sentenced as a dangerous offender to life plus consecutive terms. She maintains her innocence; the Oregon Board of Parole denied parole again in December 2025.

cases.audioScript: On January twenty-sixth, 1968, nineteen-year-old Linda Slawson vanished while selling encyclopedias door to door in southeast Portland, Oregon. Over the next fifteen months, three more young women disappeared. Jan Whitney, twenty-three, vanished after her car broke down on Interstate five near Albany. Karen Sprinker, nineteen, disappeared from a Salem department store parking lot, and Linda Salee, nineteen, vanished on a trip to a Portland mall. In May 1969, the bodies of Sprinker and Salee were found in the Long Tom River, and Whitney's was found in the Willamette River that July. Jerry Brudos was arrested in June 1969 and pleaded guilty to three murders. Oregon did not have the death penalty then, and he received three consecutive life terms. He confessed to killing Slawson too, but that charge was dropped for lack of evidence, and her body has never been found. Victims' relatives repeatedly urged the parole board to keep him locked up. He died in the Oregon State Penitentiary in March 2006, Oregon's longest-held prisoner.

Jerry Brudos was arrested in June 1969 and pleaded guilty to murdering Whitney, Sprinker and Salee (three consecutive life terms); a charge for Slawson, whose body was never found, was dropped. He died in prison Mar. 28, 2006.

cases.audioScript: On May twenty-second, 1989, Dawn Marie Mozino finished her shift in food services at Bryn Mawr Hospital, on Philadelphia's Main Line. She was in her early twenties, and she planned to take public transportation home, as she usually did. According to the FBI, Dawn was last seen at the bus stop near the hospital. She never arrived home. Dawn had a learning disability, and her family knew she always checked in. That evening, her sister and mother drove to the hospital, sensing something was wrong, and called the police from there. Searches followed, with dogs, search teams and friends hanging flyers all over town. Weeks later, in June 1989, a witness told police she had seen Dawn speaking with a man near the bus stop around the time she vanished. No one has ever been charged in Dawn's disappearance, and no suspect is named here. Dawn is about four foot ten, with curly brown hair and brown eyes. The FBI's Violent Criminal Apprehension Program still lists her as missing. If you were at the Bryn Mawr Hospital bus stop that day, please contact investigators.
cases.summary: Dawn Marie Mozino was last seen on May 22, 1989, at the bus stop near Bryn Mawr Hospital in Bryn Mawr, Pennsylvania, where she worked in food services; she never arrived home (FBI ViCAP). The FBI lists her age as 24 at the time and describes her as learning disabled; the Charley Project lists a date of birth of June 19, 1965 (making her 23) and says she planned to use public transportation. Main Line Today, interviewing her sister, reports that the family went to the hospital that evening and called police, and that in June 1989 a woman told Radnor Township Police she had seen Dawn talking with a man near the bus stop. That account and the man's identity are not confirmed by an official release, and no one has been charged; no suspect is named here. Dawn is 4'10", about 110 lbs, with curly brown hair and brown eyes.

cases.audioScript: On the afternoon of February twenty-second, 1985, eight-year-old Cherrie Mahan stepped off her school bus on Cornplanter Road in Winfield Township, Butler County, Pennsylvania. It was about five past four. Her home was just up the hill, and her mother was waiting inside, excited to take Cherrie to a friend's house. Cherrie never made it up the hill. People who saw her get off the bus said they noticed a blue or green van behind it, and a blue sedan in the area. Neither vehicle, nor their drivers, has ever been identified. Cherrie was wearing a gray jacket, a denim skirt, blue leg warmers, tan ankle boots, and carrying a blue bookbag. Pennsylvania State Police in Butler still classify the case as active. Investigators have interviewed countless people, and tips still come in from across the country. In February 2026, state police announced a five-thousand-dollar reward for information that solves the case or leads to Cherrie. The National Center for Missing and Exploited Children has released age-progressed images of her. If you know anything, call State Police in Butler at seven two four, two eight four, eight one hundred.
cases.summary: Cherrie Ann Mahan, 8, got off her school bus at about 4:05 p.m. on Feb. 22, 1985, on Cornplanter Road in Winfield Township, Butler County, Pennsylvania, at the bottom of the hill below her home, and was never seen again (CBS Pittsburgh; Butler Eagle). Witnesses reported a blue or green van behind the bus and a blue sedan in the area; neither has been identified (CBS Pittsburgh). She wore a gray jacket, denim skirt, blue leg warmers, tan ankle boots and a blue bookbag (WPXI). Pennsylvania State Police Troop D in Butler leads the case and in 2024 described it as active rather than cold; in February 2026 PSP announced a $5,000 reward, adding to a separate $100,000 offered by a private investigator (WPXI). NCMEC lists her as missing from Cabot, PA, with an age-progressed image. No one has been charged.

cases.audioScript: Late on the night of December third, 2003, Assistant U.S. Attorney Jonathan Luna was working at the federal courthouse in Baltimore, finishing a plea agreement in a drug case. He was thirty-eight, a husband and a father. He left the courthouse in his car. Hours later, around dawn on December fourth, he was found face-down in a small creek on a well-drilling company's property in Brecknock Township, Lancaster County, Pennsylvania, within earshot of the Pennsylvania Turnpike. His car was nearby, stained with blood. Investigators traced a winding route, including a credit card used at a gas station in King of Prussia. Luna had been stabbed thirty-six times, most of the wounds around his neck. The county pathologist ruled the cause of death freshwater drowning and multiple stab wounds to the neck, and the manner of death homicide. Over the years, some officials publicly raised the possibility of suicide, but the case remains an open homicide with the Pennsylvania State Police and the Lancaster County District Attorney. No suspect has ever been identified. If you know anything about what happened to Jonathan Luna, contact the Pennsylvania State Police.
cases.summary: Jonathan Luna, 38, an Assistant U.S. Attorney in Baltimore, was working late at the federal courthouse on Dec. 3, 2003, preparing a plea agreement. He left in his car, and his credit card was later used near the Pennsylvania Turnpike in King of Prussia. On Dec. 4, 2003, he was found face-down in a small creek on a well-drilling company's property in Brecknock Township, Lancaster County, with a blood-stained car nearby. Autopsy and toxicology reports unsealed by the Lancaster County DA (reported 2025) state 36 stab wounds, most to the neck, and a cause of death of freshwater drowning and multiple stab wounds to the neck; the manner was ruled homicide. Officials have publicly disagreed about how he died, and suicide was raised over the years, but the case remains an open homicide under the Pennsylvania State Police and the DA, with FBI involvement. No suspect has been identified or charged.

cases.audioScript: On April fifteenth, 2005, Ray Gricar, the longtime district attorney of Centre County, Pennsylvania, took a half day off work and drove away from Bellefonte in his red Mini Cooper. Around eleven-thirty that morning, he called his girlfriend and said he was driving east on Route 192 toward Lewisburg. He never came home. The next day, his car was found in the parking lot of the Street of Shops in Lewisburg, near the Susquehanna River. His cell phone was inside. There was no sign of him and no sign of a struggle. That summer, fishermen found his county-issued laptop in the river below a bridge, with the hard drive missing. Months later a badly damaged hard drive turned up on the riverbank nearby. Nothing on it could be recovered. Gricar was fifty-nine and had been the county's top prosecutor for about twenty years. In 2011, at his daughter's request, a judge declared him legally dead. But no body has ever been found, and no one knows whether he was harmed, took his own life, or chose to disappear. Pennsylvania State Police say the case is still open. If you know what happened to Ray Gricar, they want to hear from you.
cases.summary: Ray Frank Gricar, 59, Centre County district attorney for about 20 years, left work for a half day on April 15, 2005, driving his red 2004 Mini Cooper. Around 11:30 a.m. he called his girlfriend and said he was driving east-northeast on Route 192 toward Lewisburg (Solve the Case summary). The next day his car was found in the parking lot of the Street of Shops in Lewisburg, Union County, near the Susquehanna River, with his cell phone inside and no sign of foul play reported. On July 30, 2005, fishermen found his county-issued laptop in the river below a bridge between Lewisburg and Milton with the hard drive missing; a badly damaged hard drive later found on the riverbank about 100 yards away yielded no recoverable data. Bellefonte police led the investigation before turning it over to the Pennsylvania State Police. In July 2011 a Centre County judge declared Gricar legally dead on his daughter's petition (Daily Collegian). State police said in 2026 that the investigation is still active. No one has been charged, and no evidence has established whether he was harmed, died by suicide or left voluntarily.

cases.audioScript: On February twenty-fifth, 1957, the body of a little boy was found in a cardboard box beside Susquehanna Road, in Philadelphia's Fox Chase neighborhood. He had been severely beaten and was malnourished. No one ever came forward to claim him. For sixty-five years he was known only as the Boy in the Box, and his headstone read America's Unknown Child. His body was exhumed in 1998, and again in 2019, when a forensic anthropologist recovered enough DNA for modern testing. Genetic genealogy led investigators to his mother's family and to his birth certificate. On December eighth, 2022, Philadelphia police announced his name: Joseph Augustus Zarelli, born January thirteenth, 1953, in West Philadelphia. Police said his parents are both deceased, and did not name them out of respect for his living siblings. Then-Commissioner Danielle Outlaw called it the city's oldest unsolved homicide, and said the search for justice continues. Anyone with information can call the Philadelphia Police Homicide Unit at 215-686-3334, or call or text 215-686-TIPS.
cases.summary: On Feb. 25, 1957, the body of a young boy was found naked, severely beaten and malnourished in a cardboard box beside Susquehanna Road in the Fox Chase section of Philadelphia. An autopsy found multiple abrasions, contusions, a subdural hemorrhage and pleural effusions. He went unidentified for 65 years and was buried under a headstone reading "America's Unknown Child." He was exhumed in 1998 and again in April 2019; the 2019 DNA allowed genetic genealogy work that led to his mother's family and his birth records. On Dec. 8, 2022, Philadelphia police identified him as Joseph Augustus Zarelli, born Jan. 13, 1953, of West Philadelphia; he was never reported missing. Police said both parents are deceased and did not name them. The homicide remains open with no arrests.
cases.solvedHow: Identity solved in 2022 via exhumation, DNA, forensic genetic genealogy and court-ordered vital records; the homicide itself remains unsolved.
cases.techniques: Exhumation (1998, 2019); DNA analysis; Forensic genetic genealogy; Vital-records search; Public posters and canvassing (1957)

cases.audioScript: In September 1894, a man named Benjamin Pitezel was found dead in Philadelphia. His business partner was Herman Webster Mudgett, better known as H. H. Holmes, the man behind a notorious building in Chicago later called his "murder castle." Holmes and Pitezel had planned to fake Pitezel's death and split a ten-thousand-dollar insurance payout. Instead, Pitezel really died, and Holmes claimed the money. Holmes was arrested in Boston in November 1894, accused of insurance fraud, and Pitezel's wife told investigators she feared Holmes had killed her husband. In July 1895, the bodies of three of the Pitezel children were found buried in a basement in Toronto. That October, Holmes went on trial in Philadelphia for Benjamin Pitezel's murder, defending himself at first. On November second, 1895, the jury convicted him of first-degree murder. He was hanged at Moyamensing Prison on May seventh, 1896. He had confessed in writing to twenty-seven murders, though historians doubt much of what he claimed.
cases.summary: Benjamin F. Pitezel, a business associate of Herman Webster Mudgett ("H. H. Holmes"), died in Philadelphia on Sept. 2, 1894; the two had planned to fake Pitezel's death and split $10,000 in insurance money, and Holmes collected the payout. Holmes was arrested in Boston in November 1894 on insurance-fraud accusations; Pitezel's wife confessed to the fraud and said she feared Holmes had killed her husband. In July 1895 the bodies of three Pitezel children were found buried in a Toronto basement, and police in Chicago searched Holmes's building there, later dubbed the "castle." Holmes's murder trial began in Philadelphia on Oct. 28, 1895; he was convicted of first-degree murder on Nov. 2, 1895, denied a new trial and sentenced to death on Nov. 30, 1895. He was hanged at Moyamensing Prison on May 7, 1896, after a written confession to 27 murders.
cases.solvedHow: The insurance-fraud investigation, Pitezel's wife's confession, and the later discovery of the Pitezel children's bodies led to Holmes's prosecution in Philadelphia, where the case was strongest.

cases.audioScript: On the night of June seventh, 2021, Maggie Murdaugh, fifty-two, and her son Paul, twenty-two, were shot to death near the dog kennels on the family's hunting property, known as Moselle, in rural Colleton County, South Carolina. The family was one of the most prominent in the Lowcountry. Maggie's husband, attorney Alex Murdaugh, told investigators he had been visiting his ailing father and found the bodies when he returned. In July 2022, a Colleton County grand jury indicted Alex Murdaugh on two counts of murder. In March 2023, after a trial in Walterboro, a jury convicted him and he was sentenced to life in prison. He separately pleaded guilty to dozens of financial crimes. But in May 2026, the South Carolina Supreme Court unanimously reversed the murder convictions, finding that the county clerk of court had improperly influenced the jury, and ordered a new trial. Today, Alex Murdaugh is again presumed innocent of the murders. He denies killing his wife and son. His retrial is scheduled for April 2027 in Sumter County. He remains in prison on his financial crime sentences. Maggie and Paul are remembered by the family and friends who loved them.
cases.summary: Margaret "Maggie" Murdaugh, 52, and her son Paul, 22, were shot to death on June 7, 2021, near the dog kennels at the family's hunting property in the Islandton area of rural Colleton County, South Carolina (Live 5 News; SCAG). Alex Murdaugh told investigators he found them after visiting his ailing father. On July 14, 2022, a Colleton County grand jury indicted him on two counts of murder and two counts of possession of a weapon during a violent crime (SCAG). After a trial in Walterboro he was convicted and sentenced to life in prison in March 2023. On May 13, 2026, the S.C. Supreme Court (Opinion No. 28329) reversed the denial of his new-trial motion because of improper jury contact by former Colleton County Clerk of Court Becky Hill, and remanded for a new trial (the court also gave guidance on admitting financial-crimes evidence). The Attorney General said the state would retry him. Judge McCaslin moved the retrial to Sumter County and set it for April 5, 2027; on Nov. 20, 2026 she denied his motion to dismiss the indictments (ABC News). Murdaugh remains imprisoned on 27-year state and 40-year federal sentences for financial crimes, has admitted stealing from clients, and denies the killings. He is presumed innocent of the murder charges pending retrial.

cases.audioScript: In April 2009, seventeen-year-old Brittanee Drexel from the Rochester, New York, area went to Myrtle Beach, South Carolina, with friends for spring break. On April twenty-fifth, she was last seen outside the Blue Water Resort on Ocean Boulevard. Then she vanished. For thirteen years her family pleaded for answers. Investigators had a person of interest for more than a decade, but no charges. Investigators re-examined cell phone data and surveillance footage, and kept coming back to a man named Raymond Moody. In May 2022, Moody confessed and led investigators to her remains in a wooded area of Georgetown County. On October nineteenth, 2022, at the Georgetown County Courthouse, Moody pleaded guilty to her murder, kidnapping and rape. He was sentenced to life in prison, plus thirty years for each of the other crimes. Brittanee's mother, Dawn, spent those thirteen years keeping her daughter's name in the news. In the end, it was a long, patient investigation that finally brought Brittanee home.
cases.summary: Brittanee Marie Drexel, 17, of the Rochester, N.Y., area, traveled to Myrtle Beach with friends during spring break and was last seen on April 25, 2009, outside the Blue Water Resort on Ocean Boulevard (WMBF; Charley Project). In May 2022 the Georgetown County Sheriff announced that human remains found in the Harmony Township area were hers; Solicitor Jimmy Richardson said evidence led authorities to the site on May 4 and the remains were uncovered May 7 (WMBF). Raymond Douglas Moody, who had been a person of interest for more than a decade, confessed and led authorities to the remains (ABC News). On October 19, 2022, Moody pleaded guilty to murder, kidnapping and first-degree criminal sexual conduct and was sentenced to life in prison plus 30 years each for kidnapping and rape (ABC News; WMBF). ABC News reported investigators re-examined cell phone data and surveillance footage in 2019 and 2020 and pinned down locations of Drexel's phone; WMBF reported improved technology let investigators track her phone around Georgetown County.

cases.audioScript: On November 2, 2015, four members of one family were found shot to death inside their home near Pendleton. The victims were Mike and Cathy Scott and their mothers, Barbara Scott and Violet Taylor. The coroner said there was no sign of forced entry, and the family was likely killed on Halloween. The 911 call came from Cathy's daughter, Amy Vilardi, who lived with her husband in a separate home on the same property. For years the case went unsolved. Then, in December 2023, the Anderson County Sheriff's Office charged Amy and her husband, Rosmore "Ross" Vilardi, with four counts of murder each. In February 2026, a jury found Amy Vilardi guilty on all four counts, and she was sentenced to life in prison. Ross Vilardi has not been convicted and is presumed innocent. His trial was set to start in October 2026, but a judge suppressed evidence from a search of the couple's trailer, and prosecutors appealed, putting the case on hold.

Amy Vilardi was convicted on all four counts on Feb. 27, 2026, and sentenced to four life terms. cases.audioScript: On April seventh, 1993, forty-two-year-old Monica Wickre went out for drinks in Aberdeen, South Dakota. The state Division of Criminal Investigation says she was last seen leaving a bar with a man, or men, who were not known. News interviews later named that last stop as a bar called The Body Shop, which has since closed. A missing-person report was filed with Aberdeen police on April twenty-sixth, and searchers found no sign of her. Then, on June sixteenth, a passerby in a canoe found her body in the James River just outside town. She was identified through dental records. Because of decomposition, a cause of death could not be determined, but investigators suspected foul play and have treated the case as a homicide. More than thirty years later, no one has been charged. In 2021, her family offered a ten-thousand-dollar reward for information leading to an arrest and conviction, and a sheriff’s official said the office had never stopped working the case. If you know something, call the Brown County Sheriff’s Office at 605-626-7100, or the South Dakota DCI tip line at 605-394-1884.
cases.summary: Monica L. Bercier Wickre, 42, was last seen in Aberdeen, South Dakota, on April 7, 1993, after going out for drinks. The South Dakota Division of Criminal Investigation’s unresolved-cases page states that she was last seen leaving a bar in Aberdeen with an unknown male or males, and that her badly decomposed remains were discovered in the James River in June 1993 by a passing boater. NBC Dateline, quoting then–Chief Deputy Dave Lunzman, reports that a missing-person report was filed with the Aberdeen Police Department on April 26, 1993, that her remains were found in the James River just outside Aberdeen on June 16, 1993, by a passerby in a canoe, and that she was identified through dental records. A cause of death could not be determined because of decomposition; foul play was suspected and the case has been treated as a homicide. It remains unsolved, and no one has been charged. As of June 2024, the Aberdeen Insider reported that the Brown County Sheriff’s Office was still overseeing the unsolved homicide. In April 2021, NBC Dateline reported that the family had collected a $10,000 reward for information leading to an arrest and conviction, and directed tips to the Brown County Sheriff’s Office at 605-626-7100. The DCI also publishes a tip line, 605-394-1884, and DCITips@state.sd.us.
cases.solvedHow: Unsolved. cases.audioScript: On the morning of April twenty-ninth, 2003, thirteen-year-old Tabitha Danielle Tuders left her home in Nashville, Tennessee, to walk to the school bus. She never got on the bus, and she never arrived at school. She has not been seen or heard from since. Tabitha was a student at Bailey Middle School. The FBI describes her then as five feet one and about a hundred pounds, with sandy blonde hair and blue eyes. In 2026, twenty-three years later, Metro Nashville Police again asked for the public's help. Police said neighbors and other children reported seeing her around seven that morning as she walked toward the bus stop in East Nashville. A red car was seen near where she was last spotted. When the car drove away, Tabitha was gone. No one has ever been arrested. The FBI is offering a reward of up to fifty thousand dollars for information that leads to her recovery and to a prosecution. If you know anything, contact the FBI, Metro Nashville Police at 615-862-8600, or Nashville Crime Stoppers.
cases.summary: Tabitha Danielle Tuders, born Feb. 15, 1990, in Nashville, was 13 when she disappeared on April 29, 2003. The FBI says she was last seen early that morning at her residence in Nashville, that she left the house on her way to board the school bus, that she never got on the bus and did not arrive at school, and that she has not been seen or heard from since. The Metropolitan Nashville Police Department identifies her as a 13-year-old student at Bailey Middle School and still lists her as missing on its official page (last updated Oct. 17, 2025). The FBI lists her height at the time as 5 feet 1 inch and her weight as 100 pounds, with sandy blonde hair and blue eyes; MNPD lists her height as 4 feet 9 inches, weight 100 lbs, sandy hair and blue eyes. Both agencies note a birthmark on her stomach, a scar on her finger, and pierced ears. In April 2026, Metro Nashville Police renewed a public appeal on the 23rd anniversary of her disappearance. WSMV and FOX 17 reported that police said she was last spotted around 7 a.m. in East Nashville, that neighbors and other children saw her walking to her bus stop, that a red car was seen near where she was last seen, and that when the car drove away, she was gone. The case remains unsolved. No arrest or charges have been announced. The FBI offers a reward of up to $50,000 for information leading to her recovery and the prosecution of the person or persons responsible. Tips may be submitted to the FBI, to MNPD Youth Services at (615) 862-7417 or police at (615) 862-8600, or to Nashville Crime Stoppers (74-CRIME).

cases.audioScript: At about three twenty in the morning on April twenty-second, 2018, a man got out of his car at a Waffle House in Antioch, here in southeast Nashville, carrying an AR-15 rifle. Police said he shot two people in the parking lot, then walked inside and kept firing. Four young people were killed: Taurean Sanderlin, Joe Perez, DeEbony Groves and Akilah DaSilva. None of them was older than twenty-nine. A customer named James Shaw Junior wrestled the rifle away from the gunman. Police said his actions saved many lives. The shooter ran, and a manhunt lasting more than a day followed before police arrested Travis Reinking. At trial in 2022, his lawyers argued he was insane. Prosecutors said he had planned the shooting, packed an escape bag, and knew it was wrong. The jury found him guilty on all sixteen counts and sentenced him to life without parole. Nashville's district attorney said nothing can bring the victims back, but the sentence means Reinking will never threaten anyone again. Before the sentence, the jury heard from relatives of all four people who were killed.
cases.summary: At about 3:23 a.m. on April 22, 2018, a gunman got out of his car at a Waffle House restaurant in the Antioch area of Nashville and opened fire with an AR-15 rifle, killing two people outside before going inside and continuing to shoot, according to police. Taurean C. Sanderlin, 29, a restaurant employee, Joe R. Perez, 20, DeEbony Groves, 21, and Akilah DaSilva, 23, were killed; others were wounded. Customer James Shaw Jr., 29, wrestled the rifle away from the shooter; police said his actions undoubtedly saved many lives. The suspect, Travis Reinking, 29, of Morton, Illinois, fled, and a manhunt lasting more than a day followed before he was arrested on April 23, 2018. The Secret Service said Reinking had been arrested in July 2017 for crossing a security barrier near the White House. At a 10-day trial in 2022, the defense pursued an insanity defense; prosecutors argued he had planned a mass shooting in advance, packed an escape bag and knew his actions were wrong. On Feb. 4, 2022, the jury found Reinking guilty of all 16 counts, and on Feb. 5 sentenced him to life in prison without parole. On July 15, 2022, Davidson County Criminal Court Judge Mark Fishburn ordered the four life sentences to run consecutively, plus 114 years on the remaining counts, the Tennessean and NewsChannel 5 reported.

cases.audioScript: On July eighteenth, 2010, former Memphis Grizzlies player Lorenzen Wright was last seen leaving his ex-wife's home. Early the next morning, Germantown police received a 911 call from his cellphone, but the call was interrupted by gunfire. Ten days later, on July twenty-eighth, his body was found in a field near Hacks Cross and Winchester roads in Memphis. He had been shot multiple times. He was thirty-four. The case went unsolved for years. In November 2017, authorities announced they had found the murder weapon in a lake near Walnut, Mississippi. A month later, his ex-wife Sherra Wright and Billy Ray Turner, a Collierville landscaper who attended her church, were indicted. In July 2019, Sherra Wright pleaded guilty to facilitation of first-degree murder and was sentenced to thirty years. In March 2022 a jury deliberated less than three hours before convicting Turner of premeditated first-degree murder, conspiracy and attempted murder. He was sentenced to life in prison plus twenty-five years.

cases.audioScript: On the morning of October ninth, 2020, twenty-one-year-old Reagan Simmons-Hancock was at her home here in New Boston. She was about thirty-five weeks pregnant with a daughter she had already named Braxlynn. A woman she knew, Taylor Parker, came to the house and killed her, then cut the baby from her body and drove off toward Oklahoma. Near De Kalb, a Texas state trooper pulled Parker over and found a newborn in her lap. Parker claimed she had just given birth on the side of the road. Baby Braxlynn was pronounced dead at a hospital. Investigators found that Parker had faked a pregnancy for months, with announcements, sonogram pictures and even a gender reveal. In October 2022, a Bowie County jury took less than an hour to convict her of capital murder. A month later, the same jury sentenced her to death. Her direct appeals ended in 2026, when the U.S. Supreme Court declined to hear her case. She remains on Texas death row with no execution date. Reagan's family looked on in the courtroom as the death sentence was returned.
cases.summary: On the morning of Oct. 9, 2020, Taylor Rene Parker, then 27, killed 21-year-old Reagan Simmons-Hancock at her home in New Boston, Texas; Simmons-Hancock was about 35 weeks pregnant. Parker cut the unborn child from her body and fled toward Oklahoma; a Texas state trooper stopped her near De Kalb and found her with the newborn, whom she claimed she had just delivered. The baby, Braxlynn Sage Hancock, was pronounced dead at a hospital, and Parker was arrested the same day at a McCurtain County, Okla., hospital. Prosecutors said Parker had faked a pregnancy for months, including announcements, sonogram images and a gender reveal, to hold on to her relationship with her boyfriend. A Bowie County grand jury indicted her in December 2020, and prosecutors announced in January 2021 that they would seek the death penalty. On Oct. 3, 2022, after about three weeks of testimony, the jury deliberated less than an hour and convicted Parker of capital murder. On Nov. 9, 2022, the jury sentenced her to death; KTBS reported the trial and punishment phases spanned 49 days with 142 witnesses. The Texas Court of Criminal Appeals upheld the conviction and sentence on Nov. 6, 2025, and the U.S. Supreme Court declined to take the case on May 18, 2026; no execution date has been set.

cases.audioScript: In June 1996, in Rowlett, Texas, two young brothers, five-year-old Damon and six-year-old Devon Routier, were found stabbed to death in their family's home. Their mother, Darlie Routier, was also wounded. She said an intruder had attacked them. Prosecutors did not believe her. In February 1997, she was convicted of capital murder for Damon's death and sentenced to death. She was never tried for Devon's death. Two earlier appeals were rejected. In 2021, a Dallas County judge ordered additional DNA testing. That testing found DNA from an unidentified man on a bloody sock found in an alley near the home, and new fingerprint analysis found prints on the knife and a door that did not belong to Darlie or her then-husband. In November 2026, her lawyers asked the Texas Court of Criminal Appeals to send the case back so the new evidence can be heard. The court has not ruled, and Darlie Routier remains on death row.

cases.audioScript: Beginning in December 1970, teenage boys began disappearing from the Heights neighborhood in Houston. Parents searched and reported them missing, and some received postcards claiming their sons had left town. On the morning of August eighth, 1973, Elmer Wayne Henley called Pasadena police and said he had just shot a man. The dead man was thirty-three-year-old Dean Corll. Henley led police to a boat storage shed Corll rented in southwest Houston, where seventeen bodies were dug up over two days. Four more were found near Lake Sam Rayburn, and Henley and David Brooks led police to graves on the beach at High Island. Both teenagers admitted helping Corll lure boys and bury them. Corll was never charged. Henley was sentenced to six life terms, and Brooks got life for murder and died in prison in 2020. DNA work later raised the count to at least twenty-eight victims. Some families, including the mother of seventeen-year-old Mark Scott, are still waiting to learn where their sons are. Henley was denied parole again in November 2025.
cases.summary: From 1970 to 1973, Dean Corll, aided by teenagers Elmer Wayne Henley and David Brooks, lured and killed at least 28 boys and young men in the Houston area. On Aug. 8, 1973 Henley shot Corll dead in Pasadena, then led police to bodies in a southwest Houston boat shed, near Lake Sam Rayburn and on High Island. Corll was never charged; Henley was sentenced to six life terms and denied parole in 2025; Brooks was convicted of murder and died in prison in 2020.
cases.solvedHow: Accomplice confession: after Henley shot Corll he called police, confessed and led them to the burial sites; Brooks also confessed. Both were convicted.

cases.audioScript: On May second, 1995, fifteen-year-old Kiplyn Davis disappeared from Spanish Fork High School in Utah. She was never seen again. For years, investigators heard rumors and conflicting stories from young men around her. In 2005, five men were indicted in federal court for lying to a grand jury about the case. In 2006, one of them, Timmy Olsen, was charged with her murder. In February 2011, Olsen pleaded guilty to manslaughter. Through his attorney, he claimed he and another person drove Kiplyn up Spanish Fork Canyon, and that the other person struck her in the head with a rock. That person was never identified in court. Under the plea deal, Olsen didn't have to reveal where Kiplyn's body is. He was sentenced to one to fifteen years in prison, and in February 2026 he walked free after serving his full sentence. More than thirty years later, Kiplyn's family is still asking the same question: where is she? Anyone with information is asked to contact the Spanish Fork Police Department.
cases.summary: Kiplyn Davis, 15, vanished from Spanish Fork High School on May 2, 1995. Investigators received conflicting accounts for years. In 2005, Timmy Olsen and four other men were indicted in federal court for perjury before a grand jury and lying to a federal agent about comments on moving a female's body and creating false alibis. In 2006 Olsen was charged with murder; charging documents said he admitted to multiple people that he raped and killed Davis. Christopher Jeppson was also charged with murder but pleaded no contest to obstruction of justice in 2009. On Feb. 11, 2011, Olsen pleaded guilty to manslaughter and was sentenced to 1–15 years. His attorney said Olsen saw another, unnamed person strike Kiplyn twice in the head with a rock in Spanish Fork Canyon and then helped move her body; prosecutors said they lacked evidence to charge anyone else. The plea did not require Olsen to reveal where her body is, and it has never been found. Olsen was released Feb. 10, 2026, after his sentence expired.
cases.solvedHow: Resolved by federal perjury prosecutions followed by a state murder charge and a manslaughter plea; remains never located.

cases.audioScript: On August twenty-sixth, 1982, three-year-old Rachael Runyan was playing with her brothers at a park behind her family's home in Sunset, Utah, while her mother made lunch. At about twelve-thirty, she was abducted. Her mother says a man lured Rachael across the park with a promise of ice cream, and Rachael told him she liked bubblegum. Police released two composite sketches and said they believed the man drove a blue 1973 Ford Pinto Squire station wagon with woodgrain sides. On September nineteenth, 1982, Rachael's body was found in a remote area of Morgan County. No arrests have ever been made. Rachael's mother, Elaine, spent decades advocating for missing children, and Utah's early child abduction alert, the Rachael Alert, was later united with the national AMBER Alert. The park where she was last seen now bears her name. Sunset police say it is still an active investigation, but there is no physical evidence tying anyone to the case. If you know anything, call Sunset Police at 801-825-1620, or the Utah cold case tip hotline at 833-DPS-SAFE.
cases.summary: Rachael Runyan, 3, was abducted around 12:30 p.m. on Aug. 26, 1982, from a park in Sunset, Davis County, Utah, according to the Utah Department of Public Safety's Bureau of Criminal Identification as cited by KUTV. She had been playing near her home with her brothers; her mother has said a man lured her across the park with the promise of ice cream and put her in his car. At the time, police described the suspect as a man aged about 25 to 35, 5 feet 8 inches to 6 feet tall, with a medium brown complexion, an afro and a mustache, believed to drive a blue 1973 Ford Pinto Squire station wagon with woodgrain stripes; two composite sketches were released. Her body was found on Sept. 19, 1982, in a remote area of Morgan County, in a mountain canyon stream. No arrests have ever been made. In 2024, Sunset Police Chief Brett Jamison said it remained an active investigation but there was no physical evidence tying anyone to the case. Her case led to Utah's Rachael Alert, first used in the 2002 Elizabeth Smart abduction and later united with the AMBER Alert. Sunset police ask anyone with information to call 801-825-1620 or 801-614-9111; tips also go to the Utah BCI unsolved homicide hotline at 833-DPS-SAFE (833-377-7233).
cases.solvedHow: Unsolved. Techniques so far: composite sketches and vehicle description (1982); repeated case-file reviews and lead follow-up by Sunset police; annual public appeals on Rachael Runyan Day.

cases.audioScript: In the early morning hours of September twenty-sixth, 2021, Beaver County deputies were called to a home in Minersville, Utah. In the garage they found thirty-eight-year-old Shane Michael Davis, shot in the back. He told medical staff he did not shoot himself, and he died shortly after reaching the hospital. Davis owned the home, and he shared it with his wife, Victoria Woerth, and her lover, Mike Allen Miller. Miller was arrested that same morning and admitted the shooting, claiming self-defense. But within days, detectives got a tip about Snapchat messages between Woerth and Miller. A witness told police he heard Woerth say the only way Mike could marry her was if Shane was dead. In 2023, Miller pleaded guilty to murder and conspiracy, and Woerth pleaded guilty to criminal solicitation. In October 2023, a judge sentenced Woerth to three years to life and Miller to consecutive prison terms, and urged the parole board to keep both locked up for at least fifteen years.
cases.summary: Shane Michael Davis, 38, was found shot in the garage of the Minersville home he owned in the early morning of Sept. 26, 2021; he told medical staff he did not shoot himself and died after arriving at the hospital. Mike Allen Miller, who lived in the home and was Davis's wife's lover, was arrested that morning and admitted the shooting, claiming self-defense; investigators found there was no immediate threat. Detectives received a tip about Snapchat messages between Victoria Woerth and Miller, and a witness said he heard Woerth say Miller could marry her only if Davis was dead; Woerth was charged in November 2021 with aggravated murder, criminal solicitation and conspiracy. In August 2023, Woerth pleaded guilty to criminal solicitation, with the other charges dismissed, and Miller pleaded guilty to murder, felony discharge of a firearm and conspiracy to commit aggravated murder. On Oct. 16, 2023, 5th District Judge Ann Marie McIff Allen sentenced Woerth to three years to life and Miller to consecutive terms, recommending that neither be paroled before serving at least 15 years.

cases.audioScript: Early on March fourth, 2022, thirty-nine-year-old Eric Richins was found dead in his family's home in Kamas, Utah. An autopsy found about five times the lethal dose of fentanyl in his system, and the medical examiner said the drug had been taken by mouth. His wife, Kouri Richins, later published a children's book about grief to help their three sons cope with losing their father. Weeks after promoting it on local television, she was arrested in May 2023 and charged with his murder. Prosecutors also said she had tried to poison him weeks earlier, on Valentine's Day, after he ate a sandwich and became ill. In March 2026, after a thirteen-day trial with more than forty prosecution witnesses, a Summit County jury unanimously found her guilty of aggravated murder, attempted aggravated murder, insurance fraud and forgery. Jurors found the attempted killing was committed for financial gain. The defense rested without calling any witnesses. She was later sentenced to life in prison without parole.

cases.audioScript: On August fifteenth, 2002, deputies in Henry County, Virginia, found Michael and Mary Short shot to death inside their home in the Oak Level community. Their nine-year-old daughter, Jennifer, was gone. An Amber Alert went out, and searchers spent weeks looking for her. About six weeks later, Jennifer's remains were found near a stream in Rockingham County, North Carolina, just across the state line. She had also been shot. Investigators called the killings execution-style. More than two decades later, no one has been arrested. In 2021, Henry County Sheriff Lane Perry relaunched a task force with the Rockingham County Sheriff's Office, Virginia State Police and the FBI to re-examine the case from scratch, including roughly a thousand pieces of evidence and new DNA testing. The family's home burned down in 2019. Henry County and Martinsville-Henry County Crime Stoppers are offering a reward of sixty-two thousand five hundred dollars for information leading to an arrest and conviction. If you know anything about what happened to Michael, Mary and Jennifer Short, call the Henry County Sheriff's Office at two seven six, six three eight, eight seven five one.
cases.summary: On Aug. 15, 2002, Michael and Mary Short were found shot to death in their home in the Oak Level community of Henry County, Virginia. Their 9-year-old daughter, Jennifer, was missing. Six weeks later, her remains were found in Rockingham County, North Carolina; she had also been shot. Investigators described the killings as execution-style. The case was never solved. In February 2019 the family's former home burned down. In October 2021, Sheriff Lane Perry announced a multi-agency task force (Henry County Sheriff's Office, Rockingham County Sheriff's Office, Virginia State Police and FBI) to review the case in its entirety, including physical evidence for new forensic testing. In 2022, WFXR/WGHP reported a DOJ Sexual Assault Kit Initiative grant would fund DNA analysis of about 1,000 evidence items. A $62,500 reward is offered.

cases.audioScript: On Saturday, December fifth, 2015, nineteen-year-old Katelin Akens was supposed to fly home to Arizona after visiting her family in Spotsylvania County, Virginia. A ride had been arranged to get her to Reagan National Airport. She was supposed to catch the Metro near Springfield Mall. But according to the Spotsylvania County Sheriff's Office, Katelin never appears on mall or Metro video, she never arrived at the airport, and her plane ticket was never used. Two days later, her suitcase turned up on the side of River Road in Spotsylvania, with her ID inside and most of its contents missing. No one knows who put it there. Her bank accounts have not been touched since the day she disappeared, and she has never contacted her family or friends again. In 2021, the FBI joined the search. Nearly eleven years later, the sheriff's office still lists the case as active. If you know anything about what happened to Katelin, call the Spotsylvania County Sheriff's Office at 540-582-5822.

cases.audioScript: In January 2011, twenty-one-year-old Bethany Decker was living in Ashburn, Virginia, with her young son. She was about five months pregnant. Her live-in boyfriend, Ronald Roldan, told authorities he last saw her at their apartment on January twenty-ninth. Weeks went by without anyone hearing from her, and on February nineteenth her family reported her missing. Her car was still in the apartment complex parking lot. For nearly ten years, the Loudoun County Sheriff's Office kept looking. Then, in November 2020, Roldan was charged with abduction and brought back to Virginia from North Carolina. In 2022, he pleaded guilty to second-degree murder. Months later, he told detectives he had put her body in the apartment complex's trash compactor. In February 2023, he was sentenced to forty years, with all but twelve and a half suspended. Bethany's remains have never been found. As the judge said at sentencing, nobody in the courtroom was getting closure.
cases.summary: Bethany Anne Decker, 21, of Ashburn, Va., was the mother of a 17-month-old son and about five months pregnant. Her live-in boyfriend, Ronald D. Roldan, said he last saw her at their Ashburn apartment on Jan. 29, 2011. Her family reported her missing on Feb. 19, 2011; her car was left in the complex parking lot. In November 2020 the Loudoun County Sheriff's Office charged Roldan with abduction and extradited him from North Carolina. He pleaded guilty to second-degree murder in November 2022. In January 2023, he told detectives she tripped and hit her head and that he put her body in the complex's trash compactor; he did not call 911. On Feb. 21, 2023, Judge Alfred Swersky sentenced him to 40 years with all but 12.5 years suspended. Her remains have never been found.

cases.audioScript: On March second, 1996, Alicia Showalter Reynolds was driving south on Route 29, from Baltimore to Charlottesville, Virginia, to meet her mother. She never arrived. Witnesses saw her car stopped on the southbound shoulder of Route 29 in Culpeper County, with a white man standing outside it. Her Mercury Tracer was found abandoned there later that same day. As news spread, other women came forward to say a man had stopped, or tried to stop, them on the same route, and the case became known as the Route 29 Stalker. On May seventh, 1996, Alicia's remains were found in the Lignum area of Culpeper County. Witnesses described the man as white, thirty-five to forty-five years old, five foot ten to six feet tall, with a medium build and light to medium brown hair, driving a dark pickup, possibly a green Nissan. cases.audioScript: On the night of March nineteenth, 2004, seventeen-year-old Brianna Maitland finished her shift at the Black Lantern Inn in Montgomery, Vermont, and drove away at about eleven twenty. The car she drove, her mother's 1985 Oldsmobile, was found by state police the next day, backed in near an abandoned farmhouse about a mile from the restaurant. Because no one had reported her missing yet, the car was not treated as suspicious, and it was towed. Brianna had been staying with friends, and she was not reported missing for four days. At first police believed she had run away, but they later determined she may have been a victim of foul play. In 2022, investigators identified the source of DNA found on an item near the car, but it did not lead to a suspect. In 2024, on the twentieth anniversary, the FBI and Vermont State Police announced a reward of up to forty thousand dollars for information leading to her recovery. Her father says he still believes answers are out there. If you have information, call the Vermont State Police tip line at 1-844-84-VTIPS, or the FBI at 1-800-CALL-FBI.

cases.audioScript: On the afternoon of December first, 1946, eighteen-year-old Paula Jean Welden, a student at Bennington College in Vermont, told her roommate she was going for a hike. Several hikers later reported seeing her on the Long Trail, just off Route 9 near Glastenbury Mountain. The last confirmed sighting came around four o'clock, when she asked a man on the trail how far it went. She never returned, and her roommate reported her missing the next morning. An extensive search of the area turned up no sign of her. Because Vermont had limited police services at the time, investigators from New York, Massachusetts and Connecticut were brought in to help. Critics said the search lacked a coordinated effort, and her case led directly to the creation of the Vermont State Police in 1947. Many theories were investigated, but no conclusive outcome was ever determined. Paula has never been found, and she remains listed as a missing person. Anyone with information can submit a tip to the Vermont State Police at vsp.vermont.gov slash tipsubmit.
