Extensive searches found no trace; investigators from New York, Massachusetts and Connecticut assisted because Vermont had limited police services. According to the New England Historical Society, a $5,000 reward was raised during the search. Her case led directly to the 1947 formation of the Vermont State Police. She remains listed as missing.

cases.audioScript: On the evening of June twenty-sixth, 2009, ten-year-old Lindsey Baum left a friend's house in the small town of McCleary, Washington, to walk home. It was about nine-thirty, and she was wearing a light blue hooded pullover and blue jeans. She never made it home. Searchers combed the area for days, and for almost nine years her parents circulated fliers with her picture. Then, in the fall of 2017, hunters found human remains in a remote area of eastern Washington, in the Manastash area of Kittitas County. In May 2018, DNA analysis confirmed they were Lindsey's, and the Grays Harbor County sheriff said, we've brought Lindsey home. The case became a kidnapping and homicide investigation, led by the sheriff's office with the FBI. No one has ever been arrested. In 2026, the sheriff's office asked hunters and other outdoor recreationists to watch for more remains or evidence, and not to disturb anything they find. The sheriff's office lists a reward of up to forty thousand dollars for information leading to an arrest and conviction, and the FBI offers up to fifteen thousand dollars. If you know anything, call the Grays Harbor County Sheriff's Office tip line at 360-964-1799, or the FBI Seattle office at 206-622-0460.
cases.summary: Lindsey Jo Baum, 10, disappeared at about 9:30 p.m. on June 26, 2009, while walking home from a friend's house in McCleary, Grays Harbor County, Washington. Extensive searches in the following days found no sign of her. In fall 2017, hunters found remains in a remote area of Kittitas County in eastern Washington (the Manastash area), and in May 2018 the Grays Harbor County Sheriff's Office announced that DNA analysis had confirmed they were Lindsey's. The case is now a kidnapping and homicide investigation led by the Grays Harbor County Sheriff's Office and the FBI Seattle Field Office. On May 12, 2018, the Kittitas County Sheriff's Office ran a multi-agency search with 22 K9 teams in steep, heavily timbered terrain about 20 miles west of Ellensburg. Investigators tracked down more than two dozen possible persons of interest over the years; none was found to be connected. No one has been arrested. In April 2026 the sheriff's office renewed its appeal, asking hunters and outdoor recreationists to report possible remains without disturbing them, and listed a reward of up to $40,000 for information leading to an arrest and conviction. The FBI separately offers a reward of up to $15,000.

cases.audioScript: On March twenty-sixth, 1986, twelve-year-old Michella Welch was watching her two younger sisters at Puget Park in Tacoma, Washington. Around one o'clock she left to get them lunch. When her sisters came back from a nearby business, Michella was gone. All that was left was her bike and the lunch. Hours later, searchers found her body in a nearby gulch. For more than thirty years, the case went unsolved. Then, in 2018, Tacoma detectives turned to genetic genealogy, matching crime-scene DNA to a family tree. It pointed to a man named Gary Hartman. Detectives collected a napkin he threw away at a fast-food restaurant, and the DNA matched. He was arrested in June 2018. On March twenty-second, 2022, after a bench trial he requested, a judge found him guilty and sentenced him to more than twenty-six years in prison, a term the judge noted meant he would likely die there.

He was found guilty of first-degree murder in a bench trial on March 22, 2022 and sentenced to more than 26 years.

cases.audioScript: In early November 2024, seventy-five-year-old Richard Andrews of Moses Lake told his daughter he was going on a hunting trip. But his family noticed his glasses, wallet and phone were still at home. He had never left town. On November third, his body was found buried in a shallow grave behind his shop in Cascade Valley, just outside Moses Lake. Moses Lake police, working with Grant County deputies and the State Patrol crime lab, traced the killing to the home Andrews shared with his grandson, twenty-seven-year-old Isaiah Thomas. Investigators reported blood on the back door and a bloodied knife inside, and Thomas had been driving his grandfather's pickup, which had an axe and shovel in the bed. Thomas was arrested and charged with murder. Two days before his trial in February 2026, he pleaded guilty to second-degree murder and unlawful disposal of human remains. In March, a Grant County judge sentenced him to two hundred forty-four months in prison, the maximum term, and ordered mental health treatment.

cases.audioScript: On November twenty-fourth, 1989, eighteen-year-old Mandy Stavik went jogging near her family's home near Acme, in Whatcom County, Washington, and never came back. Three days later her body was found in the south fork of the Nooksack River. The case went unsolved for twenty-eight years. Investigators had a DNA profile from the crime but no match. Then a coworker of Timothy Bass collected a plastic cup and a soda can he threw away and gave them to detectives. His DNA matched the suspect profile, and he was arrested on December twelfth, 2017. Court records showed he watched cold case television shows and bragged he wouldn't be caught. At trial, prosecutors showed jurors the view Bass may have had of her from his room. In May 2019 a Whatcom County jury convicted him of first-degree murder, finding he had kidnapped and raped her. He was sentenced to nearly twenty-seven years, almost as long as he had been free. His appeals ended in January 2022.
cases.summary: Mandy Stavik, 18, disappeared while jogging near her home near Acme, Wash., on Nov. 24, 1989; her body was found in the Nooksack River three days later. In 2017 a coworker gave detectives a cup and can discarded by Timothy Bass; his DNA matched and he was arrested Dec. 12, 2017. He was convicted of first-degree murder May 24, 2019 and sentenced to nearly 27 years; appeals ended in 2022.

cases.audioScript: On a Saturday night in October 1953, while much of La Crosse, Wisconsin, was celebrating a college homecoming win, fifteen-year-old Evelyn Hartley was babysitting a toddler for a professor on the city's south side. She was supposed to call her parents at eight-thirty. She never did. When her father arrived, the doors were locked, the lights and radio were on, and the baby was asleep and unharmed. Evelyn was gone. Inside, he found her shoe and her broken glasses. Police found pry marks on windows and a trail of blood leading from a basement window across the yard. Tracking dogs lost her scent two blocks away. Later, a bloodstained pair of sneakers and a denim jacket turned up along Highway 14 near Coon Valley. Police asked residents to search their garages, outbuildings and basements. Evelyn has never been found, and no one has ever been charged. In 2004, DNA testing on the shoes and jacket produced only a partial result. La Crosse police say the case remains open. If you know anything, call 608-782-7575.
cases.summary: On the evening of October 24, 1953, Evelyn Hartley, 15, was babysitting for a La Crosse State College professor at a home in the 2400 block of Hoeschler Drive in La Crosse (News 8; Charley Project). She missed her 8:30 p.m. check-in call. Her father found the doors locked, the lights and radio on, the baby unharmed, and Evelyn gone; her shoes and broken glasses were inside (News 8; Charley Project). Police found pry marks on windows and a trail of blood from the basement window that ended on Coulee Drive. One witness reported a scream around 7:15 p.m. (News 8). Bloodstained sneakers matching the scene footprints and a denim jacket were later found on Highway 14 near Coon Valley (News 8). Investigators examined many leads over decades, including a 1957 check of serial grave robber Ed Gein, who was cleared (News 8). In 2004 DNA from the shoes and jacket produced only an incomplete profile (News 8). The La Crosse Police Department says it is an open investigation. Evelyn has never been found and no one has been charged.

cases.audioScript: On the night of July twenty-second, 1991, two Milwaukee police officers saw a man with handcuffs dangling from one wrist. He told them a man had threatened him inside an apartment nearby. When officers went to that apartment, they met thirty-one-year-old Jeffrey Dahmer, and what they found inside ended one of the worst killing sprees in American history. Dahmer confessed to seventeen killings, sixteen in Wisconsin and the first in 1978 at his parents' home in Bath, Ohio, where he killed an eighteen-year-old hitchhiker, Steven Hicks. One detail haunted the city. Two months before the arrest, neighbors had called police about a naked, bleeding teenager outside Dahmer's building. Officers accepted Dahmer's story and left the boy with him. The boy was fourteen-year-old Konerak Sinthasomphone, and Dahmer killed him soon after. In February 1992 a jury found Dahmer sane, and he was sentenced to fifteen consecutive life terms. On November twenty-eighth, 1994, he was killed by a fellow inmate in a Wisconsin prison.
cases.summary: Jeffrey Dahmer killed 17 men and boys between 1978 and 1991, the first in Bath Township, Ohio, and 16 in Wisconsin. He was arrested in Milwaukee on July 22, 1991, after a handcuffed man escaped his apartment and alerted police. On May 27, 1991, officers had returned 14-year-old Konerak Sinthasomphone to Dahmer after accepting his explanation; Dahmer said he killed the boy soon after, and the officers were suspended. He pleaded guilty but insane; on Feb. 15, 1992 a jury found him sane, and he received 15 consecutive life terms. He was beaten to death in prison on Nov. 28, 1994 by inmate Christopher Scarver, who pleaded no contest in May 1995 and received two more life terms.
cases.solvedHow: Solved July 22, 1991 when a man who escaped Dahmer's apartment in handcuffs led Milwaukee officers there; evidence in the apartment and Dahmer's confession followed.

cases.audioScript: In April 2024, nineteen-year-old Sade Robinson, a Milwaukee college student, went on a first date with a man at a Milwaukee restaurant. She worked two jobs and took classes at Milwaukee Area Technical College. Soon after, she was reported missing. Prosecutors said her date, Maxwell Anderson, killed her at his home on the city's south side, dismembered her body at Warnimont Park in Cudahy, and later set her car on fire. Parts of her body were found at sites across the region. In June 2025, a jury found Anderson guilty on all counts, including first-degree intentional homicide. On August first, 2025, he was sentenced to life in prison without the possibility of release. His defense attorneys had asked that he become eligible for release after twenty-five years, but the judge ruled he will never be eligible for extended supervision. At the sentencing, her father told the court about night terrors and constant mental chaos. Days later, he filed notice that he intends to appeal. The college later awarded Sade a posthumous associate's degree.

A jury convicted him on all counts in June 2025; on Aug. 1, 2025 he was sentenced to life without extended supervision. He has filed notice of intent to appeal.

cases.audioScript: On July twenty-fourth, 1997, twenty-four-year-old Amy Wroe Bechtel disappeared near Lander, Wyoming. Amy was an avid runner, and investigators believe she drove up into the Shoshone National Forest that day to check the course of a ten-kilometer race she was planning. She never came home. Searchers found her white Toyota Tercel near the turnoff to Burnt Gulch on the Loop Road. Her keys, her sunglasses and her to-do list were inside the car, but her wallet was missing. Hundreds of searchers looked for her for months, without success. Nearly three decades later, the Fremont County Sheriff's Office still has two investigators following up on leads whenever they come in. In 2025, sheriff's Lieutenant John Zerga told Cowboy State Daily he considers Dale Wayne Eaton, who was convicted in 2004 of a separate 1988 murder, a prime suspect. Eaton has never been charged in Amy's case. In 2026, detectives told ABC News they were still looking at other persons of interest, and no one has ever been charged. If you know anything about what happened to Amy on the Loop Road, call the Fremont County Sheriff's Office at 307-332-1000.
cases.summary: Amy Wroe Bechtel, 24, disappeared on July 24, 1997, near Lander, Wyoming. She was an avid runner, and investigators believe she drove to the Loop Road area of the Shoshone National Forest to check the course of an upcoming 10-kilometer run. Her white Toyota Tercel was found near the turnoff to Burnt Gulch; her keys, sunglasses and to-do list were inside, but her wallet was missing. Hundreds of searchers looked for her for months without finding her. In October 2025, Fremont County Sheriff's Office Lt. John Zerga told Cowboy State Daily that he considers Dale Wayne Eaton, found guilty in 2004 of murdering Lisa Marie Kimmel (who disappeared in 1988), a prime suspect; Eaton has never been charged in Bechtel's case (identified by police, never charged/convicted). Zerga also said the FBI had at one point ruled Eaton out as being in the area, which he disputes, and that the office has two investigators who follow up on leads. In September 2026, ABC News reported detectives describing other persons of interest; her husband has denied involvement, and a detective said he is not considered a suspect. No one has been charged and the case remains open.
cases.solvedHow: Unsolved. Techniques so far: large ground, K9 and air searches in 1997; vehicle processing; follow-up on tips, including a 2025 tip about property where Eaton stayed; national media appeals.
cases.techniques: Ground, K9 and aerial searches; Tip follow-up; Vehicle searches on property linked to a suspect; Media appeals

timeline.event: Amy runs errands in Lander; investigators believe she drove to the Loop Road area of the Shoshone National Forest to check a race course. She disappears.
Her white Toyota Tercel is found near the Burnt Gulch turnoff on the Loop Road (found that night, per later accounts).
Hundreds of searchers look for her for months without success.
Dale Wayne Eaton convicted of the 1988 murder of Lisa Marie Kimmel (separate case).
Cowboy State Daily reports FCSO considers a new tip from the owner of the property where Eaton once stayed worth checking out.
County 10 marks 29 years with no answers.
ABC News reports the case remains unsolved; detectives describe other persons of interest.
